title: Preface
text:
Turkic languages are spoken from the Balkans and Anatolia to Central Asia, western China and north-eastern Siberia. They share much of their grammar, yet the data, tools and evaluations available for them differ greatly from one language and task to the next. This book explains how to build and assess language technology with both facts in view.
General NLP is treated briefly, with Jurafsky and Martin’s Speech and Language Processing as the companion text. The chapters concentrate on what is specific to the family: agglutinative morphology and vowel harmony, the Latin, Cyrillic and Perso-Arabic scripts in which the languages are written, transfer between related languages, and the construction of corpora, treebanks and benchmarks where few exist. Johanson’s Turkic is the linguistic reference throughout. Three questions recur: how morphology affects a task, what changes when the script changes, and which knowledge transfers between related languages.
The book is written for NLP researchers and practitioners, graduate students and members of Turkic language communities. The programming sections assume intermediate Python and basic machine learning; linguistic concepts are introduced as they are needed. Book Organisation and How to Use This Book describes how the parts fit together.
Each chapter combines linguistic analysis with a practical section, most of them using TurkicNLP (version 0.5.0), an open toolkit that brings components for Turkic languages into one interface.
AI tools were used in preparing this book: for drafting and editing the text, reviewing code, checking the bibliography against publisher and index records, and style passes over the manuscript. The cover artwork was generated with an AI image tool and then edited by hand. All AI-assisted material was reviewed, corrected and checked manually.
The resources described here will change faster than the methods. The book aims to help its readers check what exists, measure what works, and build what their language communities need.

title: 1  The Turkic World: Languages, Speakers, and the Resource Reality
text:
1.1 Geographic and Demographic Overview
Turkic languages are spoken across Anatolia, the Balkans, Central Asia, Siberia and western China. Johanson calls this area Turcia (Johanson 2021, 16). Figure 1.1 gives a schematic overview.
Turkic-speaking communities also live in Iran, Iraq, Afghanistan, the Caucasus and the Volga-Ural region. Migration has established communities farther afield, including in Germany (Johanson 2021, 16).
Six states give official status to Turkic languages: Turkey (Turkish), Azerbaijan (Azerbaijani), Kazakhstan (Kazakh), Kyrgyzstan (Kyrgyz), Turkmenistan (Turkmen), and Uzbekistan (Uzbek). The family has more than a dozen standard languages (Johanson 2021, 16).
Historical varieties also matter for heritage digitisation and script conversion. The first known Old Turkic texts are the early-eighth-century inscriptions of the second Türk empire, especially those on the Orkhon River (Johanson 2021, 159). Ottoman Turkish served as the Ottoman Empire’s official and literary language; its New Ottoman period lasted until 1928 (Johanson 2021, 156, 164). In Central Asia, writers cultivated the Persian-influenced literary language Chaghatay from the fifteenth century onwards (Johanson 2021, 162).
Language policy affects which corpora can be combined and reused. Different Kazakh Latin proposals, for example, require different conversion tables (Chapter 3). Funding can support resource development. To judge what it has produced, inspect the quality, coverage and access conditions of each release.

1.2 Genealogical Classification
Genealogical classification groups languages by common descent. Historical-comparative linguistics supports the Turkic family and the reconstruction of a common ancestor, Proto-Turkic (Johanson 2021, 18).
Following Johanson (2021, 22–23), the present-day Turkic languages divide into six main branches:

These groups follow the classification in the cited reference; the northeastern (Siberian) group is genealogically less uniform than the others (Johanson 2021, 22). Johanson places South Altai with Kyrgyz in the eastern Kipchak subbranch and North Altai in the South Siberian subbranch (Johanson 2021, 22–23); the ISO code alt used by the toolkit and by corpora denotes Southern Altai. Oghuz includes Turkish, Azerbaijani, Turkmen and Gagauz; Kipchak includes languages of the Volga-Ural region, Caucasus and Central Asia. The Karluk group includes Uzbek and Uyghur, whose vowel systems and harmonic patterns must be described separately rather than treated as one contact-induced exception (Chapter 2). Chuvash and Khalaj represent the distinct Oghur and Arghu branches (Johanson 2021, 22–25).
Choosing a transfer language. Start with genealogical proximity when selecting donors, then test them on the target task. TurkicNLP uses proxy-language representations where training data are unavailable: Turkish for Gagauz and Crimean Tatar, Tatar for Kumyk, and Bashkir for Sakha (Hakimov 2026). Some of these choices cross branch boundaries. Their implementation alone tells us little about which donor would work best. Controlled comparisons are needed to separate the effects of genealogy, script and available training data.
Table 1.2 provides an overview of the major Turkic languages with selected scripts and language identifiers. The selection covers living languages only; the toolkit’s coverage list is a separate matter. section: 1.3 Mutual Intelligibility and What It Means Computationally
text:
1.3 Mutual Intelligibility and What It Means Computationally
Mutual intelligibility within the Turkic family is “very limited within the family as a whole, but it is occasionally relatively high between neighbouring speaker groups” (Johanson 2021, 16). Johanson gives examples at both ends. Kumyk has a high degree of mutual intelligibility with Azeri (Johanson 2021, 61), and the increasing mutual intelligibility of Kyrgyz and Kazakh appears to result from recent convergence (Johanson 2021, 72). Turkish and Turkmen are closer to each other than either is to Kazakh or Uyghur (Johanson 2021, 21). At the other end, Yakut (Sakha) and Dolgan are unintelligible to speakers of other Turkic languages (Johanson 2021, 24). Intelligibility between neighbouring varieties is therefore not a simple function of branch membership.
Written similarity. In TurkicNLP’s small parallel sample, conversion to a common script increased character-trigram overlap between languages written in different scripts (Hakimov 2026). Spelling had hidden some shared forms. Human intelligibility and NLP task performance require separate measurements; Section 3.6 gives the overlap method and results.
Relatedness as a transfer resource. The Kardeş-NLU benchmark (Senel et al. 2024) evaluates cross-lingual language understanding for five lower-resourced Turkic languages (Azerbaijani, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Uyghur) and shows that bringing in Turkish, their high-resource “cousin”, during intermediate training and fine-tuning improves transfer in the evaluated settings. The practical lessons are:

Before annotating data for a new Turkic language, check whether a related, better-resourced language can be used as an additional source in training.
Compare native-script and common-script versions using the same data split; conversion can expose written similarities but may hurt a model trained on national orthographies (Chapter 3).
Evaluate donors separately for Chuvash and for each Siberian language; the Siberian group is internally diverse, and branch labels alone do not predict transfer quality (Chapter 16).

Chapter 16 develops these transfer strategies in detail.

title: 1  The Turkic World: Languages, Speakers, and the Resource Reality
text:
1.4 Available Resources
Resource availability depends on the task, variety, domain, script and access conditions. Count named releases and check what they support: a web crawl, a treebank and a speech corpus serve different purposes.

1.4.1 Named Resources and What They Enable
Turkish has established resources including the Turkish National Corpus (Aksan et al. 2012), the BOUN dependency treebank (Türk et al. 2022), BERTurk (Schweter 2020) and KeNet (Bakay et al. 2021). These support different activities: corpus description, supervised parsing, representation learning and lexical-semantic applications. Their existence does not guarantee coverage of a new domain or dialect.
Kazakh resources include KazNERD for named-entity recognition (Yeshpanov, Khassanov, and Varol 2022) and the speech work described in TurkicASR and TurkicTTS (Mussakhojayeva et al. 2023; Yeshpanov, Mussakhojayeva, and Khassanov 2023). Audit each named release and its documentation to establish what it offers.
For other languages, inspect dedicated resources alongside multilingual collections. Apertium’s morphological analysers, parallel UD treebanks (Akhundjanova et al. 2025) and multilingual reading-comprehension benchmarks such as Belebele (Bandarkar et al. 2024) illustrate different kinds of coverage. Belebele’s multiple-choice comprehension task should not be confused with extractive question answering. An unsuccessful search for a dedicated dataset is not evidence that no resource exists.



Table 1.3: Named examples for a task-oriented resource audit. Treat it as a reading list. It neither exhausts the field nor ranks the work in it.

1.4.2 A Worked Resource Audit
Resource descriptions can conceal large differences in domain. In the documentation consulted on 13 October 2026, Turkish BOUN lists nonfiction and news. Azerbaijani TueCL consists of grammar examples: 148 sentences translated from Turkish. Both specify CC BY-SA 4.0. The book’s inventory uses UD 2.17 (Chapter 8). TueCL supports a controlled parallel comparison, but performance on naturally occurring Azerbaijani news needs its own evaluation.
For each candidate resource, record its URL, release or commit, language/variety, script, domain, unit of size, licence, access conditions and intended task. Mark work in progress separately from released data. Then inspect a sample: does it suit the task you have in mind?

title: 1  The Turkic World: Languages, Speakers, and the Resource Reality
text:
1.5 Key Institutions and Community Infrastructure
The following organisations maintain resources or provide venues for Turkic NLP work.
Apertium. This open-source platform provides morphological transducers and rule-based translation systems (Khanna et al. 2021; Washington, Salimzyanov, and Tyers 2014). A transducer can be built without a supervised training corpus. The work lies in its lexicon, linguistic rules, testing and maintenance. Chapter 6 and Chapter 10 distinguish analysers from released translation pairs.
SIGTURK. The ACL Special Interest Group on Turkic Languages supports workshops and community exchange. Consult its current announcements for releases, shared tasks and events; where a resource was published says little about how mature it is.
ISSAI. The Institute of Smart Systems and Artificial Intelligence at Nazarbayev University contributes datasets, models and evaluations for Kazakh and other Turkic languages, including the TurkicASR and TurkicTTS work cited above. Check each release’s access and licence independently.
Universal Dependencies. UD (Nivre et al. 2016) is the annotation framework and community behind the Turkic treebanks, with shared conventions and versioned releases. Use the release documentation to distinguish released treebanks from development repositories. Chapter 8 covers the framework and how to build new treebanks.
Turkic Interlingua. This community provides machine-translation resources for Turkic languages: the TIL corpus, baselines (Mirzakhalov et al. 2021) and the X-WMT test sets, which cover eight Turkic languages plus English and Russian in 88 directions. Chapter 10 explains the data and evaluation coverage.
Turkic UD. This group works on harmonising annotation across Turkic UD treebanks. Its parallel treebanks annotate the same sentences in several Turkic languages, starting with Azerbaijani, Kyrgyz, Turkish and Uzbek (Akhundjanova et al. 2025), so that annotation choices can be compared directly.
TurkLang. The International Conference on Computer Processing of Turkic Languages has met since 2013. It is a regular venue for work on corpora, morphology, machine translation and other language technology for Turkic languages; check individual proceedings for peer-review and publication details.
Turkic Academy. This international organisation facilitates and encourages scientific and educational cooperation among Turkic countries and communities. It is a point of contact for research collaboration across the Turkic-speaking states rather than a source of NLP datasets.

section: 1.6 Book Organisation and How to Use This Book
text:
1.6 Book Organisation and How to Use This Book
The book has 17 main chapters in seven parts, followed by four appendices. The parts cover the language family; writing systems and corpora; morphology; syntax; applications; language models; and cross-lingual methods and the resource frontier.
Choose a route according to your task:

Build a corpus: start with scripts and orthography, then corpora at scale, and consult evaluation before treating crawl labels as ground truth.
Analyse words or sentences: read the computational phenotype, morphological structure, finite-state morphology, neural morphology, and syntax and UD.
Build an application: choose sequence labelling, translation or speech.
Adapt a language model: connect pretrained models with meaning and retrieval, generation and dialogue, and evaluation.
Work with a language with limited resources: pair cross-lingual transfer with endangered languages and ethics, including community priorities and data permissions from the outset.


1.6.1 Prerequisites
This book assumes familiarity with:

Python programming at an intermediate level
Basic machine learning concepts (supervised learning, train/test splits, evaluation metrics)
Basic linear algebra and probability (vectors, matrices, conditional probability)

No NLP background beyond the introductory chapters of Jurafsky and Martin (2024) is assumed. For finite-state morphology (Chapter 6) and language models (Chapter 12), familiarity with formal automata theory and neural networks respectively will help, but the text introduces these concepts from first principles.
You need no prior knowledge of Turkic languages or of linguistics; each concept is introduced where it is first used. For a full linguistic reference on the Turkic family, see Johanson (2021) and Johanson and Csató (1998).


1.6.2 Hands-On Environment
Most chapters include a hands-on section with practical exercises; this chapter has a worked resource audit instead (Section 1.4). The code examples use:

Python 3.10+ as the primary programming language
PyTorch for neural network implementations
Hugging Face Transformers for pretrained model access and fine-tuning (Wolf et al. 2020)
Hugging Face Datasets for loading Turkic NLP datasets
TurkicNLP for morphological analysis and script processing (Hakimov 2026)
Apertium for finite-state morphology demonstrations (Khanna et al. 2021)

The code in the hands-on sections uses TurkicNLP 0.5.0.


1.6.3 A Note on Language Coverage
Turkish, Kazakh, Uzbek, Azerbaijani and Turkmen provide recurring examples. Other languages appear where documented examples, data or tools are available. The comparisons show both shared patterns and language-specific differences.


1.6.4 Recurring Example Sentences
Four short sentences recur across the book, so that one text can be followed through script conversion, morphology, tokenisation and syntax (Table 1.4). They come from UD 2.17 test treebanks, cover Cyrillic, Latin and Perso-Arabic script, and were checked by the author. They explain operations; the experiments use their own datasets and splits.

section: 1.7 Hands-On: A Procedure for Building a Task-Specific Inventory
text:
1.7 Hands-On: A Procedure for Building a Task-Specific Inventory
Question. Which resources support one chosen language, domain and task?
Inputs. The named inventories and toolkit registry in Section 1.4.
Compute. CPU and network queries; record failed requests.
Output. A dated inventory of candidates, permissions and evaluation gaps.
Interpretation. Use the inventory to select what to investigate next.
Worked row. For Kyrgyz named entity recognition, figures recorded elsewhere in the book fill the fields as follows.



Table 1.5: A filled inventory row for one language and task.









Field
Kyrgyz NER




Labelled data
KyrgyzNER: 7,033 training and 3,867 test sentences, no development split (Sequence Labelling, Exercise 3); news articles from 24.kg (KyrgyzNER README)


Licence
Dataset CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (KyrgyzNER README)


Related annotation
UD 2.17 Kyrgyz-KTMU (1,308 training and 1,222 test sentences) and Kyrgyz-TueCL (173 test sentences) (Section 8.3)


Ready-made models
No dedicated pretrained Kyrgyz NER model in TurkicNLP 0.5.0; its generic LLM backend is a separate option. Stanza’s Kazakh KazNERD model reaches 39.9 micro F1 on the KyrgyzNER test set without Kyrgyz training data (PER/LOC/ORG, gold words; Section 9.3)


Evaluation gap
One news source, and no development split: model selection needs a held-out part of the training data






Status: procedure only. The fields above define the audit, and Table 1.5 fills them for one task; Exercises 1, 3 and 5 carry it out for selected languages.

What to Take Forward
The family map suggests languages to compare. A resource audit shows which comparisons are feasible. TurkicNLP 0.5.0 lists 24 languages, with different components and evaluation evidence for each (Section 1.4). Use a dated inventory of data, permissions and results to choose a task. Chapter 2 examines the linguistic patterns that these systems must handle.

title: 1  The Turkic World: Languages, Speakers, and the Resource Reality
text:
Further Reading

Turkic language family (reference grammar): Johanson (2021) provides a systematic overview of the entire Turkic family covering structural, functional, historical, sociolinguistic, and literary aspects.
Turkic languages (individual descriptions): Johanson and Csató (1998) provides concise descriptions of individual languages.
NLP foundations: Jurafsky and Martin (2024) is the standard NLP textbook and a companion to this book for general NLP concepts.
Turkish NLP survey: Çöltekin, Doğruöz, and Çetinoğlu (2023) provides a critical survey of resources for Turkish natural language processing.
Turkish NLP (book): Oflazer and Saraçlar (2018) covers morphology, parsing, speech, NER and machine translation for Turkish with methods relevant to other Turkic languages.
Turkic NLP benchmark: Isbarov et al. (2025) presents TUMLU, a native multiple-choice benchmark; Chapter 15 explains its language coverage and release counts.
ISSAI resources: The ISSAI research group at Nazarbayev University publishes datasets, models, and papers at issai.nu.edu.kz.
Universal Dependencies: The UD project at universaldependencies.org provides treebank documentation for all Turkic UD treebanks.
Apertium Turkic: The Apertium Turkic community at turkic.apertium.org maintains morphological tools and MT systems for a range of Turkic languages; inspect the individual repository and release.

title: 1  The Turkic World: Languages, Speakers, and the Resource Reality
text:
Exercises

Language family exploration. Choose a Turkic language you are unfamiliar with from Table 1.2. Using online resources, find its Wikipedia edition (if it exists) and estimate its digital footprint. How many Wikipedia articles does it have? Is it covered by OSCAR or FineWeb2? Does it have a Universal Dependencies treebank? Locate the language on the map in Figure 1.1 and identify its branch according to Table 1.1.
Branch membership and transfer. Using Table 1.1, identify: (a) which branch contains Uzbek; (b) which branch Kazakh and Kyrgyz both belong to; (c) which branch Chuvash belongs to and why it is unusual. Based on genealogical proximity alone, predict which language would be a better transfer source for Kyrgyz NLP: Turkish or Kazakh? Justify your answer.
Resource gap analysis. Choose a language, domain and community use case. Using the audit fields in Section 1.4, identify three resources needed for that use case, search for named releases, and record any gaps as unverified until the search scope is documented. Prioritise work by user needs, permissions and feasibility.
Mutual intelligibility and NLP. The Kardeş-NLU paper (Senel et al. 2024) studies transfer to five Turkic languages with Turkish as a high-resource relative. Before reading it, rank the five languages (Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Kyrgyz, Kazakh, Uyghur) by how much you expect them to benefit from Turkish, based on genealogy, script, and resources. Then compare your ranking with the paper’s results. Which factors are confounded in this comparison, and what controlled experiment would distinguish them?
What a toolkit offers per language. Install TurkicNLP (pip install "turkicnlp==0.5.0") and run:
import turkicnlp
for lang in ["tur", "kaz", "kir", "sah", "kum", "chv"]:
    print(lang, turkicnlp.list_processors(lang))
Which processors are available for each language, and from which backends? Compare the result with Table 1.3: which tasks have both a listed backend and suitable evaluation data?
Community exploration. Visit the SIGTURK website, the Apertium Turkic page, or the Universal Dependencies project. Find a recent shared task, release, or publication related to Turkic NLP. Summarise the contribution in 2–3 sentences and explain how it addresses one of the gaps identified in Section 1.4.





Akhundjanova, Arofat, Furkan Akkurt, Bermet Chontaeva, Soudabeh Eslami, and Çağrı Çöltekin. 2025. “Parallel Universal Dependencies Treebanks for Turkic Languages.” In Proceedings of the Eighth Workshop on Universal Dependencies (UDW, SyntaxFest 2025), 129–36. Ljubljana, Slovenia: Association for Computational Linguistics. https://aclanthology.org/2025.udw-1.14/.

title: 2  The Computational Phenotype of Turkic Languages
text:
2.1 Agglutination and Productive Word Formation
This chapter introduces the linguistic patterns used throughout the book: suffixation, vowel harmony, case, word order and non-finite clauses. It explains what each pattern means for text processing, while keeping linguistic facts separate from claims about model performance.
Most worked analyses in this chapter use Turkish, giving readers a consistent starting point. Comparisons with Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, Uyghur, Turkmen and smaller languages show how far each pattern extends. Chapter 5 develops the morphology in detail; later chapters test the computational methods.
crumbs: 2  The Computational Phenotype of Turkic Languages

title: 2  The Computational Phenotype of Turkic Languages
text:
2.1.1 What Agglutination Is
A morpheme is an abstract unit of grammatical or lexical structure; a morph is a surface form used to realise it. Different surface forms of the same morpheme are allomorphs: Turkish plural -lar and -ler realise one plural morpheme. An orthographic word, a morpheme and a language-model token are different units, and their boundaries need not match.
A language is agglutinative when words are built by chaining morphs, each typically expressing one grammatical function, with clear boundaries between them. Johanson (2021, 35) characterises the Turkic word structure as based on “a juxtaposing technique with clear-cut morpheme boundaries”, with “mostly one-to-one correspondence of morphemes and their functions”. This contrasts with:

Fusional languages (German, Russian, Latin): a single morph can signal several functions at once (case + number + gender in one suffix)
Isolating languages (Chinese, Vietnamese): grammatical relations expressed by word order and separate particles, with little inflection

They describe tendencies; a language can show several at once. Polysynthesis concerns how much grammatical and lexical information a word can contain; it is a separate dimension from whether its morphs have clear boundaries. A language can be both agglutinative and polysynthetic.
A short example shows the principle. The Turkish word evlerimizden ‘from our houses’ consists of four surface pieces:



Table 2.1: The Turkish word evlerimizden ‘from our houses’. Gloss abbreviations follow the Leipzig Glossing Rules: PL plural, POSS possessive, ABL ablative, ACC accusative, GEN genitive, PASS passive, NEG negation, PST past, 3PL third person plural; the full list is in Table D.1.





Surface piece
Analysis
Contribution




ev
house
lexical stem


-ler
PL
plural


-imiz
POSS.1PL
first-person plural possessor


-den
ABL
source (ablative case)






The same structure appears across the family: Kazakh үй-лер-іміз-ден, Uzbek uy-lar-imiz-dan, with the same order of plural, possessive and case. A short verb works the same way: yaz-ıl-dı-lar ‘they were written’ is stem + passive + past + third person plural.
Turkic agglutination is productive: a single root can yield many well-formed word forms by adding suffixes in a constrained order.


2.1.2 The Suffix Template
Suffix order is constrained. A common verbal pattern is:
Root → Voice → Ability / Negation → Tense/Aspect/Mood → Person/Number
For nouns, it is:
Root → Derivation → Number → Possessive → Case
The slots in these templates interact. Ability and negation restrict one another, as the next example shows. Derivation can also change the inflection that follows: a nominalised verb takes nominal suffixes such as plural, possessive and case. Each suffix operates on the form to its left, so order affects meaning.
Negative ability illustrates both points. Turkish yaz-ıl-a-ma-dı-lar ‘they could not be written’ adds -a-ma- between the passive and the past. Positive ability is a different suffix, -(y)Abil- (yaz-ıl-abil-di-ler ‘they could be written’); the negative form is not simply -abil- plus negation. In this book we segment -a-ma- as two surface pieces, ability and negation, and treat them together as the inability construction; other analyses treat -AmA- as a single morph. Whatever the convention, it has to be stated, because it changes every morpheme count.
A statistical subword tokeniser partitions the written form without changing suffix order. Its pieces may cross morphological boundaries or combine several morphemes, leaving the model to learn the grammatical structure from those pieces.


2.1.3 An Advanced Example
The Turkish word konuşturamadıklarımızdan combines verbal derivation with nominal inflection. It means “from/among those whom we could not get to speak”:



Table 2.2: Surface pieces of konuşturamadıklarımızdan, Turkish. After the nominaliser -DIK the word continues with nominal inflection (plural, possessive-form agreement, case). The stem konuş- is treated as one unit, and -a-ma- is split under the inability convention introduced above.










Surface piece
Gloss
Function




konuş-
speak
lexical verb stem


-tur-
CAUS
causative: make/get someone to speak


-a-
ABIL
ability (with the following negation: inability)


-ma-
NEG
negation


-dık-
NMLZ
non-future nominaliser/participle -DIK


-lar-
PL
plural referents: ‘those’


-ımız-
POSS.1PL
first-person plural possessive-form agreement: ‘we’ as the subject of the relative clause


-dan
ABL
ablative case: ‘from/among’






Under this convention the word has eight surface pieces, each counted as one morpheme: one stem and seven suffixes. There is no buffer consonant in this example. The form is a headless relative clause: the people referred to are understood rather than named by a following noun. The plural -lar- marks those people, whereas -ımız- identifies the subject as ‘we’; it does not express ownership here. The k of -dık- remains unchanged before the consonant-initial plural -lar-.
-DIK is analysed here as a nominaliser; its temporal reading (often past or present relative to the main clause) depends on the construction, so the gloss NMLZ is preferred over “past participle” (Chapter 5 and Chapter 8 use the same analysis). The example is deliberately long; in running text most words carry far fewer suffixes. The long tail of rarer, longer forms is what makes the vocabulary open-ended.






Figure 2.1: Surface pieces of the Turkish form konuş-tur-a-ma-dık-lar-ımız-dan: ‘from/among those whom we could not get to speak’. Each coloured block shows one surface piece with its gloss below. Lexical stem (coral), verbal suffixes (blue), nominaliser (gold), nominal suffixes (green).









Figure 2.2: The Turkic suffix template shown as two slot diagrams. Left: nominal template (Root → Derivation → Number → Possession → Case → Copula). Right: verbal template (Root → Voice → Ability/Negation → TAM → Person/Number). These are ordering constraints, not independent or necessarily overt slots; agreement can be zero. Ability and negation interact, and nominalisation changes the following template.



The template summarises common patterns; Chuvash, for example, places possessive marking before plural (Section 5.4.5). Possessive agreement and evidentiality are expressed within suffix chains, while clitics such as Turkish question particle mI and auxiliary constructions such as Kazakh оқи ал- ‘be able to read’ extend across words. Chapter 5 explains these distinctions; Chapter 8 covers analytic predicates.


2.1.4 Unseen Word Forms
Productive suffixation creates well-formed words absent from a finite training corpus. A whole-word model needs a way to handle these unseen forms. Character-complete or byte-level tokenisers can encode them as smaller pieces; other subword tokenisers may return an unknown token. Comparing vocabulary sizes across languages requires matched corpus sizes, domains and tokenisation rules.
Morphemes per word and model tokens per word are different measures. The Hands-On section counts surface segments under an explicit convention. Section 3.6 measures how changing the script affects token counts for the same sentences. Neither, taken alone, is a measure of morphological complexity.

section: 2.2 Vowel Harmony: Rules, Exceptions, and Computational Consequences
text:
2.2 Vowel Harmony: Rules, Exceptions, and Computational Consequences

2.2.1 The Basic Mechanics
Vowel harmony is the phenomenon by which the vowels in a word are constrained to agree in some phonological property. The most general constraint in Turkic languages is front/back (palatal) harmony. Johanson (2021, 38) describes “intrasyllabic [±front] harmony, which requires the segments of a syllable to be either front or back”, and intersyllabic harmony, which neutralises the front/back distinction under the influence of a preceding syllable.
In Turkish, the eight vowels divide into two sets:

Front: e, i, ö, ü
Back: a, ı, o, u

Most native Turkish roots have vowels from one set, with exceptions such as anne ‘mother’, elma ‘apple’ and kardeş ‘sibling’. Harmony within a stem is a strong lexical tendency. Suffix selection is productive: the plural takes -ler after a front vowel (ev-ler, houses) and -lar after a back vowel (araba-lar, cars). It follows the stem’s last vowel even in disharmonic words such as elma-lar. Many other suffixes have four allomorphs, varying in both backness and rounding.
A second harmony axis, labial (round) harmony, governs high suffix vowels (i/ı/ü/u) in Turkish: after a rounded vowel they round, after an unrounded vowel they do not. This gives four-way alternation for suffixes such as the first-person singular possessive -ım/-im/-um/-üm.


2.2.2 Variation Across the Family
Vowel harmony is found throughout the family, but its scope, its exceptions and above all its spelling differ:

Turkish: backness and rounding harmony in suffixes, both written; lexical exceptions in stems (anne, elma), suffixes with limited or no vowel alternation (-yor, -ken, -ki, -leyin), and loanwords whose final consonant triggers front suffixes (saat-ler, rol-ü, hal-i)
Kazakh: backness harmony written; rounding harmony is present in pronunciation but not written in the standard orthography, whereas Kyrgyz writes it (Kazakh көзді vs. Kyrgyz көздү, ‘eye-ACC’)
Kyrgyz: backness and rounding harmony written, including in low vowels (үйлөр ‘houses’)
Uyghur: backness harmony in many suffixes, plus raising of stem vowels before suffixes, which the script writes out (bala ‘child’, balilar ‘children’)
Uzbek: suffix vowels are largely fixed in standard spelling (uylar, otlar), while front/back harmony is weaker in many urban varieties and clearer in some northern varieties; standard Uzbek has no clear-cut rounding harmony (Johanson 2021, 307, 313)
Chuvash: a vowel system that differs markedly from the other languages (Table 2.4)

Table 2.3 shows the same stems with the plural and accusative suffixes in five languages.

A vowel inventory records a language’s contrasts. Harmony governs restrictions and alternations involving those contrasts. Uzbek suffixes illustrate how a language can retain a vowel after losing a productive harmonic alternation. For written-text NLP, ask which alternations appear in the spelling.
The recurring sentences (Table 1.4) show these patterns in running text. Figure 2.3: A qualitative comparison of harmony in four Turkic languages, separating suffix alternation, spoken rounding and orthographic representation (Johanson 2021, 305–15). This is not a vowel-inventory chart.





2.2.3 Exceptions
Suffix harmony is governed by the last vowel of the stem, so loanwords with mixed vowels such as telefon or kitap are regular (telefon-lar, kitap-lar). The genuine exceptions are lexical: stems whose final consonant is pronounced palatalised and therefore takes front suffixes despite a back vowel (saat-ler ‘hours’, rol-ü ‘role-ACC’, hal-i ‘state-ACC’), and suffixes outside the regular pattern (-yor, -ken, and usually -ki). Turkish -ki has exceptions such as dünkü ‘pertaining to yesterday’ (Johanson 2021, 493).
An analyser needs lexical information about these exceptional stems. A statistical model must learn their behaviour from examples; a uniform harmony rule will miss them.


2.2.4 Computational Consequences

Suffix allomorphy. The same morpheme has two or four surface forms (more with consonant alternation). A morphological analyser must map -ler and -lar to one plural; a machine translation system generating Turkish must produce the correct allomorph.
What the representation exposes. Character representations expose the letters relevant to written harmonic alternations, usually only a few characters apart. Subword models can also learn these regularities, but their token inventory and training examples determine how directly the relevant vowels are represented: when the stem vowel and the suffix vowel fall into different tokens, the model must learn the dependency between token identities. The usefulness of either representation should be evaluated on regular forms and on lexical exceptions separately.
Allomorphs multiply vocabulary entries. Forms such as -lar/-ler and -dı/-di/-du/-dü/-tı/-ti/-tu/-tü can be represented by different subword pieces, including pieces crossing the stem–suffix boundary. They need not each occupy a whole vocabulary entry. Morphological segmentation alone does not merge allomorphs: sharing a canonical unit or grammatical label requires an additional normalisation or analysis step (Section 7.2).
Orthography differs from phonology. Whether harmony is written matters more for text NLP than whether it is pronounced. Kazakh does not spell rounding harmony while Kyrgyz does, so the same suffix has more written variants in Kyrgyz, a difference a transfer model must absorb.

section: 2.3 The Case System as Syntactic Infrastructure
text:
2.3 The Case System as Syntactic Infrastructure

2.3.1 The Case Inventory
Turkic languages use morphological case to mark the grammatical relations of noun phrases. Most Turkic languages have at least six cases: nominative, accusative, dative, locative, ablative and genitive. Some have more, such as an instrumental (Chuvash, Sakha, Kazakh), an equative or a directive. Sakha is the notable outlier: it has no genitive case but has partitive, comitative, comparative and instrumental cases [Johanson (2021), chapter 22; p. 463]. The cases are expressed by suffixes added after number and possessive marking.



Table 2.5: The word “house” (ev/үй/uy/öý) in six cases across five Turkic languages. Note allomorphic variation due to vowel harmony and consonant assimilation: Turkmen writes a rounded vowel in the genitive (öýüň) but not in the accusative (öýi). 2.3.2 How Case Does What Word Order Does in English
In English, “The dog bit the man” and “The man bit the dog” have opposite meanings because position determines grammatical role. In Turkish, the same distinction is carried largely by case suffixes:

Köpek adam-ı ısırdı. (dog man-ACC bit: the dog bit the man)
Adam-ı köpek ısırdı. (man-ACC dog bit: the dog bit the man, with a different information structure)
Adam köpeğ-i ısırdı. (man dog-ACC bit: the man bit the dog; note köpek → köpeğ- before a vowel)

Here the accusative suffix marks the direct object in either position, and the nominative subject has no suffix. Case marking is an important cue to grammatical relations, but the relationship is not one-to-one, as the next two subsections show.


2.3.3 Differential Object Marking
Not every direct object carries the accusative. Turkish marks specific objects and leaves non-specific objects bare:

Ali kitap okudu. ‘Ali read (a book / books)’: non-specific object, no suffix; the bare object normally stands directly before the verb.
Ali kitab-ı okudu. ‘Ali read the book’: specific object, accusative -ı.

A parser must combine case, position and context. The accusative does not universally mark definiteness, and an unmarked noun can be a bare preverbal object as well as a subject.


2.3.4 Case Ambiguity
A written ending can have more than one morphological analysis. Turkish ev-i can be ‘house-ACC’ (evi gördüm ‘I saw the house’) or ‘house-POSS.3SG’ (onun evi ‘his/her house’); ev-in can be ‘house-GEN’ (evin kapısı ‘the door of the house’) or ‘house-POSS.2SG’ (senin evin ‘your house’). These are homophonous suffixes of different categories rather than syncretism within the case paradigm. A morphological analyser typically returns all readings, and the sentence context selects one: onun or senin before the noun, or the verb that governs it.
Case also differs from grammatical relation and from semantic role. A dative noun phrase can be a goal (eve gitti ‘went home’), a recipient (Ali’ye verdi ‘gave to Ali’) or the experiencer-like argument of some verbs. In nominalised subordinate clauses the subject is often in the genitive rather than the nominative: Ali’nin gel-diğ-i-ni biliyorum ‘I know that Ali came’ (Ali-GEN come-NMLZ-POSS.3SG-ACC). Section 2.5 returns to these clauses.


2.3.5 Computational Consequences
These consequences are hypotheses about systems; later chapters test them.

Argument detection. English-trained parsers learn strong positional cues (subject before the verb, object after it). In Turkic languages, case, agreement and position all carry information, and their weights differ from English. Positional biases learned from English can therefore transfer poorly.
Explicit versus implicit morphology. A dependency parser can take predicted morphological features as input, predict them jointly with dependencies, or learn morphological cues within contextual representations. The biaffine parser (Dozat and Manning 2017), for example, scores learned token representations without requiring a separate morphological step. Compare otherwise matched models with and without predicted features to test their contribution (Chapter 8).
Case suffixes in NER. Named entities carry case suffixes in ordinary text: Kazakh Алматы-дан ‘from Almaty’, Абай-дың ‘of Abai’. Mention detection must preserve the original span; mapping Алматыдан to the canonical name Алматы for linking or counting is a separate step, which can use a morphological analyser (Chapter 9).
Machine translation. Translation into a Turkic language must generate the correct case and agreement on the target side. Evaluate case and agreement errors directly rather than assuming that a separate syntactic analysis of the source is required (Chapter 10).

title: 2  The Computational Phenotype of Turkic Languages
text:
2.4 SOV Base Order and Scrambling

2.4.1 Default SOV Order
The usual unmarked constituent order in Turkic is subject–object–verb (SOV). Some contact varieties also have unmarked verb-medial orders (Chapter 8). Johanson (2021, 34) describes Turkic as possessing “a basic left-branching constituent order with dependents preceding their heads” with the unmarked order being “subject + direct object + predicate.”
The same modifier-before-head principle places determiners, attributive adjectives and relative clauses before the head noun (Johanson 2021, 34), and Turkic uses postpositions rather than prepositions (Johanson 2021, 36).


2.4.2 Scrambling
While SOV is the default, constituents can be reordered for discourse purposes. The order is tied to information structure: in Turkish, the position directly before the verb is associated with focus, the sentence-initial position with topic, and material after the verb with backgrounded information (Hoffman 1994). The felicity of an order therefore depends on context, which question-answer pairs make visible:

Kitabı kim okudu? ‘Who read the book?’ → Kitabı Ali okudu. (OSV; Ali, the answer, stands before the verb)
Ali ne yaptı? ‘What did Ali do?’ → Ali kitabı okudu. (SOV)
Ali kitabı okudu mu? ‘Did Ali read the book?’ → Okudu Ali kitabı. (VSO; the verb is in focus, the rest is given)

Other permutations, such as Ali okudu kitabı (SVO, with the book as an afterthought), also occur in suitable contexts; Chapter 8 lists all six orders. Not every noun phrase can move equally freely: bare, non-specific objects such as kitap in Ali kitap okudu normally stay directly before the verb.


2.4.3 Pro-Drop
Turkic languages are pro-drop: subjects and objects may be omitted when their referents are recoverable from the context, and person-number agreement largely makes subject pronouns redundant (Johanson 2021, 35). Person-number agreement can help identify an omitted subject, while an overt pronoun can still contribute contrast or discourse information:

Ben geliyorum. (I am coming, with an explicit pronoun)
Geliyorum. (am coming; the pronoun is dropped and -um marks 1SG)
Geliyor. (is coming; 3SG, no overt subject and no agreement suffix)

In the third-person singular example Geliyor, neither a subject pronoun nor a person suffix is overt; the subject must be inferred from context. In the other persons, as in Spanish or Italian, the agreement suffix identifies the person and number of the dropped subject, but not its referent.


2.4.4 Computational Consequences

Positional features carry different information. Combine case and agreement with word order. English positional biases may transfer poorly, while Turkic patterns such as preverbal focus and adjacent bare objects can still help.
Sequence labelling. A tagger trained only on SOV-ordered text may over-rely on position relative to the verb. Training data with natural scrambling, and evaluation on non-canonical orders, show whether this happens.
Pro-drop complicates coreference resolution. With no overt subject, a system must recover the referent from context. Third-person singular forms may also lack an overt agreement suffix. Evaluate subject resolution in context, including zero arguments that systems designed around overt subjects may overlook.
Pro-drop complicates MT into non-pro-drop languages. When translating Kazakh or Turkish into English or French, the system must generate a pronoun absent in the source, which requires identifying the implicit subject from context.

title: 2  The Computational Phenotype of Turkic Languages
section: 2.5 Non-Finite Subordination: Participial and Converbal Clauses
text:
2.5 Non-Finite Subordination: Participial and Converbal Clauses

2.5.1 Subordination Without Complementisers
English subordinates clauses with function words: “the man who came”, “I know that he left”, “after he arrived”. The Turkic strategy is different: dependent clauses are headed by non-finite forms (action nominals, participles and converbs) carrying bound markers that do the work of English subordinating conjunctions (Johanson 2021, 35). The verb of the subordinate clause appears in a non-finite form, and the clause type is marked morphologically on that verb. (Finite alternatives also exist, such as Turkish ki-clauses or quotative constructions with diye ‘saying’.) Johanson (2021, 34) notes that the “left-branching constituent order” with “dependents preceding their heads” extends to clause structure: embedded clauses appear to the left of their head.


2.5.2 Participial Relative Clauses
In English, “the man who came” contains the relative pronoun who and a finite verb came. In Turkish, the equivalent is gelen adam:

gel- (come) + -en (participle) = gelen ‘who comes / who came’
gelen adam = the man who came

The participle modifies adam ‘man’. The entire clause, including its own arguments and adverbs, appears inside the noun phrase, before the noun:

Dün buraya gelen adam ‘the man who came here yesterday’ (yesterday here come.PTCP man)

Turkish participles differ according to what is relativised. In a common subject relative, the participle is -(y)An: kitabı okuyan öğrenci ‘the student who read the book’. A common non-subject relative, such as one relativising an object or location, uses -DIK for a non-future reading or -(y)AcAK for a future reading. The participle carries a possessive suffix agreeing with the genitive subject: öğrencinin okuduğu kitap ‘the book that the student read’ (student-GEN read-NMLZ-POSS.3SG book).
Kazakh and Uzbek place participles before the noun too, but without this subject/non-subject split. Both Kazakh оқушы оқыған кітап ‘the book that the student read’ and кітапты оқыған оқушы ‘the student who read the book’ use -ған. Uzbek -gan works similarly, as in oʻquvchi oʻqigan kitob.
Turkmen uses -An in both kitaby okan okuwçy ‘the student who read the book’ and okuwçynyň okan kitaby ‘the book that the student read’. In the second construction, the possessive suffix agreeing with the genitive subject attaches to the head noun, kitab-y. Turkish puts that agreement on the participle, okuduğu. Adapting a Turkish analyser or annotation scheme therefore requires changing where this agreement is represented.






Figure 2.4: Basic UD dependencies for English (top) and Turkish (bottom). English has a post-nominal relative clause with who as the subject of came; Turkish Dün gelen adam gitti has a prenominal participial clause with no relative pronoun. Each word has exactly one head; enhanced coreference edges are omitted.





2.5.3 Converbs and Nominalised Clauses
For adverbial clauses (temporal, conditional, manner), Turkic uses converbs, non-finite verb forms that mark the adverbial relation morphologically, alongside nominalised forms followed by case suffixes or postpositions:

gel-ince ‘when/as soon as (someone) came’: converb -(y)IncA
gel-erek ‘by coming, while coming’: converb -(y)ArAk
gel-ip ‘having come, and then’: converb -(y)Ip, which links clauses in a sequence
gel-dik-ten sonra ‘after coming’: nominaliser -DIK + ablative + postposition sonra, not a converb but a nominalised clause
gel-se ‘if (someone) came’: conditional -sA, which can also be fully finite

These constructions mark adverbial relations through verb morphology, sometimes together with a postposition such as sonra.


2.5.4 Long-Distance Dependencies
An embedded clause can make a noun phrase long even when the participle stays close to its head noun, as in gelen adam. Longer arcs connect the clause’s earlier dependents (Dün, buraya) to the participle, or connect the whole phrase’s head noun to the final main verb. A left-to-right processor must keep those dependents pending until it reaches their heads (Chapter 8). Postverbal and other dependents that follow their heads create a different processing pattern.


2.5.5 Computational Consequences

Clause boundaries without a marker word. Systems for event extraction, coreference and semantic role labelling that have been developed for English can use relative pronouns and complementisers as clause-boundary cues. In Turkic text the cue is a suffix on the embedded verb. Whether a given system misses non-finite clauses should be tested, for example by evaluating event recognition separately on finite and non-finite predicates.
Participial forms are morphologically ambiguous. The ending -en in Turkish can be a participle (gelen ‘who comes’) or part of other forms; the same string -DIK appears in relative clauses, complement clauses and adverbial clauses. Morphological disambiguation helps to identify clause boundaries.
Information extraction must look inside noun phrases. Events described in participial clauses are embedded inside noun phrases: öğrencinin okuduğu kitap contains a reading event. A system that only looks at finite main verbs misses them.

title: 2  The Computational Phenotype of Turkic Languages
text:
2.6 Shared Patterns and Variation

2.6.1 The Shared Computational Template
Turkic languages share broad structural tendencies, but individual constructions, varieties and contact settings require separate description. The table orients the reader to recurring patterns. Exceptions exist for almost every row:



Table 2.6: Recurring features of the Turkic profile (Johanson 2021, 34–39).










Feature
Status
Example




Agglutinative morphology
Widespread pattern
Multiple suffixes per word, clear boundaries


SOV default order
Widespread pattern
Reordering for information structure; SOV is unmarked


Vowel harmony (at least palatal)
Common, with exceptions
Weakened in standard Uzbek, whose spelling largely fixes suffix vowels (Johanson 2021, 307, 313)


Six commonly compared cases
Common, with exceptions
Nominative, accusative, dative, locative, ablative, genitive; Sakha lacks the genitive


Pro-drop
Widespread pattern
Subject pronouns routinely omitted


Participial relative clauses
Widespread pattern
Embedded clause precedes head noun


Postpositions
Widespread pattern
Spatial relations after the noun


No grammatical gender
Widespread pattern
o means he/she/it in Turkish


No definite article
Widespread pattern
Specificity expressed through case marking, word order and context








2.6.2 What Varies
The shared patterns leave room for important differences:
Vowel harmony and its spelling. Turkish and Kyrgyz write backness and rounding harmony; Kazakh writes backness but not rounding; Uzbek suffix vowels are largely fixed; Turkmen writes rounding in some suffixes but not others (Table 2.3); Uyghur writes stem-vowel raising (see the list above). Harmony-based features useful for Turkish therefore cannot be applied identically to Uzbek.
Case inventory. Most languages have the six core cases plus some extras (an instrumental in Chuvash, Kazakh and Sakha, for example). Sakha’s system differs most: it has no genitive but has partitive, comitative and comparative cases.
Morpheme inventories. While the template is shared, the specific suffixes differ: aspect markers, evidential categories and certain voice morphemes vary across branches. A morphological analyser built for Turkish cannot be applied to Sakha without new morphotactics, morphophonology and lexicon.
Script. As detailed in Chapter 3, contemporary Turkic languages are written in Latin, Cyrillic and Perso-Arabic scripts, and Old Turkic in a runic script. Kazakh has a planned transition from Cyrillic to Latin, and Uzbek uses Latin officially while Cyrillic remains in wide use. Script differences affect tokenisation and string overlap, so whether to convert scripts before cross-lingual transfer should be tested for each model and task.
Vocabulary. Related languages share vocabulary, but spelling can obscure shared forms. Section 3.6 measures written overlap before and after script conversion.


2.6.3 The Exceptional Cases: Chuvash and Khalaj
Chuvash is the only surviving descendant of the Oghur branch, which split from Common Turkic early (Johanson 2021, 20, 25). Its best-known divergences are rhotacism and lambdacism: where other Turkic languages have z, Chuvash has r, and where they have š, Chuvash has l (Chuvash χịl vs. Common Turkic ḳïš ‘winter’) (Johanson 2021, 23, 26). For NLP, the available evidence suggests testing Oghur transfer separately: on the TurkicNLP morphological challenge set, the rule-based Apertium analyser detected the target phenomena in more Chuvash sentences than the multilingual neural analyser, and the authors attribute this to Chuvash’s divergent morphology limiting transfer from the other branches (Hakimov 2026). With 20 sentences per language, the set supports a diagnostic and nothing stronger; it cannot rank languages.
Khalaj (Arghu branch) is a small language of Iran with archaic features, including the retention of primary long vowels (Johanson 2021, 26). Primary long vowels are also retained systematically in Turkmen and Sakha, so vowel length is not unique to Khalaj within the modern family (Johanson 2021, 26; Gökçür 2016). Khalaj has very few NLP resources. In TurkicNLP it has no Apertium transducer; the multilingual neural analyser serves it through Turkish as a proxy language (Hakimov 2026).


2.6.4 Why This Matters: Relatedness as a Hypothesis
Related languages offer analyses, annotation conventions and modelling experience that can be reused. Apertium’s Turkic analysers share a formalism and tag convention across about 20 languages; TurkicNLP packages 20 of them. Multilingual neural models can also serve languages with little training data through proxy-language representations (Hakimov 2026). Adaptation still requires a language-specific check of the lexicon, morphotactics, morphophonology, script and annotation assumptions.
Treat relatedness as a reason to test a donor, and use target-language evidence to decide whether it is useful. For a practitioner starting NLP work on a new Turkic language with minimal resources, a reasonable procedure is:

List candidate donors: closely related languages and the strongest available models, recording their training data, scripts and annotation conventions.
Set aside target-language development and test data before adapting anything.
Compare donors on the development set, with native-script input and, where supported, input converted to a common script (Chapter 3).
Adapt the selected donor, using separate training data where needed. Fix the system before evaluating it on the untouched test set.

The following chapters develop this procedure concretely.

title: 2  The Computational Phenotype of Turkic Languages
section: 2.7 Hands-On: Counting Segments in Turkish, Kazakh and Turkmen
text:
2.7 Hands-On: Counting Segments in Turkish, Kazakh and Turkmen
Question. Where does automatic segmentation agree with the stated surface analysis?
Inputs. The Turkish, Kazakh and Turkmen sentences below; TurkicNLP 0.5.0 and the named transducers.
Compute. CPU; download the required analyser resources first.
Output. Per-word segments, exact agreement and segments per word.
Interpretation. Inspect boundary errors and analytic constructions before comparing averages.
Start by segmenting a few words by hand under a stated convention, then compare the analyser’s output. This experiment reports surface segments for that sample and configuration. A larger corpus study would also report errors and coverage alongside the mean.
Counting convention. As in Table 2.2, count the stem and every overt affix. Attach buffer consonants to the following suffix (dığ-ı-ndan), stem-final alternations stay in the stem (kitab-ı), and zero morphemes (3SG agreement) are not counted. This is the convention of the TurkicNLP segmentation test set (Hakimov 2026); other conventions give other counts.
Setup. pip install "turkicnlp[hfst,transformers]==0.5.0". The segmenter combines Apertium readings (hfst) with a multilingual neural analyser (transformers). It runs with only one of them, so the code prints which analysers were actually loaded; report this with any result. Before the first run, download each language’s morphology resources with turkicnlp.download("tur", processors=["morph"]) and the equivalent calls for "kaz" and "tuk"; model downloads require network access.
import turkicnlp
from turkicnlp.processors.morpheme_tokenizer import MorphemeTokenizer

# Reference segmentations under the exercise convention: stem + overt affixes; buffer
# consonants go with the following suffix; zero morphemes are not counted.
reference = {
    "tur": [("Ali", "Ali"), ("kitabı", "kitab-ı"), ("okuyamadığından", "oku-ya-ma-dığ-ı-ndan"),
            ("çok", "çok"), ("üzgündü", "üzgün-dü")],
    "kaz": [("Әли", "Әли"), ("кітапты", "кітап-ты"), ("оқи", "оқ-и"),
            ("алмағандықтан", "ал-ма-ған-дық-тан"), ("өте", "өте"),
            ("қайғылы", "қайғы-лы"), ("болды", "бол-ды")],
    "tuk": [("Ali", "Ali"), ("kitaby", "kitab-y"), ("okap", "oka-p"),
            ("bilmedigi", "bil-me-dig-i"), ("üçin", "üçin"), ("gaty", "gaty"),
            ("gamgyn", "gamgyn"), ("boldy", "bol-dy")],
}

print("turkicnlp", turkicnlp.__version__)
for lang, words in reference.items():
    seg = MorphemeTokenizer(lang=lang)
    seg.load()
    # private flags in 0.5.0: which analysers were actually loaded
    print(f"{lang}: neural={seg._neural_available} hfst={seg._hfst_available}")
    n_reference = n_auto = exact = 0
    for word, g in words:
        r = seg.segment(word)
        auto = "-".join(m for m, _ in r.labeled)
        n_reference += len(g.split("-")); n_auto += len(r.labeled); exact += auto == g
        print(f"  {word:<17} reference {g:<22} auto {auto:<22} [{r.source}]")
    n = len(words)
    print(f"  exact {exact}/{n}; segments per word: reference {n_reference/n:.2f}, automatic {n_auto/n:.2f}\n")
The output below was reproduced on 13 October 2026 using the local toolkit source reporting version 0.5.0, with only the Apertium transducers available (the neural model was not installed). The package version alone is not an exact source pin:
turkicnlp 0.5.0
tur: neural=False hfst=True
  Ali               reference Ali                    auto Ali                    [hfst]
  kitabı            reference kitab-ı                auto kitab-ı                [hfst]
  okuyamadığından   reference oku-ya-ma-dığ-ı-ndan   auto oku-ya-ma-dı-ğından    [hfst]
  çok               reference çok                    auto çok                    [hfst]
  üzgündü           reference üzgün-dü               auto üzgün-dü               [hfst]
  exact 4/5; segments per word: reference 2.40, automatic 2.20

kaz: neural=False hfst=True
  Әли               reference Әли                    auto Әли                    [hfst]
  кітапты           reference кітап-ты               auto кітап-ты               [hfst]
  оқи               reference оқ-и                   auto оқ-и                   [hfst]
  алмағандықтан     reference ал-ма-ған-дық-тан      auto ал-ма-ған-ды-қтан      [hfst]
  өте               reference өте                    auto өт-е                   [hfst]
  қайғылы           reference қайғы-лы               auto қайғы-лы               [hfst]
  болды             reference бол-ды                 auto бол-ды                 [hfst]
  exact 5/7; segments per word: reference 2.14, automatic 2.29

tuk: neural=False hfst=True
  Ali               reference Ali                    auto Ali                    [none]
  kitaby            reference kitab-y                auto kitab-y                [hfst]
  okap              reference oka-p                  auto oka-p                  [hfst]
  bilmedigi         reference bil-me-dig-i           auto bil-me-di-gi           [hfst]
  üçin              reference üçin                   auto üçin                   [hfst]
  gaty              reference gaty                   auto gat-y                  [hfst]
  gamgyn            reference gamgyn                 auto gamgyn                 [hfst]
  boldy             reference bol-dy                 auto bol-dy                 [hfst]
  exact 6/8; segments per word: reference 1.75, automatic 1.88
The Turkmen lines were produced on 18 October 2026 with the same toolkit version and the Apertium Turkmen transducer (beta; SHA-256 of tuk.automorf.hfst begins 528202a5). The Turkmen sentence Ali kitaby okap bilmedigi üçin gaty gamgyn boldy ‘Ali was very sad because he could not read the book’ parallels the other two.
One reference segmentation follows the spelling rather than the morphology: Kazakh оқи is the stem оқы- ‘read’ plus the converb -й, which the orthography writes as и (ы + й → и); the convention assigns -и to the suffix. The examples show two kinds of error. Boundaries are misplaced in the nominalised forms okuyamadığından, алмағандықтан and bilmedigi. Short words can also receive the wrong reading: Kazakh өте ‘very’ is split as a form of өт- ‘pass’, and Turkmen gaty ‘very’ as an accusative of gat ‘layer’.
Word boundaries also affect the average. Turkish expresses inability in one word here; Kazakh оқи алмағандықтан and Turkmen okap bilmedigi use two. Turkmen adds the postposition üçin where the other examples use a case suffix. The resulting averages describe these sentences under this counting convention, not the languages as a whole.
For larger samples, the TurkicNLP paper reports exact segmentation of 89% for the hybrid segmenter, against 79% for Apertium alone and 68% for the neural analyser alone, on a test set of 483 words in 13 categories across 20 languages (Hakimov 2026). The authors note that the set is small, that the gold segmentations for nine languages are drafts awaiting native-speaker verification, and that it was used during development, so the scores are likely optimistic. Each result records which analysis produced it (seg.segment(word).source is "hfst", "neural" or "greedy").
Status: demonstration. The outputs above are recorded. Exercise 5 adds a related segmentation check.

title: 2  The Computational Phenotype of Turkic Languages
text:
What to Take Forward
Morphemes, written words and model tokens are different units, and a system’s score depends on which one it counts. Harmony changes suffix forms; case, word order and context express grammatical relations; participles and converbs connect clauses. The segmentation comparison illustrates how finite-state and neural analyses can complement each other, though its small, development-used set still includes draft gold analyses. Before evaluating a system, decide which construction and counting unit the task needs. Chapter 3 turns to scripts and spelling conventions.

title: 2  The Computational Phenotype of Turkic Languages
text:
Further Reading

Turkic morphology and syntax: Johanson (2021) (especially chapters 14–15 on phoneme systems and harmony) is the primary linguistic reference for the features described in this chapter.
Agglutination and NLP: Oflazer (1994) gives a two-level description of Turkish morphology, an approach that later Turkic finite-state analysers build on.
Word order and information structure: Hoffman (1994) relates Turkish word orders to topic and focus.
Subword tokenisation: Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch (2016) describes BPE; Rust et al. (2021) and Petrov et al. (2023) show how multilingual tokenisers disadvantage many languages; Hakimov (2026) measures this for 20 Turkic languages.
Kardeş-NLU: Senel et al. (2024) shows that a high-resource relative (Turkish) helps cross-lingual transfer to five other Turkic languages.
Universal Dependencies and Turkic syntax: Nivre et al. (2016) and Türk et al. (2022) cover the UD annotation framework applied to Turkish.

title: 2  The Computational Phenotype of Turkic Languages
text:
Exercises

Segmenting words. Segment evlerimizden and explain the contribution of each piece. Then compare yazıldılar and yazılamadılar. Use the analyses yaz-ıl-dı-lar and yaz-ıl-a-ma-dı-lar to identify passive voice, past and agreement, and explain how the second form adds negative ability. Under this chapter’s surface-segmentation convention, how many pieces does each word contain? Why need this count not equal the number of language-model tokens?
Vowel harmony and consonant alternation. Add the plural suffix to ev, araba, göz and kol. Separately, form the third-person singular past of gel-, bak-, gör-, bul- and git-. Identify which changes follow vowel harmony and which come from consonant assimilation. Compare a regular example with one of the exceptional stems in Section 2.2.
Case and word order. Translate Kitabı Ayşe okudu and Ayşe kitabı okudu into English. Give a question that each order would answer naturally. Then compare Ayşe kitap okudu: what changes when the accusative is absent? Write the sentence with the subject omitted (pro-drop) and explain what must be recovered from context.
Participial clauses. Translate Dün şehre gelen adam and Ali’nin okuduğu kitap. Identify the participle in each, say whether the head noun is the subject or a non-subject of the relative clause, and sketch the dependency structure.
Checking a segmenter. Run MorphemeTokenizer(lang="tur") on yazıldılar and yazılamadılar and on the Kazakh жазылды and жазыла алмады. Report which analysers were loaded. Where does the segmenter agree with your segmentation from Exercise 1, and where does it differ?
Segments per word across the family. Take the same short text in Turkish, Kazakh, Uzbek and Tatar (for example a FLORES-200 paragraph). Segment 30 words per language by hand under the chapter’s convention, then compare with the automatic output as in the Hands-On section. Report exact agreement, the gold and automatic means, and the words where analytic constructions change the word count.
Choosing a donor. You need a Kyrgyz dependency parser and have no Kyrgyz training data. Propose Turkish and Kazakh donor systems, recording their training data, input scripts and annotation conventions, and explain why either might be preferable. Design a small target-language evaluation comparing the available systems and, where supported, native-script and transliterated input. Which result would justify the cost of script conversion?

title: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering
text:
3.1 A Map of Turkic Scripts
A Turkic corpus may contain several scripts and spelling conventions for the same language. Historical collections add Old Turkic runic, Old Uyghur and earlier Perso-Arabic traditions (Johanson 2021, chap. 19). Processing these texts requires a clear record of the input script, the orthography and any conversion applied.
This chapter answers the practical question: given a corpus of Turkic text, what do you need to do before you can run any NLP tool on it?
crumbs: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering

title: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering
text:
3.1.1 Contemporary Scripts and Historical Collections
Most contemporary Turkic text uses Latin, Cyrillic or Perso-Arabic script, with conventions that vary by language, region and period. Historical collections add Old Turkic runic, Old Uyghur and other scripts. A preprocessing system must distinguish the script family, the language’s alphabet and the orthographic reform on which a conversion table is based.
Latin. Contemporary Latin orthographies include Turkish, Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Turkmen, Crimean Tatar, Gagauz and Karakalpak. Several reflect reforms after the Soviet period; others have earlier histories (Johanson 2021, 421–25). Kazakhstan has published multiple Latin designs (Section 3.2). A Latin script label alone is insufficient: Turkish ş and Uzbek sh, for example, require different conversion rules.
Cyrillic. Cyrillic-based orthographies are used for Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Tatar, Bashkir, Chuvash, Sakha and several South Siberian languages. Cyrillic alphabets were introduced for nearly all Turkic languages of the Soviet Union between 1937 and 1940, but Chuvash and Sakha have earlier Cyrillic histories (Johanson 2021, 415–20). Each orthography has its own additional letters and spelling conventions.
Perso-Arabic. This script family is used for Uyghur in Xinjiang, Azerbaijani in Iran, and Kazakh and Kyrgyz in China, as well as historical Ottoman and Chaghatay collections (Johanson 2021, 411–13, 419, 423). Modern Uyghur writes vowel qualities explicitly; this facilitates conversion but does not make its orthography a complete phonetic transcription.


3.1.2 Language-to-Script Mapping



Table 3.1: Selected language–script relationships. Historical dates follow the cited accounts; script prevalence and current legal status are not inferred from them.

The dates in Table 3.1 refer to specific reforms or source accounts. Writers may change script at different times. Record legal adoption, alphabet publication, school implementation and corpus prevalence separately; one transition date cannot describe them all.


3.1.3 Historical Scripts
Historical collections involve two further scripts and two Perso-Arabic literary traditions:

Old Turkic runic (Orkhon script): used in inscriptions from the early eighth century onward in present-day Mongolia and the Yenisei Basin (Johanson 2021, 159); it has its own Unicode block
Old Uyghur script (not to be confused with modern Uyghur Perso-Arabic): an alphabet modelled on the Soghdian script, used for Old Uyghur manuscripts (Johanson 2021, 410)
Chaghatay: the Persian-influenced literary language of Central Asia from the fifteenth century on (Johanson 2021, 162), written with Perso-Arabic conventions; a language and literary tradition, not a separate script
Ottoman Turkish: written with Perso-Arabic conventions in literature and administration until the 1928 reform

These historical scripts are relevant for heritage document digitisation and require specialised OCR (Section 17.2.2). For Ottoman Turkish, two UD treebanks exist (Chapter 8), and TurkicNLP converts Latin transcriptions into Perso-Arabic script and processes Ottoman text with a dedicated Stanza model (Hakimov 2026); Old Turkic runes can be converted to Latin transcription. An annotated Chaghatay manuscript corpus contains about 30,700 words (Steimel et al. 2020).

title: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering
text:
3.2 The Active Transitions

3.2.1 Kazakhstan: Published Designs and Implementation
Kazakh corpus processing must distinguish several published Latin designs. The following milestones explain the mappings encountered in this book; they are not a legal-status register:

2017: A first version that marked the specifically Kazakh sounds with apostrophes after a base letter (e.g., a’ for ә, s’ for ш, n’ for ң), while қ was already written q (Qazaqstan). Apostrophe-based letters are fragile in digital text: keyboard and typographic apostrophes are different Unicode characters, which breaks search and indexing.
2018: The revised alphabet used acute accents such as á, ǵ and ń, but wrote ш with the digraph Sh sh, not ś; see the reproduced appendix to Decree No. 637 of 19 February 2018.
2021: A further revision with Turkic-style diacritics, e.g. ä (ә), ğ (ғ), ñ (ң), ö (ө), ş (ш), ū (ұ), ü (ү), released as a draft for public discussion. The 2023–2029 language-policy concept makes the transition schedule depend on a further legal act. These documents show that a draft and a policy framework were published. The current legal status of any later alphabet has to be checked elsewhere.
2026: The Turkish Language Association reports that the common-alphabet commission accepted Kazakh and Kyrgyz alphabet proposals as reference documents at its meeting on 15 June 2026. A commission recommendation is not national enactment. The toolkit mapping described below does not implement a newly inferred 2026 standard.

For Kazakh-to-Latin conversion, this book uses the toolkit’s table based on the 2021 proposal. Record that mapping version with the corpus. It identifies how the text was converted, without implying national adoption or widespread use.
What this means for corpus building. A Kazakh corpus may contain: 1. Cyrillic 2. Latin text following one of the published Latin designs 3. Informal Latin, including ASCII approximations without diacritics (a for ä, s or sh for ş)
A Kazakh pipeline can convert text to a shared script in a derived view, or train on the scripts it expects to encounter. Compare the two approaches on the intended task. Assuming a single spelling convention will leave mismatches in a mixed corpus.


3.2.2 Uzbekistan: The Persistent Cyrillic
The transition to the Uzbek Latin alphabet was adopted in 1993 and revised in 1995 as a replacement for Cyrillic (Johanson 2021, 424). More than three decades later, both scripts are still in everyday use: the relevant corpus may include both Latin and Cyrillic documents. How widely writers in a given domain actually follow the legal standard is a separate, empirical question.
This duality creates a potential distribution shift for a model trained in one script. Compare native-script processing, transliteration and mixed-script training on a held-out sample from the intended domain before choosing a pipeline.


3.2.3 Corpus Implications
For any NLP practitioner working with Kazakh or Uzbek:

Detect the script of each document, and of each span in mixed documents, before processing (Section 3.4 shows the toolkit functions)
Keep the original and create converted text only as a derived view, or train script-robust models
Test transliteration to use resources from one script variant for the other (Section 3.4)
Do not assume that a web-crawled corpus is monoscript; even within a single document, informal text mixes scripts. A change of script is not necessarily a change of language: record script and language as separate metadata

3.3.2 The Turkish İ/I Problem
Turkish has four distinct characters where English has two:









Character
Unicode
Name
Example




İ
U+0130
Latin Capital Letter I with Dot Above
İstanbul


I
U+0049
Latin Capital Letter I (dotless)
Isparta


i
U+0069
Latin Small Letter I (dotted)
istanbul (lowercase of İstanbul)


ı
U+0131
Latin Small Letter Dotless I
ısparta (lowercase of Isparta)



The pairs are: İ ↔︎ i (dotted I, both cases) and I ↔︎ ı (dotless I, both cases).
Python’s str.lower() and str.upper() apply the language-independent Unicode case mappings. They are not locale-aware (unlike, e.g., Java’s toLowerCase(Locale)). For Turkish this gives two different errors:
"ISPARTA".lower()        # → "isparta"   WRONG: should be "ısparta" (I ↔ ı)
"İstanbul".lower()       # → "i̇stanbul"  WRONG: 'i' + U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE
len("İ".lower())         # → 2  — the string even changes length
"istanbul".upper()       # → "ISTANBUL"  WRONG: should be "İSTANBUL"
A correct helper must also handle the decomposed spelling of İ (I followed by U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE), which is canonically equivalent to U+0130. Normalising to NFC first takes care of it:
import unicodedata

def turkish_lower_nfc(text: str) -> str:
    """Turkish/Azerbaijani lowercasing for ordinary text; returns an NFC view."""
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text)
    text = text.translate(str.maketrans({"İ": "i", "I": "ı"}))
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text.lower())

def turkish_upper_nfc(text: str) -> str:
    """Turkish/Azerbaijani uppercasing for ordinary text; returns an NFC view."""
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text)
    text = text.translate(str.maketrans({"i": "İ", "ı": "I"}))
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text.upper())

assert turkish_lower_nfc("ISPARTA") == "ısparta"
assert turkish_lower_nfc("İSTANBUL") == "istanbul"
assert turkish_lower_nfc("I\u0307STANBUL") == "istanbul"      # decomposed İ
assert turkish_upper_nfc("istanbul ısparta") == "İSTANBUL ISPARTA"

# TurkicNLP ships the mapping step as a helper: it maps İ → i and I → ı
from turkicnlp.utils.unicode_utils import normalize_turkish_i
normalize_turkish_i("ISPARTA").lower()   # → "ısparta"
These helpers handle the ordinary Turkish dotted/dotless pairs and canonical normalisation. Unicode’s SpecialCasing includes further context-sensitive rules. Apply the helpers only after identifying the language: even English or Russian material within a Turkish corpus can contain INFO, which they turn into ınfo. Casing may also change string length, so offsets must identify the text view they refer to.
The combining-dot result can be hard to spot: it survives into vocabularies and makes "i̇stanbul" != "istanbul". The dotted/dotless distinction applies to Turkish, Azerbaijani, Crimean Tatar, Gagauz, Tatar Latin and the Kazakh Latin proposals. For these orthographies, calling lower() without an explicit mapping introduces systematic errors in case folding, vocabulary building and string comparison. Lowercasing itself is optional: cased models and annotation tasks often need the original case, so keep it unless the task requires folding.


3.3.3 Cyrillic/Latin Homoglyphs
Several characters appear visually identical in Cyrillic and Latin but have different Unicode codepoints:

U+0440
p U+0070

ə U+0259
