These homoglyphs cause subtle failures:

Mixing Cyrillic а and Latin a can change tokenisation and cause dictionary lookup failures
Script detection based on character statistics may misclassify mixed-script text
String comparison ("alma" == "аlma" is false: the second string starts with Cyrillic U+0430)

Unicode normalisation does not help here: NFC and NFKC leave Latin a and Cyrillic а distinct, because they are different characters. To find them, inspect the characters themselves:
import unicodedata
for ch in "аa әə":
    if not ch.isspace():
        print(repr(ch), hex(ord(ch)), unicodedata.name(ch))
# 'а' 0x430 CYRILLIC SMALL LETTER A
# 'a' 0x61 LATIN SMALL LETTER A
# 'ә' 0x4d9 CYRILLIC SMALL LETTER SCHWA
# 'ə' 0x259 LATIN SMALL LETTER SCHWA
For a general script test, use the Unicode Script and Script_Extensions properties (UAX #24) rather than block ranges. Latin letters span several blocks. Many digits and punctuation marks have the Script value Common, and many combining marks have Inherited; others are script-specific. Script_Extensions records use across scripts. Character names, as above, are a teaching approximation. Repairing look-alikes is a separate, language-dependent decision (Section 3.5).


3.3.4 Arabic-Script Text: Uyghur and Ottoman
Uyghur text in the Perso-Arabic script is written right-to-left (RTL). Three issues matter in practice:

Presentation forms: older Uyghur web text and PDFs were often produced with fonts and converters that store contextual glyph shapes (Arabic Presentation Forms-A/B) instead of the base letters. Visually identical words then have different code points. NFKC normalisation maps them back to the base letters; NFC does not.
Letter variants: Uyghur-specific letters (ۆ ۈ ې ۋ) are in the basic Arabic block, but look-alike Persian, Arabic, and Kazakh/Kyrgyz Arabic letters (e.g., different yeh and kaf forms) occur in real text and need a mapping table.
Joiners and punctuation: zero-width joiners/non-joiners (U+200C/U+200D) and Arabic punctuation (، ؛ ؟) must be handled by the tokeniser; TurkicNLP uses a separate Arabic-script tokeniser for this reason (Hakimov 2026).

Because the reformed Uyghur orthography marks vowels explicitly (Johanson 2021, 413), modern Uyghur does not have the same systematic missing-vowel problem as unvocalised Arabic or Persian. Missing vowels remain an issue for Ottoman Turkish and Chaghatay, whose Perso-Arabic orthography leaves many vowels unwritten.


3.3.5 Unicode Normalisation: NFC vs. NFD
Unicode allows characters to be represented in different ways. For example, the Turkish ş can be represented as:

Precomposed (NFC): a single code point U+015F
Decomposed (NFD): the base letter s (U+0073) followed by a combining cedilla (U+0327)

Much modern text is in NFC, but text from some sources (older databases, some operating systems and input methods) can contain NFD. An NLP system that encounters both will treat ş (NFC) and ş (NFD) as different strings. The failure is silent and hard to debug.
Best practice: keep the original text, and apply unicodedata.normalize('NFC', text) as the first step in building the processing view of it. NFC makes canonically equivalent strings identical; it does not correct spelling, repair look-alike letters or decide the language (UAX #15).
import unicodedata
from turkicnlp.utils.unicode_utils import normalize_nfc, strip_diacritics

def normalize_unicode(text: str) -> str:
    """Apply NFC normalisation as the first preprocessing step."""
    return unicodedata.normalize('NFC', text)     # same as normalize_nfc(text)

strip_diacritics("Türkçe")    # → "Turkce": a lossy view for a declared purpose; retain the original
When NFC is not enough: NFC leaves compatibility characters untouched: Arabic presentation forms, full-width Latin letters, ligatures such as ﬁ. NFKC folds them, but it also folds characters you may want to keep (superscripts, some punctuation), including in the Latin and symbol content embedded in an Arabic-script document. A practical recipe is NFC for all text, plus NFKC applied only to the characters in the Arabic Presentation Forms blocks, and an explicit, context-aware treatment of apostrophe variants (Section 3.5).


3.3.6 Encoding, Display Order and Visible Characters
Three further problems come before any of the above.
Wrong decoding. Text decoded with the wrong encoding (“mojibake”) is a different string, and no Unicode normalisation can repair it. Kazakh UTF-8 bytes read as Windows-1251 look like this:
s = "Қазақстан".encode("utf-8").decode("cp1251")
print(s)                                        # ТљР°Р·Р°Т›СЃС‚Р°РЅ
print(s.encode("cp1251").decode("utf-8"))       # Қазақстан  (reversible only if no byte was lost)
Decode with the known encoding, record failures instead of silently dropping bytes, and check samples of every source; a UTF-8 byte-order mark (U+FEFF) at the start of a file should be removed on decoding (encoding="utf-8-sig").
Logical versus visual order. Uyghur Perso-Arabic text is stored in logical order (the order in which it is read) and displayed right to left; numbers and embedded Latin words are displayed left to right inside it, following the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm (UAX #9). The string "ئۇيغۇرچە 2024-يىلى Python" is stored with ئۇيغۇرچە first, whatever it looks like on screen. Never reverse stored strings for NLP; only display software applies the visual order.
Characters versus what the reader sees. len() counts code points, not visible characters: decomposed ş is two code points, and an Arabic letter with a combining mark is one visible unit. User-facing offsets and truncation should use grapheme clusters (UAX #29; e.g. the regex module’s \X).

title: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering
text:
3.4 Bidirectional Transliteration

3.4.1 Why Transliteration Matters Computationally
Shared morphology and vocabulary offer little direct help to a model if unfamiliar spelling hides them. A multilingual or byte-level model can accept Kyrgyz Cyrillic, yet a model fine-tuned on Turkish Latin may still represent it poorly. Transliteration offers one possible remedy. Test it against the same model with native-script input.
Transliteration maps one written representation to another; transcription, by contrast, aims to represent sounds. Алматы (Cyrillic) becomes Almaty (Latin). A good mapping preserves the information in the spelling, but some mappings are lossy: where two source letters map to one target letter, the distinction is gone (see the hard cases below).
The TurkicNLP toolkit (Hakimov 2026) supports conversion for ten multi-script Turkic languages, following national standards or, for Kazakh, the 2021 proposal, plus conversion of 23 languages into the toolkit’s Common Turkic Script (CTS) (Section 3.6). Two of the pairs (Ottoman Turkish, Old Turkic) work in one direction only:



Table 3.3: Transliteration pairs and mapping standards in TurkicNLP 0.5.0. Ottoman Turkish (Latin transcription to Perso-Arabic) and Old Turkic (runes to Latin transcription) are one-way reconstructions, not reversible conversions.

3.4.2 The Greedy Longest-Match Algorithm
The core of a table-driven converter fits in a few lines:
def longest_match(text: str, mapping: dict[str, str]) -> str:
    """Table lookup only: no case handling, context rules or restoration."""
    if "" in mapping:
        raise ValueError("Mapping keys must be non-empty")
    keys = sorted(mapping, key=len, reverse=True)
    out, pos = [], 0
    while pos < len(text):
        for key in keys:
            if text.startswith(key, pos):
                out.append(mapping[key]); pos += len(key)
                break
        else:
            out.append(text[pos]); pos += 1          # unmatched: copied, and should be logged
    return "".join(out)

# A small demonstration table, not a complete Uzbek converter
demo = {"sh": "ш", "ch": "ч", "oʻ": "ў", "s": "с", "h": "ҳ", "o": "о", "a": "а", "q": "қ", "i": "и", "l": "л"}
longest_match("sh", demo)                        # 'ш'   (digraph matched as a unit)
longest_match("sh", {"s": "с", "h": "ҳ"})         # 'сҳ'  (without the digraph entry)
longest_match("oʻqish", demo)                     # 'ўқиш'
longest_match("Shahar", demo)                     # 'Sҳаҳаr'  (capitals and 'r' missing from the table)
An empty key would consume no input and loop forever, so the code rejects it. With no mappings, it copies the input; with no input, it returns an empty string. A practical converter also needs capitalisation rules, a complete table and a record of characters copied unchanged. Those copies show where conversion fell back to the source. Some letters need context rules too: Uzbek Cyrillic е becomes ye initially and after a vowel, but e elsewhere.
TurkicNLP extends this greedy longest-match algorithm. At each input position it tries the longest sequence first, up to four characters in this source version, then shortens the match. Uzbek sh, ch and oʻ can thus map as units to ш, ч and ў. Context rules handle position-dependent letters: Cyrillic е can be initial ye or elsewhere e in Uzbek, Turkmen and Tatar; Crimean Tatar ё/ю represent ö/ü after consonants (Hakimov 2026).






Figure 3.2: Greedy longest-match lookup for a versioned transliteration mapping. At each position the longest matching non-empty key is consumed; otherwise one character is copied. The maximum key length comes from the mapping. Contextual spelling, normalisation and case policies are separate from this kernel.



The algorithm handles capitalisation by checking whether the first character of the source sequence is upper-case and applying the same capitalisation to the output sequence; all-capital words are handled separately. Test any converter on title case, all capitals, digraphs versus separate letters (Uzbek sh versus sʼh in Isʼhoq), unknown characters, and decomposed input.


3.4.3 Code Example: Script Detection and Transliteration
The following example demonstrates automatic script detection and Kazakh Cyrillic↔︎Latin transliteration using the TurkicNLP toolkit (adapted from the companion library):
from turkicnlp.scripts import Script
from turkicnlp.scripts.detector import detect_script
from turkicnlp.scripts.transliterator import Transliterator

# --- Script Detection ---
cyrl_text = "Мен Алматыда тұрамын."  # Kazakh Cyrillic: "I live in Almaty."
print(detect_script(cyrl_text))       # Script.CYRILLIC

# --- Cyrillic → Latin (toolkit mapping based on the 2021 proposal) ---
t_cyrl_latn = Transliterator("kaz", Script.CYRILLIC, Script.LATIN)
latin_text = t_cyrl_latn.transliterate(cyrl_text)
print(latin_text)   # Men Almatyda tūramyn.   (ұ → ū in the 2021 alphabet)

# --- Latin → Cyrillic (reverse direction) ---
t_latn_cyrl = Transliterator("kaz", Script.LATIN, Script.CYRILLIC)
restored = t_latn_cyrl.transliterate(latin_text)
print(restored)     # Мен Алматыда тұрамын.

# --- Script bridging inside a pipeline ---
# The Kazakh models are trained on Cyrillic. For Latin input the pipeline
# transliterates to Cyrillic, runs the models, and maps the results back:
# word texts, lemmas and character offsets refer to the original Latin text.
import turkicnlp
nlp = turkicnlp.Pipeline("kaz", script="Latn", processors=["tokenize", "morph"],
                       tokenize_backend="rule", morph_backend="apertium")
doc = nlp("Men Almatyda tūramyn.")
print(doc._model_text)          # Мен Алматыда тұрамын.  (what the models saw)
for w in doc.words:
    print(w.text, w.lemma, w.upos, w.feats, w.start_char)
# Men      men      PRON  Case=Nom|Number=Sing|Person=1|PronType=Prs  0
# Almatyda Almaty   PROPN Case=Loc                                     4
# tūramyn  tūr      VERB  Aspect=Hab|Number=Sing|Person=1|Tense=Pres   13
# .        .        PUNCT _                                            20
The same mechanism covers Uzbek in Cyrillic, which this toolkit configuration routes to Latin-script models: turkicnlp.Pipeline("uzb", script="Cyrl") analyses the text with the Latin-script models. The output above was reproduced with the local 0.5.0 source, the rule-based tokeniser, and the Apertium analyser.


3.4.4 Hard Cases and Limitations
Many-to-one mappings (Kazakh). In the 2021 Kazakh Latin proposal both Cyrillic и and й are written i, and Cyrillic у can stand for a vowel or a glide. Converting Latin back to Cyrillic therefore needs context rules or a lexicon, and Russian loanwords (with ц, щ, ё, ъ, ь) need exception lists.
Information lost in one direction (Crimean Tatar). Crimean Tatar Cyrillic writes word-initial ö and ü as о and у, so ötmek comes back from a Latin → Cyrillic → Latin round trip as otmek. In the TurkicNLP evaluation on its parallel sample, this is the only language whose round trip did not recover every word (97.6% of words, versus 100% for the other languages and pivots) (Hakimov 2026). A perfect round trip on a sample shows that those inputs were recovered; it does not prove that a mapping is invertible on arbitrary text, nor that the converted spelling is the one a writer of the target script would use.
Perso-Arabic diacritics (harakat) in Ottoman Turkish. Ottoman Turkish texts sometimes include Arabic diacritics that provide vowel information absent from the base consonantal script. In TurkicNLP 0.5.0 the Ottoman converter runs only from Latin transcription to Perso-Arabic, so vowel diacritics in Perso-Arabic input are not used to recover Latin vowels.
Loanwords in the Latin→Cyrillic direction. For Uzbek, the Latin digraph sh maps unambiguously to Cyrillic ш, but Russian loanwords keep their Russian spelling in Cyrillic (film → фильм, with a soft sign the Latin form does not show). TurkicNLP’s Uzbek conversion agrees with the independent UzTransliterator on 99.4% of words (Cyrillic→Latin) and 98.4% (Latin→Cyrillic); the remaining differences are such loanwords (Hakimov 2026). Agreement between two converters is not accuracy against checked spellings, since both can make the same mistake. Evaluate forward conversion, reverse conversion and round-trip recovery separately, on text with loanwords, names and mixed case. An exception lexicon or learned model may resolve some differences; check its output against independently verified spellings.

title: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering
text:
3.5 Text Normalisation for Turkic

3.5.1 Spell-Checking in Agglutinative Languages
A spell-checker that looks words up in a list of full word forms is impractical for Turkish or Kazakh: productive suffixation creates forms absent from a finite word list. Practical checkers therefore model morphology. Hunspell combines a stem list with affix rules, and morphological spell-checking accepts a word if a morphological analyser can parse it; Zemberek-NLP does this for Turkish, and Apertium transducers can be used the same way for other Turkic languages.
Acceptance by the analyser is not the same as correctness, in either direction. A real-word error passes: Turkish evde ‘at home’ typed for ev de ‘the house too’ is a valid word, and only context shows the mistake. An unknown proper name or a new loanword fails, although it is spelled correctly, because it is missing from the lexicon. Correction candidates (all strings within edit distance 1 or 2 that the analyser accepts) must be ranked with context, typically by a language model.


3.5.2 Orthographic Variation in Web-Crawled Text
Web-crawled corpora for Turkic languages contain significant orthographic variation:
Turkish apostrophe usage. Turkish orthography separates certain inflectional suffixes on proper names with an apostrophe, as in Ankara’dan (from Ankara), Türkiye’de (in Turkey). This is not a rule for every suffix or every named expression; derivation and institution names require separate treatment. In informal digital text, this apostrophe is frequently omitted (Ankaradan, Türkiyede), producing forms that a morphological analyser may not recognise as proper noun inflections.
Cyrillic/Latin mixing. Uzbek and Kazakh online text can mix scripts within a post or even within a sentence, for example Latin-script loanwords or technical terms in Cyrillic text. Script detection must operate at the word level, not just the document level, for such text.
Punctuation and whitespace. Arabic-script Uyghur text uses Arabic punctuation conventions (distinct comma, semicolon and question mark characters). Uyghur web text often mixes Arabic and ASCII punctuation, which can change punctuation attachment and token boundaries depending on the tokeniser.


3.5.3 Diacritic Dropping
A frequent form of informal orthographic variation is diacritic dropping: omitting the diacritics that distinguish some characters from their base letters. Typical substitutions are:

Turkish: ğ→g, ş→s, ç→c, ö→o, ü→u, ı→i (the dotless I becomes a regular i)
Kazakh (2021 Latin): ä→a, ğ→g, ş→s, ñ→n, ū→u, ü→u, ö→o; in Cyrillic, Kazakh-specific letters are replaced by their Russian look-alikes (қ→к, ң→н, ү→у, ұ→у, ө→о, і→и) on keyboards without a Kazakh layout
Uzbek: oʻ→o, gʻ→g

The Uzbek apostrophe problem. The official spelling rules distinguish the letters oʻ, gʻ and the separating sign tutuq belgisi (maʼno), but do not prescribe Unicode code points. A common convention uses U+02BB (ʻ) for the letter mark and U+02BC (ʼ) for the separating sign. Toolkit output and some linguistic examples in this book retain ASCII U+0027.
Real text also uses backticks, curly quotes and acute accents for these marks. Normalise them according to a documented corpus convention, using word and quotation context. A mark after o or g may belong to a letter, but a mark at a word boundary may be quotation punctuation. Global replacement can erase that distinction. TurkicNLP 0.5.0 uses ASCII apostrophes in Uzbek conversion; adapt its output if the corpus uses another convention.
Diacritic-dropped text occurs where keyboards or habits make the special letters inconvenient. A morphological analyser built for correctly diacritised text may fail to parse such forms; measure how often on a sample of the target data.
Diacritic restoration, recovering the correct form from the dropped version, can be approached as a sequence-to-sequence task. For Turkish, vowel harmony provides strong constraints on the restored vowels. Kazakh also needs lexical and contextual evidence, because the dropped distinctions (к/қ, у/ү/ұ) are not all predictable from harmony.


3.5.4 Ordering the Pipeline
Preserve the original, diagnose its encoding, and build a conservative processing view. Then assess script and language. Turkish casing, Kazakh look-alike repairs and Uzbek apostrophe handling depend on those decisions. Each subsequent change should produce a view that can be inspected and traced back to its source.

Preserve the source. Save the source identifier, acquisition date, licence information and the original bytes. Decode with the known encoding and record decoding failures.
Build an NFC view. Apply NFC; apply NFKC only to Arabic presentation-form characters. Keep the previous view.
Assess script and language. Detect scripts per span, and identify the language with an unrestricted label set or an explicit “unknown” option (Section 3.7). Use source metadata as evidence (a Kazakh news site), and abstain when metadata and text disagree.
Split mixed content. Treat spans in different languages or scripts separately; protect URLs, code and quoted foreign text. Choose a language and orthography version only for spans the evidence supports.
Propose language-specific repairs. Casing, apostrophes and look-alike letters, as candidates with their positions. Keep uncertain cases for review, and re-run language identification if a repair changes the evidence it used.
Restore and convert. Apply a restoration model only in the representation it was trained on (a model trained on noisy and corrected Cyrillic expects Cyrillic). Convert to the downstream model’s script, if a task comparison supports conversion.
Tokenise with the downstream model’s tokeniser, keeping view and offset metadata, and evaluate on held-out original-language examples.

Restoration and transliteration. Suppose a writer types Kazakh к for қ. A Cyrillic-to-Latin converter produces k; recovering the intended q requires restoration. A model tolerant of noisy spelling may need neither repair. When restoration is useful, apply it in the representation the restoration model expects: before conversion for a model trained on Cyrillic, afterwards for one trained on Latin. A joint model may perform both operations.
Code Example: Script Spans and Look-Alike Letters
The toolkit’s detect_script(text) returns the dominant script of a whole text and raises ValueError if the text contains no characters recognised as letters in a supported script. detect_script_segments(text) returns (text, script) pairs:
from turkicnlp.scripts.detector import detect_script, detect_script_segments

detect_script("Мен Алматыда тұрамын.")                # Script.CYRILLIC
detect_script_segments("Мен iPhone сатып алдым, бағасы 500 $.")
# [('Мен ', CYRILLIC), ('iPhone ', LATIN), ('сатып алдым, бағасы 500 $.', CYRILLIC)]
detect_script_segments("«Salom» — dedi u.")
# [('Salom» — dedi u.', LATIN)]   the leading « is not in any segment
Neither function gives character offsets, and leading neutral characters can be dropped, so the segments are not a complete map of the input. Do not reconstruct the original by joining them; retain the original and track offsets, including neutral characters, if annotations must be mapped back. iPhone is genuine Latin text in a Cyrillic sentence and must not be “repaired”.
Look-alike letters inside a Cyrillic word are a different case. The function below only suggests a repair, and only when the repaired form is a known word; it never edits a document:
import unicodedata

_LATIN_TO_CYRILLIC = {"a": "а", "e": "е", "o": "о", "p": "р", "c": "с",
                      "x": "х", "y": "у", "i": "і", "h": "һ", "ə": "ә"}
_LATIN_TO_CYRILLIC.update({k.upper(): v.upper() for k, v in list(_LATIN_TO_CYRILLIC.items())})

def is_cyrillic(ch: str) -> bool:
    return "CYRILLIC" in unicodedata.name(ch, "")

def suggest_cyrillic_token(token: str, trusted_forms: set[str]) -> str | None:
    """Suggest a repair for a mixed-script token; never edits a document."""
    token = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", token)
    if not token or not all(ch.isalpha() for ch in token):
        return None                                   # URLs, numbers, punctuation
    if not any(is_cyrillic(ch) for ch in token):
        return None                                   # all-Latin: a name, a loanword, English
    if any(not is_cyrillic(ch) and ch not in _LATIN_TO_CYRILLIC for ch in token):
        return None                                   # a Latin letter without a look-alike
    candidate = "".join(_LATIN_TO_CYRILLIC.get(ch, ch) for ch in token)
    if candidate == token:
        return None                                   # nothing to repair
    return candidate if candidate in trusted_forms else None

trusted = {"Алматы", "Қара"}                          # e.g. from a lexicon or the analyser
assert suggest_cyrillic_token("Aлматы", trusted) == "Алматы"   # Latin A at the start
assert suggest_cyrillic_token("Қapa", trusted) == "Қара"       # two Latin letters in a row
assert suggest_cyrillic_token("Алматы", trusted) is None       # already clean
assert suggest_cyrillic_token("web", trusted) is None          # genuine Latin word
assert suggest_cyrillic_token("https://example.org", trusted) is None
assert suggest_cyrillic_token("Қapa", set()) is None           # unknown form: no suggestion
The small confusable table proposes candidates for review. A known word can still be wrong in context, and an absent lexicon entry leaves the repair unsupported. Store each candidate’s offsets, replacement and acceptance decision. Apply accepted edits in a new view with a span map, so annotations such as NER spans can be traced back to the original.






Tip



Practice note. Synthetic pairs made by removing diacritics from clean text can train a restoration model. Test on real informal text as well: artificial corruption does not capture every typing error. Apply language-specific repair only after identifying the language.

section: 3.6 A Common Script as an Interoperability Layer
text:
3.6 A Common Script as an Interoperability Layer

3.6.1 The Common Turkic Alphabet
The Common Turkic Alphabet began as a 34-letter Latin proposal from a 1991 symposium in Istanbul (Devlet 1992; AKIpress 2024). In 2024 the Turkic World Common Alphabet Commission agreed on a revised version. Its declaration presents recommendations to member states rather than a binding orthography (Turkic World Common Alphabet Commission 2024).
The toolkit implements its own common-script representation, called CTS in this book. The local source snapshot reports version 0.5.0 and supplies CTS-target mappings for 23 languages (Hakimov 2026). Table 3.4 lists the case pairs and code points. The accompanying snapshot also records the full source hash and mapping tables, since local changes can leave the package version unchanged. Keep this implementation distinct from both alphabet proposals.

The implementation uses ä (U+00E4), not Azerbaijani ə (U+0259), and ñ (U+00F1), not ŋ (U+014B). It distinguishes dotless ı (U+0131) and dotted i (U+0069), with capitals I and İ (U+0130). Uyghur additionally uses é (U+00E9) to distinguish its closed vowel from e. Kazakh ұ maps to CTS u, while the national-2021 conversion uses ū; CTS also maps Kazakh у to u, so this conversion is lossy. These choices describe the toolkit’s implemented mapping; whether it conforms exactly to the 2024 commission’s recommendation has not been checked. Unsupported input is copied by the converter, so arbitrary output need not contain only letters from this alphabet.
The mapping gives some corresponding letters a shared representation: Kazakh Қазақстан becomes Qazaqstan, Azerbaijani Azərbaycan becomes Azärbaycan, Turkmen baý becomes bay. This works only as far as the source spelling goes: phoneme inventories differ across the family, and a distinction a national orthography does not write (Kazakh rounding harmony, Section 2.2) is not recovered by conversion.
from turkicnlp.scripts import Script
from turkicnlp.scripts.transliterator import Transliterator

Transliterator("kaz", Script.CYRILLIC, Script.COMMON_TURKIC).transliterate("Қазақстан")
# 'Qazaqstan'
Transliterator("aze", Script.LATIN, Script.COMMON_TURKIC).transliterate("Azərbaycan dili")
# 'Azärbaycan dili'
Transliterator("tuk", Script.LATIN, Script.COMMON_TURKIC).transliterate("Türkmen dili baýdyr")
# 'Türkmen dili baydır'
For the recurring sentences (Table 1.4), TurkicNLP 0.5.0 gives these CTS views:
kaz  Qazaqstan osı öñirdegi beybitşilikti qoldaydı.
kir  Menin maşinam bar.
uzb  Toşkentda dzyudo böyiça Gran-pri musobaqasi bölib ötmoqda.
uig  u şeher sirtidiki bir at harvisini köridu.
Two details matter for a pipeline. Only the Uyghur conversion has a reverse table in this version: CTS→Perso-Arabic restores the original exactly, while the Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Uzbek CTS views cannot be converted back with the toolkit, so the original must be stored. CTS is also not the treebank’s own romanisation: Uyghur-UDT transliterates the same sentence as u sheher sirtidiki bir at harwisini köridu (ULY), with sh and w where CTS has ş and v.
CTS gives models and string-matching tools a common written input. Keep the original orthography, store CTS as a derived view and make conversion an explicit option. Community decisions about writing systems belong to speakers (Section 17.4).


3.6.2 How Script Conversion Changes Tokenisation Cost
Chapter 7 shows that multilingual LLM tokenisers need far more tokens per word for some Turkic languages than for others. Is that because of morphology? On a parallel sample, Turkish needs 1.95–2.33 tokens per word across four tokenisers while Uyghur needs 3.38–6.85. Latin-script languages with few resources, such as Crimean Tatar and Gagauz, are as cheap as Turkish; the expensive languages are those written in Cyrillic or Arabic script (Hakimov 2026).
Converting the same sentences to CTS lets us compare their tokenisation cost under two written representations (Table 3.5). Conversion may lose distinctions: Kazakh у and ұ, for example, both become u. The comparison therefore says nothing by itself about meaning preservation.
Fertility is the total token count divided by the number of Unicode alphanumeric runs. Python’s re.findall(r"[^\W_]+", text) extracts those runs from the concatenated sample, excluding underscores. Each run is tokenised separately, without special tokens. The word count is recomputed after conversion and may change if separators change; averages are macro-averages over languages.
Across the 13 Cyrillic- and Arabic-script languages, fertility drops by 22–41%, depending on the tokeniser. The gap between Latin-script and non-Latin-script languages falls from 0.62–1.70 to at most 0.03 tokens per word. CTS has roughly the compactness of the national Latin orthographies. Under Qwen3.5 it uses fewer tokens than the 2021 Kazakh Latin alphabet (2.28 vs. 2.48 per word), but slightly more than Uzbek Latin (2.30 vs. 2.12).

The frozen full-precision results and a copy of the experiment method are stored beside the table. The historical run does not record tokeniser commit hashes or the mapping revision used at execution time, so these assets reproduce the reported table, not a byte-exact rerun of tokenisation. The measured OpenAI encoding is o200k_base; the table names the encoding directly.
A common script can also expose cognates to string-based methods. Here, overlap is computed on each language’s concatenated sample: regex-extracted words are lowercased with ordinary Python str.lower() and joined with spaces; the character-trigram Dice score uses sets of trigrams, including those crossing word boundaries. Word overlap is Jaccard similarity of lowercased word sets. Cross-script summaries average unordered language pairs, not aligned sentence-level scores. For language pairs written in different national scripts, character-trigram overlap on the parallel sentences rises from 0 to 0.30 on average after conversion to CTS (Turkish–Kumyk: 0.42), and word-type overlap more than doubles (Hakimov 2026).






Figure 3.3: Character-trigram overlap (Dice coefficient) between each Turkic language and Turkish on parallel sentences, in the native script and after conversion to CTS. Every Cyrillic- and Arabic-script language starts at zero. Data: figures/fig-cts-overlap/data.csv, from Hakimov (2026).



Figure 3.3 shows written overlap after conversion. Gagauz has the highest overlap with Turkish (0.77), followed by Crimean Tatar (0.54) and Azerbaijani (0.46); Chuvash is lowest (0.13). This ordering is not a genealogy: the sample, shared vocabulary and conversion conventions all affect it.
The sample contains only 20 sentences per language. What it shows is a change in token cost for the tested mappings and tokenisers. Separating the causal contributions of script and morphology would need a different design. Lower fertility also need not improve task accuracy: a model trained on native orthographies may handle CTS poorly.
To test CTS for a new model, train native-script and converted conditions with matched data and splits. Keep all versions of a document in the same split, and report task quality alongside token cost (Chapter 7 and Chapter 16).

title: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering
text:
3.7 Language Identification and Corpus Construction

3.7.1 Why Identification Is Hard Inside the Family
Language identification is difficult when neighbouring languages share function words, suffixes and scripts. TurkicNLP wraps GlotLID (Kargaran et al. 2023), which has more than 2,000 labels. By default, LanguageDetection() restricts predictions to the toolkit’s Turkic labels and renormalises their scores. Russian text, English text and boilerplate must then receive a Turkic label too. The score expresses a preference within that restricted set. Use it only for input already known to be Turkic; for a web crawl, start with the unrestricted model:
# pip install "turkicnlp[lid]==0.5.0"   # GlotLID needs the lid extra (fastText + Hub download)
import turkicnlp
from turkicnlp.scripts.detector import detect_script

lid = turkicnlp.LanguageDetection()            # restricted to Turkic labels
text = "salam, hemmelere!"

def identify_with_abstention(text, lid, *, min_full_score, min_margin):
    """Thresholds must be calibrated on labelled target-domain text."""
    full_labels, full_probs = lid.model.predict(text.replace("\n", " "), k=3)
    supported = set(lid.available_labels())
    accepted = (len(full_labels) >= 2
                and full_labels[0] in supported
                and float(full_probs[0]) >= min_full_score
                and float(full_probs[0] - full_probs[1]) >= min_margin)
    if not accepted:
        return {"language": None, "full_labels": full_labels, "full_scores": full_probs}
    labels, probs = lid.predict(text, k=3)
    return {"language": labels[0], "labels": labels, "restricted_scores": probs,
            "full_labels": full_labels, "full_scores": full_probs}

# Inspect the unrestricted candidates before choosing thresholds.
# Invoke the function only with thresholds selected on held-out calibration data.
print(lid.model.predict(text.replace("\n", " "), k=3))

# Alternatively, keep the contact languages in the restricted label set,
# so that Russian or Persian text is not forced into a Turkic label:
lid_contact = turkicnlp.LanguageDetection(
    languages=lid.available_labels() + ["__label__rus_Cyrl", "__label__pes_Arab"])
On the sentences of the parallel UD Turkic test treebanks, GlotLID restricted to Turkic labels is correct for 85.7% of sentences; on the short parallel challenge sentences it reaches only 69.2% (Hakimov 2026). The two figures come from test sets with different language compositions and sentence lengths, so they should not be read as a difference between “natural” and “artificial” text. Per-language results for the challenge sample appear in Figure 3.4. The errors are systematic: smaller languages are absorbed by a close neighbour written in the same script (Figure 3.4, Table 3.6).

Kazakh (9/20)
35%


Kumyk
Karachay-Balkar (7/20)
25%






Three practical lessons follow:

Identify before you transliterate. On text that has been converted to another script, accuracy drops to 48.1% (Hakimov 2026). Conversion changes the native-script letter sequences used by the identifier. This result does not isolate which individual cues caused the drop.
Restrict the label space only for text known to be Turkic. On the Turkic test sets, restricting GlotLID to Turkic labels gave small gains (+0.6 to +2.0 points) (Hakimov 2026), because it removes confusions with unrelated languages written in the same script. On a web crawl the same restriction mislabels every non-Turkic document. Establish the family first, keep the top-k candidates, allow abstention, and calibrate thresholds on labelled target-domain text that includes Russian and English distractors, short strings, names, boilerplate and code-switching.
Do not trust language labels in web corpora for the small languages. Large multilingual web corpora assign languages with identifiers of this kind, so a subset may contain another language, while genuine target-language text may be assigned elsewhere. These error rates require a corpus audit; the challenge set does not measure them. Inspect samples, and for the smaller languages prefer sources with language evidence at the document level (checked news articles, Wikipedia pages or digitised books); a national website may also publish in Russian or other languages.



3.7.2 From Single Texts to Corpora
These lessons apply to every document that enters a corpus. Section 4.3 turns them into an ordered pipeline for building a corpus: provenance, NFC, language identification before transliteration, script and orthography metadata, quality filtering, deduplication across scripts, and conversion only in a derived copy.

title: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering
text:
3.8 Hands-On: Checking a Text Pipeline
Question. Which text changes are justified, and what information do they lose?
Inputs. The Unicode and conversion examples above, with the declared toolkit mappings.
Compute. CPU; some exercises download language-identification models or task data.
Output. Original and derived strings, conversion failures and language-ID decisions.
Interpretation. Round trips and downstream scores answer different questions, so inspect each on its own.
Worked step. Replace the first Cyrillic а (U+0430) in the recurring Kazakh sentence (Table 1.4) with a Latin a (U+0061), a common copy-and-paste corruption, and run the checks (output abridged):
clean      NFC unchanged: True; Latin letters: none
           detect_script: Cyrl
           CTS: Qazaqstan osı öñirdegi beybitşilikti qoldaydı.
corrupted  NFC unchanged: True; Latin letters: ['a U+0061']
           detect_script: Cyrl
           segments: [('Қ', Cyrl), ('a', Latn), ('зақстан осы өңірдегі бейбітшілікті қолдайды.', Cyrl)]
           CTS: Qazaqstan osı öñirdegi beybitşilikti qoldaydı.
strings equal: False | CTS views equal: True
NFC normalisation and whole-text script detection both miss the corruption; only the per-segment check finds it. The CTS view hides it entirely, because Latin a and Cyrillic а map to the same letter. Run homoglyph checks on the original text, before any conversion, and keep the original.
Status: demonstration. The checks above are recorded output. Exercises 1–5 work through text handling; Exercises 6, 8 and 9 extend the comparison to language identification and tagging.
crumbs: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering

title: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering
text:
What to Take Forward
A reliable text pipeline keeps the original and records every derived view, with the direction and convention of each conversion. Conversion can reduce token counts: for the 13 Cyrillic- and Arabic-script languages in the TurkicNLP measurements, CTS lowers tokeniser fertility by 22–41% (Hakimov 2026). It can also lose information, which is why round trips and downstream scores are checked separately. Convert only when the task benefits and the loss is recorded, and let the language identifier abstain when it is uncertain. Chapter 4 makes these decisions part of corpus metadata.
crumbs: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering

title: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering
text:
Further Reading

Script history: Johanson (2021, chap. 19) covers the history of Turkic writing systems from Old Turkic runic to the 20th century.
Unicode standard: The Unicode Consortium’s The Unicode Standard (current version) documents all relevant code blocks. Use the Old Turkic code chart for character identities and code points.
Turkish casing: Unicode’s SpecialCasing file lists the language-specific dotted/dotless I mappings for Turkish and Azerbaijani; Çöltekin, Doğruöz, and Çetinoğlu (2023) surveys Turkish NLP resources more generally.
TurkicNLP toolkit: Hakimov (2026) describes the transliteration, script detection, CTS conversion and language identification used in this chapter, with their evaluation.
Language identification: Kargaran et al. (2023) describes GlotLID.
Transliteration for transfer: Muller et al. (2021) show for Uyghur, among other languages, that transliterating an unseen script into Latin helps multilingual models.
Apertium transliteration: Khanna et al. (2021) covers the Apertium approach to script conversion as part of MT pipelines.
crumbs: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering

title: 3  Scripts, Encoding, and Orthographic Engineering
text:
Exercises

Unicode investigation. Run "İstanbul".lower(), "ISPARTA".lower() and turkish_lower_nfc("I\u0307STANBUL") from Section 3.3. Print repr, len and the code points of each result. Explain why the standard str.lower() is incorrect for Turkish, and why the helper normalises to NFC first.
Homoglyph detection. Write a Python function detect_homoglyphs(text) that returns a list of (position, character, codepoint) tuples where the character is a Cyrillic/Latin homoglyph (use the table in Section 3.3). Test it on a string that mixes Cyrillic а (U+0430) and Latin a (U+0061).
Transliteration by hand. Using the toolkit’s Kazakh mapping (based on the 2021 proposal; print the table from Transliterator("kaz", Script.CYRILLIC, Script.LATIN)), convert Алматы, Қазақстан, Астана and киім (‘clothes’) by hand, then check your answers with the toolkit. Identify one mapping whose reverse is ambiguous and explain what additional information would be needed to convert back. Why does implementing a mapping say nothing about its legal status?
Pipeline ordering. You have Kazakh text in Cyrillic and Latin, some of it diacritic-dropped, and a restoration model trained on noisy Cyrillic paired with corrected Cyrillic. Design a pipeline that preserves the original and records the script of each span. Where can that restoration model be applied, and why? How would the design change if the restoration model had been trained on Latin text instead?
Round trips. Take 50 Uzbek sentences in Latin script (for example from FLORES-200, uzn_Latn). Convert them to Cyrillic and back with Transliterator("uzb", …). Which sentences do not survive the round trip unchanged? Classify the differences (apostrophe variants for oʻ/gʻ, the tutuq belgisi, loanwords, capitalisation), and say which ones matter for a corpus.
Identify, then transliterate. Choose 20 Kyrgyz sentences. Run turkicnlp.LanguageDetection() on them as they are, then again after converting them to CTS. How does accuracy change, and which wrong labels appear? Relate the result to Section 3.7.
Script transition implications. In this hypothetical exercise, a researcher has scraped Kazakh web text in which 60% of the documents are in Cyrillic and 40% in Latin (following the 2021 proposal plus informal variants). Describe three specific problems this mixed-script corpus will cause if used without preprocessing, and propose a concrete solution for each. Would your answer change if the 60/40 split counted words instead of documents?
Abstention in language identification. Build a sample of 100 short texts: 60 in Turkic languages, 20 in Russian, 10 in English and 10 mixed Kazakh–Russian. Run LanguageDetection() restricted to Turkic labels and the unrestricted model. For a range of thresholds, report precision for each Turkic language and the share of non-Turkic texts that are accepted. Which threshold and abstention rule would you choose for a crawl, and why?
Does conversion help the task? Choose a task with data in a Cyrillic-script Turkic language (for example POS tagging of Kazakh). Train and evaluate the same model on native-script and CTS versions of the same split. Report task accuracy and tokens per word for both. Is the conversion worth it?

title: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale
text:
4.1 What Exists: Turkic Text in Multilingual Web Corpora
A web-corpus label is an automatic prediction. This chapter shows how to compare corpus releases, check a sample and build a processing pipeline. The first checks are simple: is the text in the intended language, and which script does it use?
The chapter has three parts. The first surveys what the large web corpora contain for each Turkic language and how much (Section 4.1). The second shows how to check those claims by auditing a sample (Section 4.2). The third describes how to build and release a cleaner corpus: the processing pipeline, script choice, parallel data, and licensing (Section 4.3 to Section 4.6).
crumbs: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale

title: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale
text:
4.1.1 Successive web-corpus releases
The collections below draw on multilingual web archives, including Common Crawl. They differ in how they extract text, which language identifier they use, how they filter for quality, and how they remove duplicates:

CC-100 (Conneau et al. 2020) was built to train XLM-R. It includes Turkish, Azerbaijani, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, and Uyghur, but not Tatar, Bashkir, Turkmen, Chuvash, or Sakha.
mC4 (Xue et al. 2021) was built to train mT5. It has five Turkic languages: Turkish, Azerbaijani, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, and Uzbek.
CulturaX (Nguyen et al. 2024) combines and re-cleans mC4 and OSCAR, another Common Crawl corpus. It lists 14 Turkic languages; ten of them have fewer than 250,000 documents, and Tuvan has 23.
MADLAD-400 (Kudugunta et al. 2023) covers more than 400 languages, and its authors audited samples of each language by hand.
HPLT is represented here by three releases: v1.2 (Gibert et al. 2024), v2.0 (Burchell et al. 2025), and v3.0 (HPLT Consortium 2025; Oepen et al. 2026). Each re-extracts text from web archives. The language identifier changed between releases: CLD2 for v1.2, a modified OpenLID (Burchell et al. 2023) for v2.0, and OpenLID-v2 for v3.0.
FineWeb2 (Penedo et al. 2025) adapts its filtering pipeline to each language. Its language identifier, GlotLID (Kargaran et al. 2023), has many more labels than OpenLID, and FineWeb2 provides the language/script subsets listed in the inventory below, several of them in more than one script.



4.1.2 How much text: HPLT v3.0 as a worked example
HPLT v3.0 publishes a machine-readable manifest with the size of every language subset: documents, characters, and tokens under the Gemma 3 tokeniser. Table 4.1 lists the Turkic subsets, and Figure 4.1 shows their sizes on a logarithmic scale.

Three observations follow.
The sizes span more than three orders of magnitude. Turkish has about 1,600 times as many characters as Crimean Tatar and 1,700 times as many as South Azerbaijani. Kazakh has 3% of the Turkish total. Russian, the main contact language of Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Tatar and Bashkir, has about 900 (Kazakh) to 20,000 (Bashkir) times as many characters in the same release.
Count subsets before counting languages. The manifest separates North (azj) and South Azerbaijani (azb) and lists eleven Turkic subsets altogether. A language without its own subset may still have pages in the crawl, assigned another label, filtered out or left unclassified. Define the release-specific mapping from subsets to languages before reporting coverage.
Characters per token vary across the HPLT language subsets. Dividing character totals by Gemma 3 token totals gives 1.80 for Uyghur, 3.42 for Turkish and 4.44 for English (Figure 4.2). This measures text length per token in different corpora; it is not the tokens-per-word fertility measure of Section 7.1 and does not isolate a causal script effect. Corpus composition, orthographic conventions and tokeniser behaviour can all affect the ratio.

Which languages appear depends on the language identifier. Five languages (Turkish, Azerbaijani, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek) are in all eight sources. CC-100 and HPLT v1.2 each have six Turkic languages, mC4 five. FineWeb2, whose identifier has the largest label set, is the only one of these web corpora with Nogai, Kumyk, Khakas, Altai, Gagauz, and Karakalpak. That cleaning stage filters low language-identification probabilities, low Web Docs Scorer values and other signals (Burchell et al. 2025, sec. 4.2).
Most of the apparent decline therefore occurred within v2.0. We have not established which filter removed those documents or what languages they contained. Against cleaned v2.0, every other Turkic subset grows in v3.0. Uzbek rises from 707,000 documents to 1.9 million.

4.1.4 Common Crawl itself
Common Crawl publishes, for every snapshot, the number of pages per primary language as detected by CLD2. Figure 4.4 shows the Turkic shares in all 77 snapshots from August 2018 to September 2026.






Figure 4.4: Share of pages per Turkic language in each Common Crawl snapshot (CLD2 primary language, log scale). In the legend: the share in the latest snapshot, CC-MAIN-2026-39. Source: Common Crawl crawl statistics (plots/languages.csv), accessed 12 October 2026.



Turkish makes up 1.28% of the pages in the latest snapshot. Every other Turkic language is below 0.1%: Azerbaijani 0.061%, Kazakh 0.043%, Uzbek 0.031%, and Uyghur 0.0016%. Russian, for comparison, has 6.7%. Between the first and the latest snapshot, the reported shares of Kazakh, Uzbek, and Kyrgyz roughly tripled, while Turkish grew by about half. The statistics report only nine Turkic CLD2 labels, so the rest of the family is invisible in them: those pages are counted under other labels or as unknown.


4.1.5 National and curated corpora
Web corpora are not the only source. Several Turkic languages have national reference corpora, built by language institutes with documented sources and annotation. The Turkish National Corpus is one example (Aksan et al. 2012). Wikipedia is another candidate source: its provenance is known, but language and quality still require checking, and its article counts (Table 4.2) do not measure running text.

title: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale
section: 4.2 What the Labels Hide: Auditing a Corpus
text:
4.2 What the Labels Hide: Auditing a Corpus

4.2.1 Why labels fail for Turkic languages
A language label in a web corpus is the output of an automatic classifier applied to each document. Kreutzer et al. (2022) audited samples of several multilingual corpora by hand and found that, for many low-resource languages, a large share of the text was in the wrong language or was not language at all. For Turkic languages, seven sources of error need checking:

A close neighbour gets the label. Shared spellings can make related languages hard to distinguish. On a 20-sentence challenge set, GlotLID restricted to Turkic labels assigned Turkish to 18 of 20 Gagauz sentences; its most frequent wrong label was Karachay-Balkar for Kumyk and Kyrgyz for Nogai, Altai, and Tuvan (Table 3.6, Figure 3.4).
Russian inside Cyrillic pages. Pages from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tatarstan, Bashkortostan, and Sakha can mix Russian and the Turkic language: bilingual navigation, comments, and quotations. A script detector sees only Cyrillic. Only a word- or sentence-level language check finds the Russian.
Several scripts and orthographies for one language. Uzbek is written in Latin and Cyrillic; Kazakh in Cyrillic and in Latin text that may follow different proposals or informal conventions; Uyghur in Arabic script, Latin, and Cyrillic; Azerbaijani in Latin and, in Iran, Arabic script (Section 3.2). A corpus may keep only one script, mix them silently, or split them into separate subsets.
Lookalike letters. Special letters such as Kazakh ә ғ қ ң ө ұ ү һ і or Bashkir ҙ ҫ can be replaced in web text by Latin lookalikes or other substitutes (Section 3.3).
Informal Latin typing. Text in a Cyrillic-script Turkic language may be typed in an ad hoc Latin transcription, and Turkish may be typed without its special letters.
Machine-translated and automatically generated text. Machine-translated pages and automatically generated articles can enter web subsets and Wikipedias. Their share in Turkic corpora has not been measured here.
Arabic-script confusion. South Azerbaijani, Uyghur, Persian, and Ottoman Turkish share a script.



4.2.2 A Method for Auditing
Define the sampling unit (document), corpus revision, subset and complete population before sampling. Keep original IDs and raw text. A document sample estimates document shares, not token shares. Human labels from qualified evaluators are the reference; automatic scores are screening signals.
The functions in corpus.py report script shares over letters, sentence-level target/Russian/other shares, and raw FST coverage over alphabetic word tokens. Empty denominators return None. A recognised word needs a finite, non-failure FST reading. A copied surface form, truthy lemma or nonempty UD field is insufficient. The helper also excludes <unk> guesses, such as the Bashkir analyser’s Weezy<np><unk>. These choices define lookup coverage; analysis accuracy and language labels still need independent reference data.
Construct the tokeniser, sentence splitter, unrestricted language identifier and target-language FST once and reuse them. Pass the exact expected label (for example __label__kir_Cyrl) rather than a prefix test. Rebuild all language-dependent objects when changing language; changing only a global LANG leaves the old analyser active. Newlines are not automatically sentence boundaries.
from corpus import audit  # code/ch04-corpus on PYTHONPATH

def audit_document(row, splitter, tokenize, lid_model, fst_lookup, target_label):
    return {"id": row["id"], **audit(
        row["text"], splitter(row["text"]), target_label,
        predict_all=lambda s: lid_model.predict(s, k=1)[0][0],
        lookup=fst_lookup, words=tokenize(row["text"]))}
lid_model here is the underlying unrestricted model, not a Turkic-only candidate wrapper. Otherwise Russian text is forced into a Turkic label and a target-share estimate becomes misleading. Save model/transducer revisions, segmentation policy, raw labels and denominators in the audit manifest. Compare signals on separately labelled development and test samples before choosing thresholds.


4.2.3 HPLT’s quality bins
HPLT v3.0 sorts the documents of each language into Web Docs Scorer quality bins; the release contains bins 5 to 10, with higher bins for higher scores (Oepen et al. 2026). Figure 4.5 shows how the data of each Turkic subset is distributed across the bins.






Figure 4.5: Share of each Turkic subset of HPLT v3.0 (compressed bytes) per Web Docs Scorer quality bin, from 5 (lowest in the release) to 10 (highest).



Nine of the eleven subsets place 56–72% of their compressed bytes in bins 8–10. South Azerbaijani has 48%. Uyghur has just 1%, with almost all its data in bins 5–7. Several explanations remain possible: scorer calibration on Arabic-script text, domain composition or extraction quality. If calibration is responsible, a strict threshold could discard useful Uyghur text. If the subset is noisier, more cleaning may help. Inspect samples to distinguish these cases. Compression ratios vary too, so the byte shares cannot be read as document or token shares.

title: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale
text:
4.3 A Pipeline for Turkic Text

4.3.1 Order matters
The steps of a corpus pipeline interact. The following order avoids most of the problems discussed here and in Chapter 3:

Collect from sources whose language and orthography are documented, and keep the URL, date, licence or terms, and the original bytes.
Decode and normalise to a known encoding and create an NFC copy, with selective NFKC for Arabic presentation-form characters (Section 3.3). Keep the raw text; delay language-specific repairs (lookalike letters, apostrophes) until step 4.
Identify the language before any transliteration, at sentence or document level. An unrestricted model can predict Russian or English; it may still assign noise a language label. Add an explicit rejection policy and use a Turkic-only label set only for text already established as Turkic (Section 3.7). Record candidates and scores, and route uncertain text to an “unknown” bin. Conversion changes native-script cues: on converted text, GlotLID accuracy fell to 48.1% in the TurkicNLP evaluation (Hakimov 2026).
Detect the script per document and per span, and record the orthography version as metadata (for example Kazakh Cyrillic, 2018 Latin or 2021 Latin; Uzbek Cyrillic or Latin) rather than silently converting (Section 4.4).
Handle mixed-language segments and boilerplate under the collection’s declared inclusion policy; Russian quotations are not automatically corrupt text.
Filter for quality, with thresholds set per language (below).
Deduplicate with a derived key that unifies apostrophe variants and, where needed, converts to one script, so that the same text in two variants counts once (below). Make the train/dev/test split at the level of duplicate clusters or sources, before creating script variants, so that a native and a converted copy cannot end up on opposite sides of the split.
Normalise orthography and convert scripts in a derived copy only: the Turkish İ/ı casing rules, the Uzbek apostrophe variants for oʻ, gʻ and the tutuq belgisi, and optionally conversion to a common script (Section 3.5). The archival copy keeps the original.
Document permissions and personal data: record the licence or terms of each source, and remove or mask personal data before releasing a derived corpus (Section 4.6).



4.3.2 Adapting English-Derived Quality Filters
Some web-corpus filters use word length, common words, repetition and symbol counts. The Gopher rules (Rae et al. 2021), as implemented in datatrove, include a mean word length of 3–10 characters and at least two words from an eight-word English list. These defaults need checking before use on Turkic text. FineWeb2 estimates language-specific thresholds (Penedo et al. 2025).
The aligned FLORES measurement below compares word lengths without mixing release and development treebanks. How many web documents a filter would reject is another matter. In particular, a rule requiring English stop words can reject valid Turkic text. FineWeb2 instead estimates thresholds and word lists per language (Table 4.4).
Some estimated stop-word lists suggest which domains to inspect. Among the first eight entries for Cyrillic Azerbaijani, Cyrillic Gagauz and Khakas are јеһова ‘Jehovah’, иисус ‘Jesus’ or худай ‘God’; Cyrillic Crimean Tatar includes рабби ‘Lord’. Kazakh, Bashkir and Chuvash lists contain words for ‘water’ and ‘river’ (су, өзен; һыу, йылға; шыв, юханшыв, respectively). They tell you where to sample; they say nothing about how large each domain is. FineWeb2 derived the lists from its own data; this chapter supplies no independent audit.



Table 4.4: Quality-filter thresholds that FineWeb2 estimated for the primary Turkic subsets, against the English defaults of the same datatrove filters. Avg word length: allowed range of a document’s mean word length; alpha words: minimum share of words containing a letter (called max_non_alpha_words_ratio in datatrove); line punct.: minimum share of lines ending in punctuation (off = disabled; a threshold of 0.0 has the same effect); dup. lines: maximum share of duplicated lines; top 2-gram: maximum share of characters in the most frequent word bigram (values above 1 disable the rule); LID score: minimum language-ID confidence; stop words: size of the list (a document needs at least 2 of them). Sources: github.com/huggingface/fineweb-2 configs/*.yml and datatrove filter defaults (main branch), accessed 12 October 2026.

4.3.3 A source-aligned orthographic-length check
A complementary measurement uses all 1,012 aligned rows of original FLORES-200 devtest in eleven Turkic varieties, English and Russian (NLLB Team et al. 2024). The count covers Unicode letters in each whitespace-delimited unit containing at least one letter, after NFC normalisation. It averages units within each sentence and then weights sentences equally. This definition excludes punctuation from the length count; it does not segment morphemes.






Figure 4.6: Measured difference from English in mean letters per orthographic unit on original FLORES-200 devtest. Bars use the same 1,012 aligned sentence rows in each variety. Intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 2,000 paired sentence bootstrap samples (seed 20261017); English is the zero reference.



Spacing anomalies dominate the South Azerbaijani bar: 83 of 1,012 rows contain only one whitespace unit, and 128 average more than 30 letters per unit (audit_spacing.py). Row 198, for example, has 227 letters without an internal space. The audit retains and lists these rows. The bar thus shows how formatting affects the measurement; it cannot serve as a language-level word-length estimate.
Matching the translated source rows removes one source of content variation, but translations and orthographic conventions still differ. The intervals describe resampling these sentences, not uncertainty over the population of web documents; source-article clustering is not modelled. The saved results also include a contiguous-letter-run definition for sensitivity checking. Neither definition measures morphological complexity, and neither validates a quality filter. That requires independently labelled documents.


4.3.4 Deduplication across scripts
Character-overlap methods can miss duplicates published in different scripts. An Uzbek story in Latin and Cyrillic may share little written text even when the content is the same. After both versions are converted to one script, the overlap can be measured. The same holds for Kazakh text in Cyrillic and in one of the Latin designs. Figure 3.3 showed the effect of conversion for related languages; its effect on duplicate detection for the same language in two scripts can be measured on labelled document pairs.
After a versioned script conversion, a deduplication key can normalise Uzbek o/g letter marks with uzbek_letter_apostrophes in corpus.py. The helper maps apostrophe variants after o or g to U+02BB, while TurkicNLP uses U+0027 (Section 3.5). Either convention can work if applied consistently. Keep tutuq signs and quotation punctuation distinct.
MinHash requires further choices: character shingles, hash count and similarity threshold, tuned on labelled pairs. Since conversion can merge different originals, treat key matches as candidates and measure false merges. Build duplicate/source clusters before assigning train/dev/test splits.


4.3.5 Personal data
Web text contains names, phone numbers, addresses, and identity numbers. Turkic-specific patterns include national identification numbers with fixed formats, such as the Turkish T.C. kimlik numarası and the Kazakh individual identification number (IIN). Remove or mask these before releasing any derived corpus.

title: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale
section: 4.4 Choosing a Script for the Corpus
text:
4.4 Choosing a Script for the Corpus
For a language written in more than one script, the corpus builder has to decide what to store and what to release. Three rules work well:

Keep the original. Store every document in the script it was published in, with the detected script and orthography version as metadata. Conversion can lose information: in the toolkit’s CTS mapping, for example, Kazakh у and ұ both become u (Section 3.6), so the original cannot always be recovered from the converted text.
Release conversions as derived data. A version in a common script, such as the toolkit’s CTS mapping (Section 3.6) or an official Latin alphabet, is useful for training. Release it next to the original, not instead of it.
Say what was merged. If Uzbek Latin and Cyrillic are merged into one training set, or Kazakh text in several Latin designs is normalised to the 2021 design, document the conversion and the mapping version.
crumbs: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale

title: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale
text:
4.5 Parallel and Comparable Data
Parallel text expresses corresponding content in two languages. It provides supervision for machine translation (Chapter 10) and cross-lingual sentence embeddings (Section 13.3), though both also have methods that learn without sentence-aligned data. For Turkic languages, useful sources include:

Curated collections: OPUS (Tiedemann 2012), the TIL corpus with its X-WMT test sets (Mirzakhalov et al. 2021), and FLORES-200 (NLLB Team et al. 2024).
Bilingual institutional websites: governments and news agencies that publish in a Turkic language and in Russian or English.
Religious texts: translated texts are one possible source; FineWeb2’s word lists suggest checking for them in some subsets (Table 4.4). Check their licences before including them.
Comparable text, such as Wikipedia articles on the same topic, from which parallel sentences can be mined.

Mining parallel sentences usually relies on multilingual sentence embeddings such as LaBSE or LASER (Feng et al. 2022; Heffernan, Çelebi, and Schwenk 2022), scored with a margin criterion (Artetxe and Schwenk 2019). For very close pairs, such as Turkish–Gagauz or Kazakh–Kyrgyz, string similarity after conversion to a common script (Figure 3.3) is a candidate retrieval signal or extra filter; its precision has to be checked by hand (Exercise 3).
crumbs: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale

title: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale
text:
4.6 Licensing, Provenance, and Sovereignty
Check the terms for both the corpus release and its source material. A licence on the compilation may not cover redistribution of every source page.

Prefer releasing IDs and labels. When an audit or a filtered subset is shared, consider sharing document identifiers, scores and labels when the text cannot be redistributed. It does not remove rights or privacy obligations.
Check religious and literary texts individually. A text that is free to read online may come with terms that forbid text and data mining or redistribution.
National law differs. Copyright exceptions for text and data mining differ between the countries where Turkic languages are spoken.
Document the corpus. A datasheet records sources, collection dates, filters, known problems, and intended uses. For a small language, record the community’s position on its use as well (Section 17.4).

title: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale
text:
4.7 Hands-On: Auditing a Corpus Sample
Question. What kinds of unwanted text do the audit signals detect?
Inputs. A documented sample, unrestricted language identification, script checks and an analyser.
Compute. CPU inference and resource downloads; size the sample before processing a full corpus.
Output. Per-document signals, reviewed errors and a provenance manifest.
Interpretation. Calibrate decisions against reviewed documents before selecting thresholds.
Worked step. Exercise 1 first runs the audit on documents of known composition: five-sentence X-WMT documents in Kyrgyz, in its neighbour Kazakh, in Russian, mixed (three Kyrgyz and two Russian sentences), and Kyrgyz converted to CTS, 20 of each. The recorded output uses GlotLID v3 and the Apertium Kyrgyz analyser; the illustrative “kept” rule requires a target share and an analyser coverage of at least 0.6.
document type           target  Russian  FST cov.  Cyrillic   kept
target                    1.00     0.00      0.83      0.98  20/20
neighbour                 0.00     0.00      0.28      0.97   0/20
Russian                   0.00     1.00      0.09      0.97   0/20
target 3 + Russian 2      0.60     0.40      0.52      0.97   4/20
target in CTS             0.00     0.00      0.00      0.00   0/20
Language identification separates whole documents cleanly, and analyser coverage agrees with it. Mixed documents are the hard case: the rule keeps only 4 of 20, although 60% of their sentences are Kyrgyz. Kyrgyz in CTS is lost entirely: GlotLID labels it mostly as Turkish or Gagauz, and the Cyrillic analyser rejects it. Audit before converting. These are constructed documents; a real corpus needs a hand-labelled sample to set thresholds.
Status: demonstration. The table is recorded output of Exercise 1 on constructed documents; an audit of a real web corpus is a procedure to run on its own sample.

title: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale
text:
What to Take Forward
Start an audit from the corpus label, then inspect what it contains. The Uzbek counts in Section 4.1 show how widely collections can differ. Sample documents for the intended task, preserve their provenance through processing, and check permissions before release. Chapter 5 introduces the word analyses used in later text-processing methods.

title: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale
text:
Further Reading

Kreutzer et al. (2022) is the reference audit of multilingual web corpora and the model for Section 4.2.
The corpus papers describe their pipelines and language identifiers: CC-100 (Conneau et al. 2020), mC4 (Xue et al. 2021), CulturaX (Nguyen et al. 2024), MADLAD-400 (Kudugunta et al. 2023), HPLT (Gibert et al. 2024; Burchell et al. 2025; Oepen et al. 2026), and FineWeb2 (Penedo et al. 2025).
GlotLID (Kargaran et al. 2023) and OpenLID (Burchell et al. 2023) are used by the corpora discussed here.
Glot500 (Imani et al. 2023) built a corpus and a model for more than 500 languages; its language list shows which smaller Turkic languages it covers.
crumbs: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale

title: 4  Building Turkic Corpora at Scale
text:
Exercises

Audit another language. Use the method in Section 4.2 to audit samples for two Turkic languages in the same corpus. Which contamination type dominates in each, and how do they compare?
Lookalike letters. For Kazakh or Bashkir, count the tokens in a corpus sample that mix Latin and Cyrillic letters. Build a repair table for the 20 most frequent substitutions, and measure how much the repair raises analyser coverage.
Mining with a shared script. Mine Kazakh–Kyrgyz sentence pairs from comparable Wikipedia articles in two ways: character overlap after conversion to CTS, and LaBSE similarity. Check 100 pairs from each method by hand. Which is more precise, and where does each fail?
Absent languages. Choose one language that is absent from HPLT v3.0 (Table 4.1). Find three web sources for it, estimate how much text they hold, and run GlotLID on a sample. Under which labels would this text end up in a web corpus?
