title: 5  Morphological Structure: A Linguistic Foundation
text:
5.1 The Morpheme Inventory
Morphological analysis identifies the stem and grammatical information in a word. Turkish okuyamıyor, for example, expresses reading, inability and progressive aspect. An NLP system may model this structure explicitly or learn it from data. This chapter explains suffix ordering, alternations and ambiguity; the next two chapters show computational methods.
The basic definitions of agglutination, case and harmony are in Chapter 2. Here we use them to read complete analyses, compare suffix sequences and resolve ambiguity.
crumbs: 5  Morphological Structure: A Linguistic Foundation

title: 5  Morphological Structure: A Linguistic Foundation
text:
5.1.1 Derivational vs. Inflectional Morphology
A useful starting distinction is between derivation and inflection.
Derivational morphemes change the lexical category or meaning of the base. They create a new word, often with a new part of speech. Examples from Turkish:



Table 5.1: Selected derivational suffixes in Turkish











Input
Suffix
Output
Function




ev (house, N)
-li
evli (married, Adj)
denominal adjective


yaz- (write, V)
-ı
yazı (writing, N)
deverbal noun


güzel (beautiful, Adj)
-leş-
güzelleş- (become beautiful, V)
deadjectival verb


git- (go, V)
-mek
gitmek (to go, V→infinitive)
infinitive nominalisation






In the simple pattern illustrated here, derivational morphemes precede the outer inflection and can be stacked: güzelleştir- (to make beautiful) adds a causative to the deadjectival verb. The resulting derived stem behaves as a new root for subsequent affixation.
Inflectional morphemes mark grammatical categories such as number, case, tense and agreement. They usually follow derivation in the patterns shown here. The boundary is not absolute: a category change can introduce another inflectional domain, and individual stems or constructions restrict which suffixes can follow.
An analyser often needs lexical entries for derived meanings: composition alone cannot tell it that ev-li means ‘married’. Inflection is more systematic, so rules can generate many forms without listing each one. Grammars and treebanks draw the boundary differently, especially for infinitive -mAk, voice suffixes and copular forms. State which convention the analyser follows.


5.1.2 The Suffix Template
Turkic suffix ordering follows regular patterns. Johanson (2021, 37) notes that the high degree of synthesis “allows combinations of a large number of bound denominal and deverbal markers to form long sequences”. In the common patterns below, derivational material comes before inflectional material, and each suffix applies to the form on its left. For noun inflection, “Common Turkic follows the ordering number-possessive-case”; Chuvash is the exception, with possessive before number (Johanson 2021, 452) (Section 5.4.5).
Nominal template (for nouns and adjectives):
\[\text{Root} \rightarrow [\text{Derivation}]^* \rightarrow \text{Number} \rightarrow \text{Possessive} \rightarrow \text{Case} \rightarrow [\text{Copula}]\]

Derivation (optional, repeatable): changes stem meaning or category
Number (-lar/-ler plural): absence of plural marking need not mean singular reference
Possessive (1sg, 2sg, 3sg, 1pl, 2pl, 3pl): marks possessor agreement
Case (nominative, accusative, dative, locative, ablative, genitive)
Copula (optional): predicative forms -dır/-dir/-dur/-dür or evidential -(y)mış

Example: Turkish ev-ler-imiz-den (from our houses):



Slot
Morpheme
Gloss




Root
ev
house


Number
-ler
PL


Possessive
-imiz
POSS.1PL


Case
-den
ABL



Verbal template (for verbs):
\[\text{Root} \rightarrow [\text{Derivation}]^* \rightarrow \text{Voice} \rightarrow \text{Ability/Negation} \rightarrow \text{TAM} \rightarrow \text{Person/Number}\]

Derivation (optional): lexical derivation such as güzel-leş- ‘become beautiful’
Voice (passive -Il/-In, causative -DIr/-t, reciprocal -Iş, reflexive -In). Some grammars treat voice as derivation, because it changes the valency of the stem; this book lists it as a separate slot. Apertium encodes voice with tags, while UD uses features such as Voice=Cau and Voice=Pass
Potential (-(y)a/-(y)e, the ability marker that precedes negation in gel-e-me- “be unable to come”; the positive -(y)abil/-(y)ebil “can” goes back to the same marker plus the verb bil- “know”)
Negation (-ma/-me)
TAM (tense, aspect, mood: one slot, complex inventory)
Person/Number (agreement with subject: 1sg, 2sg, 3sg, 1pl, 2pl, 3pl; two paradigms, see below)

Read the diagrams as summaries of common sequences. Which suffix can follow depends on the stem, the construction and the morphology already present. TAM may have several exponents (gel-iyor-du ‘was coming’, progressive + past), agreement has several paradigms, and a nominalised verb takes nominal inflection (oku-duk-lar-ı-n-dan). Chapter 6 shows how continuation classes encode the combinations licensed by a language.






Figure 5.1: Common nominal and verbal suffix sequences. Ability and negation interact; nominalised verbs enter nominal inflection. Boxes describe morphological domains, not a requirement for an overt suffix in each position.





5.1.3 Nominal Morphology in Detail
Number. The plural is marked by -lar/-ler (the two forms differ by vowel harmony). The form without a plural suffix is unmarked for number, and its reference can include more than one entity: Turkish Ali gazete okudu can mean that Ali read a newspaper or newspapers (Johanson 2021, 945). In Turkish, a noun after a numeral normally takes no plural suffix: beş kitap (five book), not beş kitaplar. A system that reads plural marking as a count of referents will therefore be wrong in both directions.
Possessive. The Turkish possessive suffixes have different shapes after consonant-final and vowel-final stems. In the abstract notation used here, I stands for the four-way harmonising vowel (ı/i/u/ü) and A for the two-way one (a/e):



Table 5.2: Turkish possessive suffixes after consonant- and vowel-final stems. I = four-way harmony (ı/i/u/ü), A = two-way harmony (a/e). With a plural noun the plural comes first: ev-ler-im ‘my houses’.





Possessor
After a consonant
After a vowel
Examples




1sg
-Im
-m
ev-im, araba-m ‘my house/car’


2sg
-In
-n
ev-in, araba-n


3sg
-I
-sI
ev-i, araba-sı


1pl
-ImIz
-mIz
ev-imiz, araba-mız


2pl
-InIz
-nIz
ev-iniz, araba-nız


3pl
-lArI
-lArI
ev-leri, araba-ları






The third person plural is a source of ambiguity: evleri can be ev-leri ‘their house’ (POSS.3PL) or ev-ler-i ‘his/her houses’ or ‘their houses’ (PL + POSS.3, with a singular or plural possessor), and Turkish does not write a second plural for ‘their houses’. Johanson describes the same three-way reading for the type ‘horse-PL-POSS3’ and notes that a form with two plurals is illicit (2021, 459). A possessive pronoun resolves it for nouns: onların evi only means ‘their house’, and onların evleri only ‘their houses’ (2021, 459). The number of the possessed noun and the number of the possessor cannot be read off as independent slots.
Possessive suffixes come between number and case, and a third-person possessive is followed by a buffer n before a case suffix: araba-sı-n-ı ‘his/her car’ (ACC), araba-sı-n-da ‘in his/her car’. For segment counts, this book attaches the buffer to the following suffix, as in Section 2.7: araba-sı-nı has three counted pieces. A finer notation, araba-sı-n-ı, shows the buffer separately but does not count it as another morpheme.
Case. Six commonly compared cases (not present in every language) are introduced in Chapter 2 (Section 2.3). Their suffixes in Turkish are:








Case
Suffix
Function




Nominative
∅
Subject; predicate nominal


Accusative
-(y)ı/i/u/ü
Specific direct object


Dative
-(y)a/e
Indirect object; goal; experiencer


Locative
-da/de/ta/te
Location; point in time


Ablative
-dan/den/tan/ten
Source; material; comparison


Genitive
-(n)ın/in/un/ün
Possession; complement of some postpositions after pronouns (benim için ‘for me’)



Note the consonant alternation in locative and ablative: -da after voiced consonants and vowels, -ta after voiceless consonants. This is consonant assimilation, discussed in Section 5.2.
Copula. Nominal predicates in Turkic languages can take a copular suffix directly on the noun: Turkish doktor-um (I am a doctor), doktor-sun (you are a doctor), doktor-dur (he/she is a doctor). Third-person present predication can also be unmarked (O doktor, “He/she is a doctor”); -DIr is not an obligatory third-person ending and can add assertive or inferential force. Identifying a nominal predicate therefore requires constructional context (Johanson 2021, chap. 27, pp. 555–571).


5.1.4 Verbal Morphology in Detail
Voice. The following table illustrates an unmarked active stem and four voice-related patterns:



Table 5.3: Turkish verbal voice suffixes (allomorphs vary by phonological context)





Voice
Suffix
Example
Gloss




Active
∅
sev-
love


Passive
-il/-ın
sev-il-
be loved


Reflexive
-In
yıka-n-
wash oneself


Reciprocal
-Iş
gör-üş-
see each other, meet


Causative
-dir/-tir/-ir/-t
sev-dir-
make (s.o.) love






Voice suffixes can be stacked: sev-dir-il- (to be made to love) places passive outside causative, and öl-dür-t- (“have someone killed”) contains successive causatives. No single exhaustive ordering rule follows from such examples. What can come next depends on the stem, valency and construction. This stacking produces the long verb chains discussed in Chapter 2.
Negation. The negation suffix -ma/-me follows voice morphemes and the potential marker and precedes TAM in the ordinary synthetic forms illustrated here: sev-me- (not love), sev-il-me- (not be loved), sev-dir-me- (not cause to love). The template covers verbal -mA- only; other negative constructions work differently. Its surface shape also varies: before progressive -Iyor, its vowel is absent (gel-m-iyor).
Ability and inability. Turkish expresses these meanings with suffixes; other Turkic languages also use auxiliary constructions:

gel-ebil- (to be able to come): the stem gel- + ability suffix -ebil- (historically involving bil- “know”)
gel-e-me- (to be unable to come): the stem gel- + -e- + negative -me-; the segmentation convention distinguishes the ability component from negation

The sequence -(y)eme-/-(y)ama- (potential + negation) is formally distinct from the bare negative -me-/-ma-, so inability and simple negation are not confused: gel-me-di “did not come” vs. gel-e-me-di “could not come”.
Tense, Aspect, and Mood (TAM). TAM occupies a single slot in the verbal template but with a complex inventory. Turkish distinguishes:



Table 5.4: Selected Turkish TAM suffixes. A = a/e, I = ı/i/u/ü, D = d/t according to voicing; (y) appears where required.










Category
Suffix
Meaning




Simple past
-DI
Past; not restricted to witnessed events


Indirective/perfect
-mIş
Inference, report or perfect reading, depending on construction


Aorist
-Ar/-Ir/-r (stem-dependent)
Habitual/generic present


Present progressive
-Iyor (with stem-vowel adjustments)
Ongoing action now


Future
-(y)AcAk
Future tense


Conditional
-sA
Conditional mood


Optative
-(y)A
Wish/exhortation






Kazakh, Kyrgyz, and other Kipchak languages share many of these distinctions but with different suffix shapes, and many Turkic languages express aspect partly through converb + auxiliary constructions with verbs such as ‘lie’ (Kazakh оқып жатыр ‘is reading’, Turkmen okap ýatyr; Johanson (2021), p. 646). Some of these have fused into one word (Uzbek oʻqiyapti ‘is reading’, historically from oʻqi-b yot-). Analysers must treat them as multi-word or grammaticalised forms.
Person/Number agreement. The final slot marks the agreement of the verb with its subject. Turkish has two main agreement paradigms. Suffixes of the “pronominal type” follow the aorist, the progressive, -mIş, the future and the necessitative, and also mark nominal predicates; suffixes of the “possessive type” follow the past -DI and the conditional -sA (Johanson 2021, 439, 555):



Table 5.5: Turkish verbal agreement: the two main paradigms, shown with gel- ‘come’ (Johanson 2021, 439).





Person
After the aorist (gel-ir-)
After the past (gel-di-)




1sg
gelir-im (-(y)Im)
geldi-m (-m)


2sg
gelir-sin (-sIn)
geldi-n (-n)


3sg
gelir (∅)
geldi (∅)


1pl

2pl
gelir-siniz (-sInIz)

3pl

geldi-ler (-lAr)






In the two paradigms shown, third person singular has no overt agreement suffix, a fact with consequences for pro-drop and coreference (see Section 2.4 and Chapter 8).

title: 5  Morphological Structure: A Linguistic Foundation
text:
5.2 Morphophonological Alternations
The same morpheme appears in multiple surface forms depending on phonological context. Three types of alternation are most important for Turkic NLP: vowel harmony in suffixes, consonant assimilation, and stem alternations.

5.2.1 Vowel Harmony in Suffixes
Covered in Section 2.2, the harmonising vowels of Turkish suffixes commonly alternate in two-way or four-way sets. Invariant suffixes and consonantal alternations require separate rules. The pattern is:

2-way suffixes (back vs. front only): e.g., Turkish plural -lar/-ler

kitap-lar (books, back vowel root)
ev-ler (houses, front vowel root)

4-way suffixes (back/front × round/unround): e.g., Turkish 1sg possessive -ım/-im/-um/-üm

kol-um (my arm, back round)
kitab-ım (my book, back unround)
göz-üm (my eye, front round)
ev-im (my house, front unround)


For most stems, native or borrowed, the last vowel of the stem determines the harmony class of the suffix, even when earlier syllables mix classes (kitap-lar, telefon-lar). The exceptions listed in Section 2.2 must be marked in the lexicon: stems whose final consonant selects front suffixes (saat-ler ‘hours’, rol-ü ‘role-ACC’) and suffixes outside the regular pattern (-yor, -ken, and usually -ki). A regular stem and an exceptional one can look alike: saat and sabah both have a back vowel in their final syllable, but only sabah-lar follows the regular rule.
For morphological analysis, harmony is a strong constraint: if an analyser sees evlerde, it can rule out analyses in which the locative should be -da, because ev is a front-vowel root. Rule-based analysers encode the constraint explicitly; neural analysers can learn it from data.


5.2.2 Consonant Alternations
Beyond vowel harmony, consonant alternations are common at morpheme boundaries.
Voicing assimilation. The Turkish past tense suffix is -di/-dı/-du/-dü after voiced consonants and vowels, but -ti/-tı/-tu/-tü after voiceless consonants:



Verb
Past form
Rule




gel- (come)
gel-di
l is voiced → d


git- (go)
git-ti
t is voiceless → t


oku- (read)
oku-du
u is a vowel → d


iç- (drink)
iç-ti
ç is voiceless → t



The same assimilation applies to the locative (-da/-ta), ablative (-dan/-tan), and several other suffixes. For the morphological analyser, this means tracking the voicing of the final consonant of the stem. That information is phonologically transparent in the surface form.
Buffer consonants. Turkish uses y before vowel-initial accusative and dative suffixes after a vowel-final stem. The n following a third-person possessive is a separate pattern: it also occurs before a consonant-initial case suffix, as ev-i-n-de shows:



Form
Analysis




araba-y-ı
car-(y)-ACC ‘the car’ (not araba-ı)


araba-sı-n-ı
car-POSS.3SG-(n)-ACC ‘his/her car’ (object)


ev-i-n-de
house-POSS.3SG-(n)-LOC ‘in his/her house’



Stem-final consonant alternation. Turkish kitap (book) alternates with kitab- before a vowel-initial suffix: kitab-ı (book-ACC). This can be represented with an underlying voiced consonant and a devoicing rule, or with stem allomorphs. It is lexically conditioned; not every stem-final obstruent alternates. The kitap/kitab- alternation must therefore be tracked in the morphological lexicon as a property of the stem.
Other stem patterns. Some stems alternate before suffixes; others remain unchanged:








Root
Suffixed form
Pattern




renk (colour)
renk-li / reng-in
k → g in rengin


yüz (face)
yüzü / yüz-de
no alternation in this root


ağız (mouth)
ağzı
vowel deletion: underlying /ağız/ + ACC → ağz-ı



The vowel deletion in ağız → ağz- is a stem alternation triggered by the attachment of a vowel-initial suffix. An analyser must identify which stems license this alternation; it cannot apply deletion to every matching vowel sequence.


5.2.3 Why Productive Generalisation Matters
The alternations described above mean that the same morpheme can appear in multiple surface forms, and conversely that similar surface strings can correspond to different underlying morphemes. Consider:

kitap-ta (book-LOC) vs. kitab-ı (book-ACC): the same stem surfaces as kitap- and kitab-
ev-de (house-LOC) vs. at-ta (horse-LOC): the same locative morpheme surfaces as -de and -ta

A whole-word vocabulary stores these forms separately. Their relationships must be learned from context or supplied as features, and new texts can always contain unlisted forms. Finite-state rules (Chapter 6) and character or subword representations (Chapter 7) offer different ways to generalise. The next chapters evaluate their coverage, handling of ambiguity and usefulness for particular tasks.

title: 5  Morphological Structure: A Linguistic Foundation
section: 5.3 What a Full Morphological Analysis Looks Like
text:
5.3 What a Full Morphological Analysis Looks Like

5.3.1 From Surface Form to Feature Bundle
A morphological analysis maps a surface word form to a triple: (lemma, part-of-speech, morphological features). In Universal Dependencies notation:
\[\text{surface form} \rightarrow (\text{lemma, UPOS, FEATS})\]
The FEATS field is a set of attribute-value pairs using the Universal Dependencies morphological feature vocabulary (Marneffe et al. 2021). For Turkic languages, the relevant feature categories include:

Number: Sing, Plur
Case: Nom, Acc, Dat, Loc, Abl, Gen
Person: 1, 2, 3
Tense: Past, Pres, Fut, Pqp (pluperfect, Turkish IMST)
Aspect: Perf, Imp, Prog, Hab, Prosp
Mood: Ind, Cnd, Opt, Imp, Pot (ability), Nec, Des, Gen
Evident: Fh (firsthand), Nfh (non-firsthand; used for -mIş in these annotations)
Voice: Pass, Cau, Rcp, Rfl, and combinations such as CauPass
Polarity: Pos, Neg
VerbForm: Fin, Part, Conv, Vnoun (Turkish), Ger, Inf (Kazakh KTB)
Person[psor], Number[psor]: possessor person and number (distinct from Poss=Yes)
NumType, PronType, etc.

The values beyond the core set were counted in the Turkish IMST and BOUN training files and the Kazakh KTB test file (UD GitHub master branch, accessed 19 October 2026). Treebanks of the same language do not use the same subset: BOUN uses Evident=Fh and Voice=Rfl, IMST does not.


5.3.2 Three Levels of Representation
A UD feature bundle describes selected grammatical properties of a syntactic word. A transducer may additionally expose derivational steps, surface boundaries and competing readings. We will compare three representations: surface segmentation, morphological analysis (lemma and analyser tags), and UD annotation. For evlerimizden ‘from our houses’:



Table 5.6: Three levels of representation for evlerimizden. The Apertium reading is ev<n><pl><px1pl><abl> (TurkicNLP 0.5.0).










Surface piece
Analysis (Apertium tag)
UD feature




ev
lemma ev, noun (<n>)
UPOS=NOUN


-ler
plural (<pl>)
Number=Plur


-imiz
possessor 1st person plural (<px1pl>)
Person[psor]=1, Number[psor]=Plur


-den
ablative (<abl>)
Case=Abl






The UD line, as TurkicNLP 0.5.0 outputs it:
form:   evlerimizden
lemma:  ev
upos:   NOUN
feats:  Case=Abl|Number=Plur|Number[psor]=Plur|Person[psor]=1
Note Number[psor] and Person[psor]: UD distinguishes the number of the noun itself (Number=Plur, ‘houses’) from the person and number of the possessor (‘our’).


5.3.3 An Advanced Example: Ambiguity in a Long Form
Consider okuyamadıklarından, a nominalised verb with several possessive readings. Three levels must be kept apart: the readings the grammar allows, the readings the analyser returns, and the features a treebank records.
Grammatical readings. The form is oku-ya-ma-dık ‘read-ABIL-NEG-NMLZ’ followed by possessive agreement and the ablative. The nominal can head a headless relative clause, ‘from/among the things that … could not read’, or denote the event; an ablative event nominal commonly expresses a cause, ‘because … could not read’. The possessive identifies the subject of the clause (Section 2.1): -lar-ın PL + 2SG (‘you’, with plural -lar marking the things), -lar-ı PL + 3 (‘he/she’ or ‘they’), or -ları 3PL (‘they’, with a singular nominal).
Analyser readings. The Turkish Apertium transducer returns these three readings (ignoring readings with a copula added):
oku<v><tv><abil><neg><ger_past><pl><px2sg><abl>    -lar-ın   PL + POSS.2SG   'from what you could not read'
oku<v><tv><abil><neg><ger_past><pl><px3sp><abl>    -lar-ı-n  PL + POSS.3     'from what he/she/they could not read'
oku<v><tv><abil><neg><ger_past><px3pl><abl>        -ları-n   POSS.3PL        'because they could not read'; 'from what they could not read'
The boundaries differ according to whether -lar marks the nominal’s plural or belongs to third-person plural agreement, and whether -n- is a buffer or part of the second-person possessive. Context narrows the choice. Senin okuyamadıklarından selects the second person (‘from what you could not read’); onun okuyamadıklarından selects a plural nominal with a singular possessor (‘from the things he/she could not read’). Onların okuyamadıklarından can still mean ‘from the things they could not read’ or, with -ları as third-person plural agreement, ‘because they could not read’.
Apertium lists the morphological possibilities but assigns the same analysis to relative-clause and event readings. Its tag ger_past names -DIK, whose temporal interpretation depends on the construction. Turkish UD treebanks annotate such forms as participles with Aspect=Perf|Tense=Past|VerbForm=Part. Their treatment of ability differs: IMST gives anlayamadığı (sentence 00006231_29) Mood=Pot, while BOUN gives damgalayamadığını (sentence news_128) no Mood feature (Chapter 8). The following illustrates an IMST-style bundle for the POSS.3PL reading:
form:   okuyamadıklarından
lemma:  oku
upos:   VERB
feats:  Aspect=Perf|Case=Abl|Mood=Pot|Number[psor]=Plur|Person[psor]=3|Polarity=Neg|Tense=Past|VerbForm=Part


5.3.4 The Same Analysis Across Three Languages
To illustrate the shared template, consider the parallel: “from our houses” in Turkish, Kazakh, and Uzbek:



Language
Form
Morphemes




Turkish
ev-ler-imiz-den
house-PL-POSS.1PL-ABL


Kazakh
үй-лер-іміз-ден (üi-ler-ımız-den)
house-PL-POSS.1PL-ABL


Uzbek
uy-lar-imiz-dan
house-PL-POSS.1PL-ABL



Latin forms in parentheses use the toolkit’s Kazakh transliteration (Section 3.2). The Apertium analysers for the three languages return the same tag sequence for these forms (<n><pl><px1pl><abl>, TurkicNLP 0.5.0).
The order of plural, possessive and case is the same in all three languages, as in Common Turkic generally (Johanson 2021, 452). The differences are in the surface forms: Kazakh -іміз harmonises with front stems, Uzbek -imiz is invariant, and the ablative suffix varies. An analyser design for Turkish can therefore be reused for Kazakh and Uzbek by adjusting harmony rules, suffix shapes and lexicon; whether the result works must be validated on the target language, as the next comparison shows.
For a more demanding comparison, consider the Turkish sentence Kitabı okuyamıyorum (I cannot read the book), its Kazakh equivalent Кітапты оқи алмаймын (Kıtapty oqi almaimyn) and its Turkmen equivalent Kitaby okap bilmeýärin:










Turkish
Kazakh
Turkmen




Object
kitab-ı (book-ACC)
кітап-ты (kıtap-ty, book-ACC)
kitab-y (book-ACC)


Verb
oku-ya-m-ıyor-um (read-ABIL-NEG-PROG-1SG)
оқи ал-ма-й-мын (оқы- ‘read’ + converb, take-NEG-PRS-1SG; analytic)
oka-p bil-me-ýär-in (read-CVB know-NEG-PRS-1SG; analytic)



Turkish packs inability into okuyamıyorum. Kazakh uses a converb and auxiliary ал- ‘take’: оқи алмаймын, literally ‘reading I do not take’. Turkmen also uses an auxiliary, bil- ‘know’, cognate with Turkish -(y)Abil-. Johanson lists ‘take’, ‘know’ and ‘become’ as ability auxiliaries, including Kazakh žaz-a al- ‘be able to write’ and Uzbek ȯḳi-y-ål- ‘be able to read’ (2021, 613).
The Kazakh analyser returns ал<vaux><neg><aor><p1><sg> as one of two readings of алмаймын. Its tense tag is aorist, where our gloss uses present. Both the word structure and the annotation convention need checking when adapting an analyser across languages.


5.3.5 Morphological Ambiguity
A single surface form can have multiple valid analyses. This is morphological ambiguity, and it is pervasive in Turkic text. Two useful distinctions are:
Analysis ambiguity: The same segmentation can carry different features. Turkish evi is: - ev-i = house-ACC (‘the house’, as a specific object) - ev-i = house-POSS.3SG (‘his/her house’)
The boundaries are identical; only the analysis differs. evleri has three readings without a + continuation in the Turkish Apertium transducer: ev-ler-i (house-PL-ACC ‘the houses’), ev-ler-i (house-PL-POSS.3 ‘his/her houses’ or ‘their houses’; Apertium <px3sp>), and ev-leri (house-POSS.3PL ‘their house’). Here the readings also differ in where the boundary falls.
Category ambiguity: The same form can belong to different categories. Turkish yazar can be: - A noun: “author” - A verb: yaz-ar “writes” (aorist, 3SG)
and okuma can be the verbal noun “reading” or the negative imperative “don’t read!”.
On the Turkish TueCL test file (UD 2.17), 608/730 eligible tokens (83%) receive multiple raw readings; 399/730 (55%) still do after excluding every reading containing a + continuation. On the Kazakh-KTB test file (UD 2.17), a different and larger sample of mostly encyclopaedic and literary sentences, the counts are 6,313/7,667 (82%) and 5,071/7,667 (66%). The denominator consists of integer-ID syntactic words except PUNCT, NUM and SYM, including unknown words (41 Turkish and 56 Kazakh). Thus “without +” is a reproducible filter, not a linguistic test for copulas alone. Lookup uses NFC surface spelling, then Turkish-aware lowercasing for Turkish or ordinary lowercasing for Kazakh only if the surface has no reading. code/ch05-ambiguity/ contains the script, exact counts, per-token readings and SHA-256 hashes of the two test files and transducers. Because the samples differ in genre and size, the Turkish–Kazakh difference is not a language comparison; read the figures as properties of these samples. They do not generalise to Turkish or Kazakh text at large. Disambiguation requires context, typically the surrounding words and their likely analyses.


5.3.6 The Disambiguation Problem
Given a set of possible analyses for each word in a sentence, the disambiguation problem is to select the correct analysis for each word. The constraints are mutual: the analysis of one word affects the analyses of its neighbours. For example, a noun in the accusative makes a following transitive verb more likely.
Classic approaches train statistical models over sequences of morphological tags on manually disambiguated corpora; for Turkish, Hakkani-Tür, Oflazer, and Tür (2000) model the tags of each word as a sequence of inflectional groups (see also Oflazer and Saraçlar (2018), chapter 3). More recent work uses neural taggers trained on Universal Dependencies data (Qi et al. 2020). Supervised taggers need labelled training data, but those labels can come from manual annotation or automatic methods with different error rates. A target-language learning curve shows how additional annotation affects accuracy. This motivates the cross-lingual transfer strategies discussed in Chapter 7.

title: 5  Morphological Structure: A Linguistic Foundation
text:
5.4 Cross-Language Morphological Comparison

5.4.1 The Shared Template
Use the templates in Section 5.1 to organise comparisons, then check each construction. Chuvash changes nominal suffix order (Section 5.4.5); Kazakh expresses the inability example above analytically. These differences guide what can be reused in the transfer methods of Chapter 6 and Chapter 16.
What differs across languages is:

The inventory of morphemes in each slot (which suffixes mark which distinctions)
The allomorphic rules (how harmony and assimilation apply)
The productivity of some slots (which suffixes combine freely and which are restricted to particular stems)
The degree of analyticity (how much is expressed by suffixes vs. auxiliary verbs)



5.4.2 Where Uzbek and Uyghur Diverge
Uzbek and Uyghur (Karluk branch) diverge from the Oghuz-Kipchak norm most visibly in vowel harmony. In standard written Uzbek, suffix vowels are largely fixed: the Uzbek plural is always -lar regardless of root vowel (unlike Turkish -lar/-ler), and standard Uzbek lacks a clear-cut rounding harmony (Johanson 2021, 313). The writing understates the pronunciation, however: front/back harmony has not vanished in spoken Uzbek, and Johanson calls the impression that it has ceased to function a “false impression” supported by the orthography (2021, 245, 307). For text processing, the written form is what an analyser sees: fewer written vowel alternations, even where pronunciation varies.
Uyghur writes front/back suffix variants (iš-lar ‘works’ vs. bir-gä ‘to one’; Johanson (2021), p. 245). Its Perso-Arabic orthography, unlike Arabic or Persian, writes every vowel, which makes conversion into Latin or Cyrillic largely table-driven (Chapter 3). The complication for analysis is rather vowel raising in stems (bala ‘child’ → balilar ‘children’; cf. ati-si ‘his/her father’ ← ata, Johanson (2021), p. 27), which creates stem alternants an analyser must list or derive. The Apertium Uyghur analyser reads بالىلار (balilar) as بالا<n><pl><nom>.
Uzbek, Uyghur and the Kipchak languages express some verbal categories, particularly aspect and modality, with converb + auxiliary constructions rather than suffix stacking (Kazakh оқи ал- ‘be able to read’, Uzbek oʻqiy ol- ‘be able to read’, Turkmen okap bil- ‘be able to read’; Uzbek after Johanson (2021), p. 613). A form that Turkish expresses as a single verb may require two words.


5.4.3 Selected Cross-Language Differences
Table 5.7 lists only contrasts that are illustrated in this chapter or in Chapter 2; each cell refers to the standard written language.

Row sources: backness examples in Table 2.3; rounding patterns in Johanson (2021, 311–15); plural harmony in Section 2.2.
Differential object marking affects parsing and translation. Turkish usually marks specific objects with the accusative (kitabı okudum ‘I read the book’) and leaves non-specific objects bare (kitap okudum ‘I read a book / I did book-reading’). A specific indefinite can also take the accusative: bir kitabı okudum ‘I read a certain book’. Kazakh (кітап оқыдым vs. кітапты оқыдым) and Uzbek (kitob oʻqidim vs. kitobni oʻqidim) show the same basic contrast.
The conditions depend on language, discourse and construction. For parsing, accusative marking is one cue to objecthood; word order and context help identify bare objects. For translation, preserve the intended reference. English articles cannot be mapped directly onto Turkic case suffixes.


5.4.4 The Recurring Examples Analysed
The recurring sentences of Table 1.4 show several of these contrasts together. Hyphens separate morphs, and glosses follow the Leipzig conventions (abbreviations in Table D.1); ATTR marks the attributive suffix (Kazakh -ГІ, Uyghur -diki). The Uyghur line uses the treebank’s ULY transliteration.
Қазақстан   осы   өңір-де-гі        бейбітшілік-ті  қолда-й-ды
Kazakhstan  this  region-LOC-ATTR   peace-ACC       support-PRS-3

Мен-ин  машина-м      бар
I-GEN   car-POSS.1SG  existent

Toshkent-da   dzyudo  boʻyicha  Gran-pri    musobaqa-si         boʻl-ib  oʻt-moqda
Tashkent-LOC  judo    on        Grand.Prix  competition-POSS.3  be-CVB   pass-PROG.3

u    sheher  sirt-i-diki              bir  at     harwi-si-ni      kör-i-du
3SG  town    outside-POSS.3-LOC.ATTR  a    horse  cart-POSS.3-ACC  see-PRS-3

Locative + attributive. Kazakh өңір-де-гі and Uyghur sirt-i-diki turn a locative into a noun modifier with the same suffix order.
Possessive marking in compounds. Uzbek Gran-pri musobaqa-si and Uyghur at harwi-si mark the head of a noun compound with the 3rd-person possessive and no genitive. In Kyrgyz Мен-ин машина-м, by contrast, a genitive possessor agrees with a 1st-person possessive suffix.
Analytic predicates. Kyrgyz expresses possession with the existential бар, without a verb ‘have’; Uzbek boʻl-ib oʻt- ‘take place’ is a converb + verb combination of the kind described above.
Person without number. Kazakh -ды and Uyghur -du mark the 3rd person but not number.

The treebank annotations differ from these analyses in places: Kyrgyz-KTMU tags машинам as genitive and бар as a verb with tense and aspect; Uyghur-UDT tags sirtidiki as nominative and bir as an ordinal; Kazakh-KTB marks only the locative of өңірдегі. A released annotation documents a convention and can contain errors; Section 8.2 returns to this point.


5.4.5 Chuvash: The Exceptional Case
Chuvash is agglutinative, with phonology and morphotactics that differ from Common Turkic. Oghur sound changes give Chuvash r where Common Turkic has z (rhotacism) and l where Common Turkic has š (lambdacism) (Johanson 2021, 25). Its plural is -сем (-säm), becoming -сен before case suffixes (Johanson 2021, 453). Possessive marking comes first: кил-ӗм-сен-чен ‘from my houses’ (house-POSS.1SG-PL-ABL), compared with Turkish ev-ler-im-den (Johanson 2021, 452, 455). A transducer must encode this order along with Chuvash rules and vocabulary.
On the 20-sentence-per-language TurkicNLP challenge set, Apertium detected the target phenomenon in 80% of the Chuvash sentences and the multilingual neural analyser in 60% (Hakimov 2026). The authors suggest that divergent Oghur morphology limits transfer. A comparison this small cannot settle the cause, so test transfer to Chuvash directly.


5.4.6 Practical Guidance: Starting from a Close Relative
An existing analyser can provide a starting design for a related language. Choose it by documented structural similarities and tool quality, then check the following parts:

Reuse the tag set and the morphotactic design of the relative’s analyser, and check each continuation against the target language.
Build a new lexicon for the target language; cognate roots speed this up but must be checked one by one.
Write the target language’s own alternation rules: harmony dimensions (and whether they are written), consonant assimilation, stem alternations.
Adjust suffix shapes. The Kazakh locative -da/-de/-ta/-te matches Turkish, but the Kazakh accusative -ны/-ні/-ды/-ді/-ты/-ті differs from Turkish -(y)ı/i/u/ü.
Add language-specific morphemes and constructions not present in the relative.

The Apertium Turkic analysers were built in this spirit: each language has its own lexicon and rule files, but they follow shared formalisms and tag conventions (Washington, Salimzyanov, and Tyers 2014). Chapter 6 develops this architecture in detail.

section: 5.5 Hands-On: Walking Through a Morphological Analysis
text:
5.5 Hands-On: Walking Through a Morphological Analysis
Question. How does the analyser represent ambiguity and choose a reading?
Inputs. The Turkish and Kazakh sentences below and their Apertium resources.
Compute. CPU with TurkicNLP and downloaded transducers.
Output. Selected lemmas, parts of speech, feature bundles and alternative readings.
Interpretation. Compare each field with the sentence context and inspect processor provenance.
The TurkicNLP toolkit (Hakimov 2026) provides rule-based morphological analysis via Apertium transducers for 20 Turkic languages and a multilingual neural analyser for 22. The following example analyses a Turkish and a Kazakh sentence with TurkicNLP 0.5.0 and the Apertium backend (pip install "turkicnlp[hfst]==0.5.0"; fetch the transducers with turkicnlp.download(lang, processors=["morph"]) for each language before running) and prints the selected analysis of each token. Missing values are printed as _.
from turkicnlp import Pipeline

# --- Turkish ---
tr_pipeline = Pipeline("tur", processors=["tokenize", "morph"], tokenize_backend="rule", morph_backend="apertium")
doc_tr = tr_pipeline("Evlerimizden çok uzaklaşmıştık.")

print("Turkish morphological analysis:")
for word in doc_tr.words:
    print(f"  {word.text:<16} lemma={word.lemma or '_':<10} upos={word.upos or '_':<6} feats={word.feats or '_'}")

# --- Kazakh (Cyrillic) ---
kz_pipeline = Pipeline("kaz", processors=["tokenize", "morph"], tokenize_backend="rule", morph_backend="apertium")
doc_kz = kz_pipeline("Үйлерімізден өте алыс кеткенбіз.")

print("\nKazakh morphological analysis:")
for word in doc_kz.words:
    print(f"  {word.text:<16} lemma={word.lemma or '_':<10} upos={word.upos or '_':<6} feats={word.feats or '_'}")

# --- All readings of an ambiguous word (private API in 0.5.0) ---
apertium = next(p for p in tr_pipeline._processors if hasattr(p, "_analyze"))
for reading in apertium._analyze("evleri"):
    print(reading["raw"])
Output (local TurkicNLP 0.5.0 checkout and Apertium backend):
Turkish morphological analysis:

  çok              lemma=çok        upos=ADV    feats=_
  uzaklaşmıştık    lemma=uzaklaş    upos=VERB   feats=Evident=Nfh|Number=Plur|Person=1|Tense=Past
  .                lemma=.          upos=PUNCT  feats=_

Kazakh morphological analysis:
  Үйлерімізден     lemma=үй         upos=NOUN   feats=Case=Abl|Number=Plur|Number[psor]=Plur|Person[psor]=1
  өте              lemma=өте        upos=ADV    feats=_
  алыс             lemma=алыс       upos=NOUN   feats=_
  кеткенбіз        lemma=кет        upos=VERB   feats=Number=Plur|Person=1|Tense=Past
  .                lemma=.          upos=PUNCT  feats=_
ev<n><pl><acc>
ev<n><pl><px3sp><nom>
ev<n><pl><px3sp><nom>+i<cop><aor><p3><sg>
ev<n><px3pl><nom>
ev<n><px3pl><nom>+i<cop><aor><p3><sg>
The pipeline selects one analysis per word using transducer weights and heuristic context. The transducer can offer several: for evleri, plural accusative, plural with a third-person possessor, a third-person plural possessor, and copular continuations. Check the selected reading against a manually reviewed reference and discuss mismatches, as the exercises do.
With the PyPI release of TurkicNLP 0.5.0 and the pure-Python pyhfst reader, the readings of evleri are printed in a different order and алыс gets feats=Case=Nom; the selected lemmas and parts of speech are the same.
Evlerimizden and Үйлерімізден receive parallel FEATS bundles for the same structure in different surface forms. Other outputs reveal errors. In uzaklaş-mış-tı-k, -mIş-DI expresses the pluperfect, ‘we had moved far away’. The transducer instead reads -mIş as evidential past (Evident=Nfh|Tense=Past, Section 5.1); Turkish IMST uses Tense=Pqp. Kazakh алыс ‘far’ is tagged NOUN despite its adverbial use here. The toolkit chooses among transducer readings with heuristics, without a trained syntactic disambiguator (Chapter 7). Inspect word._provenance and doc._processor_log to see which processor supplied each field.
Status: demonstration. The displayed output is recorded and includes the backend and version differences. Exercise 3 develops the ambiguity comparison.

title: 5  Morphological Structure: A Linguistic Foundation
text:
What to Take Forward
A morphological analysis links a stem and its affixes to grammatical functions, and context selects among competing readings. Ambiguity is the normal case: in the UD test samples above, 55% of eligible Turkish tokens and 66% of Kazakh ones keep several readings even after continuation readings are removed. Surface segments, analyser tags and UD features answer different questions, so state which representation a tool produces before comparing it with another. Chapter 6 shows how finite-state analysers produce these readings, and Chapter 7 how neural models select them.

title: 5  Morphological Structure: A Linguistic Foundation
text:
Further Reading

Turkic morphology: Johanson (2021), chapter 20 (pp. 431–439), introduces morphology; chapter 22 (pp. 452–478) treats noun inflection, and chapter 27 (pp. 555–571) treats copular devices.
Turkish morphological analysis: Oflazer (1994) is the foundational computational paper on Turkish two-level morphology; Oflazer and Saraçlar (2018, chaps. 2–3) gives a modern treatment of morphological processing and disambiguation for Turkish, and the rest of the book covers parsing, semantic processing and speech.
Universal Dependencies morphological features: Marneffe et al. (2021) defines the UD feature inventory; the UD guidelines for Turkic languages at universaldependencies.org provide language-specific annotation decisions.
Cross-lingual morphology: Hakimov (2026) compares finite-state and multilingual neural analysers on a parallel 20-language challenge set, including languages without training data.

title: 5  Morphological Structure: A Linguistic Foundation
text:
Exercises

Template exercise. Analyse kitaplarımıza as kitap-lar-ımız-a. Write a proposed UD feature bundle, then run the analyser of the Hands-On section and compare. Distinguish the noun’s number, the possessor’s person and number, and case. Explain any mismatch, and record the toolkit version and backend.
Allomorphy tables. For the Turkish dative suffix (-a/-e) and the locative suffix (-da/-de/-ta/-te), fill in the correct allomorph for each of the following roots: ev (house), araba (car), göz (eye), kapı (door), çiçek (flower), kuş (bird). State the rule governing each allomorph choice.
Morphological ambiguity. List all readings the Turkish transducer returns for yazar, çalışır and evleri (use the readings call of the Hands-On section, or Zemberek). For each word: (a) gloss each reading; (b) write two sentences in which different readings are correct; (c) say which reading the pipeline selects in each sentence, and whether it is right.
Cross-language comparison. Segment the Kazakh word кетпегендіктен ‘because (someone) did not leave’ as кет-пе-ген-дік-тен (leave-NEG-PTCP-NMLZ-ABL): it contains both a participle -ген and a nominaliser -дік. (a) Give an equivalent Turkish construction and compare the order of the pieces. (b) Propose a UD annotation under the conventions of the Kazakh KTB treebank, and explain which pieces the UD bundle does not show. Compare it with what the Apertium Kazakh analyser returns for the word. (c) Compare Turkmen gitmedigi üçin ‘because (someone) did not go’ (git-me-dig-i üçin, go-NEG-PTCP-POSS.3 for), which expresses the cause with a postposition instead of the ablative.
Morphophonological rule writing. Write a formal rule (in prose or as a conditional) for Turkish consonant alternation in the locative suffix (-da/-ta): state the trigger (what phonological property of the preceding consonant) and the two output forms. Then apply your rule to the following stems: el (hand), kap (lid), göl (lake), at (horse), iç (inside).

title: 6  Finite-State Morphology: The Rule-Based Approach
text:
6.1 Why Finite-State Methods for Turkic
Chapter 5 described Turkic morphology. This chapter implements part of it with finite-state transducers, following work such as Oflazer’s Turkish analyser (Oflazer 1994) and the Apertium Turkic modules (J. Washington, Salimzyanov, and Tyers 2014). A small grammar shows how to encode suffix order, vowel harmony and consonant alternation.
Finite-state morphology is a practical option when explicit linguistic knowledge is available and labelled data are scarce. Multilingual neural and hybrid approaches (Chapter 7) are alternatives, and their costs and errors should be compared on the language at hand.
crumbs: 6  Finite-State Morphology: The Rule-Based Approach

title: 6  Finite-State Morphology: The Rule-Based Approach
text:
6.1.1 The Transparency Argument
A finite-state transducer (FST) relates two string representations. A morphological transducer maps surface forms to analyses and can be inverted for generation. Its source lexicon and rules can be inspected and tested when a form is missing or has an unwanted analysis. Tracing a compiled path back to a source rule may still take work.
For a language without annotated training data, a linguist can build a transducer from grammars and speaker consultation. When it fails, the analysis can be traced to a rule or lexicon entry. Error analysis also helps with learned models, although it rarely identifies an explicit rule in the same way.


6.1.2 The Reversibility Argument
An FST relates two sets of strings. Inverting it swaps input and output, allowing the same relation to support analysis and generation. Ambiguity survives the swap: one analysis may have several surface forms, and one surface form may have several analyses. Composing the relation with its inverse therefore need not give the identity relation. In practice:

Analysis: surface form ev-ler-imiz-den → ev<n><pl><px1pl><abl>
Generation: ev<n><pl><px1pl><abl> → surface form evlerimizden

This chapter writes analyses in the Apertium tag format, as the Turkish transducer returns them.
Generation supports spell-checking, data augmentation and machine translation. Acceptance means that a form is licensed by the implemented grammar; the spelling or the choice of word can still be wrong in context (Section 3.5).


6.1.3 The Low-Data Argument
Neural morphological analysers require training data: annotated word forms with their morphological analyses. For Turkish, Kazakh, and a few others, such data exists (Universal Dependencies treebanks provide morphological annotation). For a new target language, inspect separately the available treebanks, labelled paradigms and unannotated text; absence of a treebank does not imply absence of every kind of morphological supervision.
Building an FST draws on linguistic knowledge: the suffix inventory, harmony rules and lexicon. Grammar descriptions, fieldwork and speaker consultation can supply it without an annotated training corpus. The work still takes time, and independent test data are needed to assess the resulting rules and coverage.


6.1.4 The Coverage Argument
An FST generalises to every combination licensed by its lexicon and rules, including forms absent from the development texts. That behaviour is inspectable. Missing stems and constructions cause failures; overly permissive rules can admit forms speakers would reject. A neural model may handle the test distribution well while making less predictable errors on unusual forms.
crumbs: 6  Finite-State Morphology: The Rule-Based Approach

title: 6  Finite-State Morphology: The Rule-Based Approach
text:
6.2 Two-Level Morphology: The Core Formalism
A widely used formalism for finite-state morphology in Turkic NLP is two-level morphology, introduced by Koskenniemi (1983) and applied to Turkish by Oflazer (1994). The name refers to the two levels of representation:

Lexical level: the canonical, underlying form (morphemes listed in the lexicon)
Surface level: the realised form (what appears in actual text)

The two levels are related by two-level rules that map lexical sequences to surface sequences, encoding phonological alternations.

6.2.1 The Lexicon (lexc)
The lexicon file (written in the lexc formalism) defines:

Lexemes: root morphemes with their lexical representation and continuation class
Continuation classes (also called sublexica): the sets of suffixes that can follow a given form
Morpheme entries: individual suffix morphemes, each with its lexical representation, surface representation (if different), and next continuation class

The following schematic notation explains the architecture; it is not a compilable HFST grammar (a complete, tested one follows below). A simplified excerpt of a Turkish noun lexicon:
LEXICON NounRoot
ev    NounInfl;    ! "house", continues to noun inflection
araba NounInfl;    ! "car"
göz   NounInfl;    ! "eye"

LEXICON NounInfl
<PL>:ler  NounCase;   ! plural suffix (front), continues to case
<PL>:lar  NounCase;   ! plural suffix (back)
          NounCase;   ! singular (empty suffix)

LEXICON NounCase
<LOC>:de  #;          ! locative (front voiced)
<LOC>:da  #;          ! locative (back voiced)
<LOC>:te  #;          ! locative (front voiceless)
<LOC>:ta  #;          ! locative (back voiceless)
<ABL>:den #;          ! ablative ...
...
The # symbol marks the end of a word. The continuation class mechanism encodes the suffix template: NounRoot continues to NounInfl, which continues to NounCase, which terminates. A suffix from NounCase cannot appear before one from NounInfl because the continuation classes do not allow it.


6.2.2 Phonological Rules (twolc)
The twolc component constrains pairs of lexical and surface symbols in context. For example, an abstract suffix vowel can surface as a or e according to harmony, and an abstract suffix consonant as d or t according to voicing.
The schematic lexicon above lists the allomorphs separately. The complete grammar below instead writes each suffix once with archiphonemes, symbols that stand for its alternating sounds. The two-level rules select the permitted surface forms.


6.2.3 A Complete Toy Grammar
The following grammar compiles with HFST and is small enough to read in full. It has four stems, the plural and two cases. The lexicon writes the harmonising vowel as {A} and the suffix-initial d/t as {D}; two rules choose their surface forms. The files are in code/ch06-toy-fst/ of the book repository.
! tr-toy.lexc — upper side = analysis (lemma + tags), lower side = morphophonemic form
! {A} = harmonising vowel a/e;  {D} = suffix-initial d/t

Multichar_Symbols
%<n%> %<pl%> %<loc%> %<abl%> %{A%} %{D%}

LEXICON Root
Nouns ;

LEXICON Nouns
ev%<n%>:ev         Number ;   ! house
araba%<n%>:araba   Number ;   ! car
göz%<n%>:göz       Number ;   ! eye
kitap%<n%>:kitap   Number ;   ! book

LEXICON Number
%<pl%>:l%{A%}r     Case ;     ! plural -lAr
                   Case ;     ! singular: no suffix

LEXICON Case
                       # ;    ! nominative: no suffix
%<loc%>:%{D%}%{A%}     # ;    ! locative -DA
%<abl%>:%{D%}%{A%}n    # ;    ! ablative -DAn
! tr-toy.twolc — backness harmony of {A} and voicing of {D}

Alphabet
a b c ç d e f g ğ h ı i j k l m n o ö p r s ş t u ü v y z
%{A%}:a %{A%}:e %{D%}:d %{D%}:t ;

Sets
FrontV = e i ö ü ;
Cons = b c ç d f g ğ h j k l m n p r s ş t v y z ;
Voiceless = ç f h k p s ş t ;

Rules

"{A} is e after a front vowel, otherwise a"
%{A%}:e <=> :FrontV [ :Cons ]* _ ;

"{D} is t after a voiceless consonant, otherwise d"
%{D%}:t <=> :Voiceless _ ;
The harmony rule looks back over any number of consonants to the nearest vowel; because the surface vowel of a preceding {A} counts, ev-l{A}r-{D}{A} becomes evlerde in one pass. The Python bindings compile and test the grammar (pip install hfst; tested with HFST 3.16.0.1). Run this inline block from code/ch06-toy-fst/:
import hfst

lexicon = hfst.compile_lexc_file("tr-toy.lexc")              # analysis:morphophonemic
hfst.compile_twolc_file("tr-toy.twolc", "tr-toy.twol.hfst")
stream = hfst.HfstInputStream("tr-toy.twol.hfst")
rules = []
while not stream.is_eof():
    rules.append(stream.read())
stream.close()

generator = hfst.HfstTransducer(lexicon)
generator.compose_intersect(tuple(rules))                    # analysis:surface
generator.minimize()
analyser = hfst.HfstTransducer(generator)
analyser.invert()                                            # surface:analysis
analyser.minimize()
# Optimized-lookup format, the format of Apertium's .automorf/.autogen files
analyser.convert(hfst.ImplementationType.HFST_OLW_TYPE)
generator.convert(hfst.ImplementationType.HFST_OLW_TYPE)

def analyse(word):
    return sorted(a for a, _ in analyser.lookup(word))

def generate(analysis):
    return sorted(s for s, _ in generator.lookup(analysis))

accept = {"evler": "ev<n><pl>", "arabalar": "araba<n><pl>", "evlerde": "ev<n><pl><loc>",
          "arabalarda": "araba<n><pl><loc>", "gözden": "göz<n><abl>", "kitapta": "kitap<n><loc>",
          "kitaplardan": "kitap<n><pl><abl>"}
reject = ["evlar", "arabaler", "evlarda", "kitapda", "arabade"]
for word, gold in accept.items():
    assert analyse(word) == [gold], (word, analyse(word))      # the analysis, not just acceptance
for word in reject:
    assert analyse(word) == [], (word, analyse(word))
assert generate("göz<n><pl><loc>") == ["gözlerde"]
print("all tests passed")
The displayed checks cover representative cases. From any working directory, python code/ch06-toy-fst/build_and_test.py verifies all 24 cells of the four-stem paradigm in both directions. Accepted forms must receive the expected analysis; harmony and voicing errors must be rejected. The grammar leaves out the kitap/kitab- alternation before vowels. Exercise 2 adds it with an accusative suffix.
Apertium grammars extend this design with larger lexicons and language-specific rules. Throughput depends on transducer format and hardware, so measure it on your own text when speed matters. As checked on 19 October 2026, PyPI’s hfst package had wheels for Python 3.11 but none for Python 3.13. The pure-Python pyhfst can read compiled transducers; it cannot compile lexc or twolc.


6.2.4 The Analysis Operation
Given the compiled FST, analysis works by composition: input the surface string and read out all lexical paths that the transducer accepts. For evlerimizden:

The FST traverses the transitions that match e-v-l-e-r-i-m-i-z-d-e-n
At each step, valid continuation classes constrain which transitions are available
All accepting paths (paths that reach a final state after consuming all input characters) are returned as analyses

The output is a set of analysis strings from accepting paths; multiple paths can yield the same string. The Apertium Turkish transducer returns two (shown in Section 6.3):
ev<n><pl><px1pl><abl>
ev<n><pl><px1pl><abl>+i<cop><aor><p3><sg>
If the word is unrecognised (no accepting path), the FST returns an empty set. The word may be a loanword or a typo, or it may use a suffix or root missing from the lexicon.


6.2.5 The Generation Operation
Generation uses the inverse relation: swap the input and output labels, then look up the lexical analysis to obtain its surface form(s). This preserves string order; it does not reverse the transitions or the spelling. For ev<n><pl><px1pl><abl>:

The harmony rules select -ler (front plural, since ev has a front vowel) and -imiz (front unrounded, after -ler)
The voicing rule selects -den, because -imiz ends in the voiced consonant z
The transducer returns evlerimizden

A fully specified lexical analysis often has one standard surface realisation, although the relation can encode variants (spelling variants, or optional forms that the grammar allows), in which case generation returns several surface forms.

title: 6  Finite-State Morphology: The Rule-Based Approach
text:
6.3 The Apertium Turkic Project

6.3.1 Overview
Apertium is an open-source rule-based machine translation platform that includes, as one of its core components, a collection of morphological analysers and generators implemented as FSTs (Forcada et al. 2011; Khanna et al. 2021). TurkicNLP loads Apertium transducers for 20 Turkic languages (Hakimov 2026).
The analysers use the lexc/twolc formalism compiled with HFST. Each language module consists of:

A language-specific lexicon file (apertium-tur.tur.lexc, apertium-kaz.kaz.lexc, etc.)
A phonological rule file (apertium-tur.tur.twolc, etc.)
Depending on the module, disambiguation rules and test suites

Bilingual dictionaries and transfer rules for machine translation live in separate pair modules (e.g., apertium-kaz-tat). Although every language has its own lexicon and rules, the Turkic modules follow common formalisms and tag conventions, and several were developed together (J. Washington, Salimzyanov, and Tyers 2014); J. N. Washington, Tyers, and Kuyrukçu (2020) describe multi-script transducers and transcribers for seven of them. This shared design is what makes it realistic to start a new language from the module of a close relative.


6.3.2 How Good Are the Analysers?
The 20 analysers differ widely in lexicon size and maturity. Because gold morphological annotation is missing for most Turkic languages, the TurkicNLP evaluation uses a parallel challenge set: the same 20 sentences translated into 20 languages, each targeting one phenomenon (five cases; past, progressive, future, negation, question, imperative, conditional, evidential, passive; plural, possessive, pronoun, reciprocal, numeral, converb). It compares the Apertium analysers with the toolkit’s multilingual neural analyser (Hakimov 2026).

Each metric answers a narrow question. Det% records whether the target feature appears anywhere in a sentence. Feat% records any non-empty feature bundle, regardless of correctness. Assess full-analysis accuracy on representative running text separately, along with coverage, recall of the gold reading among candidates and contextual disambiguation.
On this diagnostic, mean target-feature detection is 74% for the transducers and 67% for the neural analyser; the corresponding non-empty-feature rates are 65% and 88%. The ordering varies by language (Table 6.1). Analyser maturity, correct disambiguation and the reasons for a cross-language gap all lie beyond what these measures can show. A full evaluation of an analyser would annotate tokens in held-out natural sentences per language, retain legitimate alternative readings, and report unknown-word rate, gold-candidate recall and selected-reading accuracy.
The Kazakh and Kyrgyz transducers were developed by the community that also produced the Kazakh UD treebank and its UD feature mapping (J. Washington, Salimzyanov, and Tyers 2014; Tyers and Washington 2015; J. Washington, Ipasov, and Tyers 2012); TurkicNLP converts module tags into UD-shaped feature strings. This does not guarantee agreement with every treebank’s annotation conventions; audit the mapping before scoring.


6.3.3 Using Apertium FSTs via HFST Python Bindings
The HFST toolkit (Lindén et al. 2011) provides Python bindings that allow Apertium FST binaries to be loaded and queried without a system-level Apertium installation (pip install turkicnlp[hfst]). The TurkicNLP toolkit wraps these bindings with a unified API, downloads the GPL-licensed transducers separately at run time, converts input to the script each transducer expects, and scores competing readings with transducer weights and heuristics (Hakimov 2026).

6.3.3.1 Direct HFST Access
For users who want direct control over the FST:
import hfst
from turkicnlp.resources.registry import ModelRegistry

# Folder of the Apertium Turkish transducers fetched by turkicnlp.download("tur")
tur_dir = ModelRegistry.get_model_path("tur", "morph", "apertium", script="Latn")

def load(path):
    stream = hfst.HfstInputStream(str(path))
    fst = stream.read()
    stream.close()
    return fst

analyser = load(tur_dir / "tur.automorf.hfst")
print(hfst.__version__ if hasattr(hfst, "__version__") else "", tur_dir)

for word in ["evlerimizden", "yüzü", "xyzqw"]:
    for analysis, weight in analyser.lookup(word):     # (output string, weight) pairs
        print(f"{word}\t{analysis}\t{weight}")

# evlerimizden  ev<n><pl><px1pl><abl>                      0.0
# evlerimizden  ev<n><pl><px1pl><abl>+i<cop><aor><p3><sg>  0.0
# yüzü          yüz<n><acc>                                0.0
# yüzü          yüz<n><px3sp><nom>                         0.0
# yüzü          yüz<num><subst><acc>                       0.0
# ...           (six readings in total)
# xyzqw         (no output: unknown word)
lookup() returns each analysis with its weight; the input is already known. evlerimizden has two readings: the noun ‘from our houses’, and the same noun followed by the copula, ‘it is from our houses’. yüzü has six: ‘face’ or the numeral ‘hundred’, each as an accusative, a third-person possessive, or a possessive plus copula. An unknown word returns nothing. Choosing between readings is the disambiguation problem of Chapter 7. The output above was produced with HFST 3.16.0.1 and the Apertium Turkish transducer distributed with TurkicNLP 0.5.0.


6.3.3.2 Via TurkicNLP
The TurkicNLP pipeline routes morphological analysis through the Apertium backend automatically, converting the Apertium-native tag format to Universal Dependencies features:
from turkicnlp import Pipeline

# Kazakh morphological analysis with UD feature output
pipeline = Pipeline("kaz", processors=["tokenize", "morph"], tokenize_backend="rule", morph_backend="apertium")   # "morph" = Apertium FST

doc = pipeline("Ол кітабымды оқып жатыр.")

for word in doc.words:
    print(f"{word.text:<12} {word.lemma or '_':<8} {word.upos or '_':<6} {word.feats or '_'}")
Output (TurkicNLP 0.5.0):
Ол           ол       PRON   Case=Nom|PronType=Dem
кітабымды    кітап    NOUN   Case=Acc|Number[psor]=Sing|Person[psor]=1
оқып         оқы      VERB   VerbForm=Conv
жатыр        жат      AUX    Number=Plur|Person=3|Tense=Pres
.            .        PUNCT  _
The analyser correctly recognises оқып жатыр ‘is reading’ as a converb followed by auxiliary жат- ‘lie’. Its selected Number=Plur is wrong for the subject Ол ‘he/she’. Kazakh third-person forms do not distinguish singular from plural here, so the transducer returns both жат<vaux><pres><p3><sg> and жат<vaux><pres><p3><pl>. The toolkit chooses the plural reading. Compare this decision with Stanza or Glot500 (Chapter 7) and check the feature mapping against the intended treebank.



6.3.4 Extending Coverage to a New Language
The common formalism and tag conventions make it feasible to extend Apertium Turkic coverage to new languages. The process, documented in the Apertium developer documentation and described practically for Kypchak languages by J. Washington, Salimzyanov, and Tyers (2014), involves:

Create a new language directory following the Apertium naming convention.
Write a new lexicon file with the target language’s root morphemes. For Kipchak languages, many roots are shared with Kazakh or Kyrgyz, reducing the lexicographic work.
Model the suffix inventory on a close relative’s lexicon (continuation classes and tags), then replace the allomorphs with the target language’s own.
Write or adapt the phonological rules for the target language’s harmony system.
Compile and test against known forms. The test suite (a list of surface forms with expected analyses) is the primary quality assurance mechanism.

The work includes lexicon building, grammatical description, implementation and speaker validation. Which part takes most time depends on the available resources.

title: 6  Finite-State Morphology: The Rule-Based Approach
text:
6.4 Language-Specific Tools
Beyond Apertium, several language-specific morphological tools exist for the best-resourced Turkic languages.

6.4.1 Zemberek-NLP (Turkish)
Zemberek-NLP (Akın and Akın 2007) is a Java library for Turkish NLP; the 2007 paper describes the earlier Zemberek framework from which it developed. Its repository states that the project “is now in slow maintenance mode” (checked 19 October 2026). It provides:

Morphological analysis: a Java-native implementation of Turkish morphology that implements Turkish suffix rules and includes a contextual disambiguator
Morphological generation: generates forms from a dictionary item and requested morphological tags
Spell-checking: based on morphological analysis rather than dictionary lookup
Tokenisation: handles Turkish-specific patterns including acronyms, numbers, and clitic punctuation

Zemberek operates independently of Apertium and uses its own internal rule representation rather than lexc/twolc. It is written in Java; a separate project provides a Python implementation.
Zemberek integrates morphological disambiguation, selecting an analysis in sentence context. Evaluate candidate generation and contextual selection separately; having a disambiguator says nothing yet about its accuracy on a new domain.


6.4.2 TRmorph (Turkish)
TRmorph (Çöltekin 2010) is an open-source finite-state morphological analyser for Turkish. The 2010 paper describes an implementation in SFST; the current repository is a rewrite in lexc/xfst developed with foma, with a new lexicon, a revised tag set, a stemmer, a segmenter and an unknown-word guesser (README, checked 19 October 2026). Results reported for one version do not carry over to the other.


6.4.3 Google’s Turkish Morphological Analyser
Ozturel, Kayadelen, and Demirsahin (2019) describe a “syntactically expressive” finite-state analyser for Turkish developed at Google and released as open source (google-research/turkish-morphology). Its analyses are designed to be compatible with Universal Dependencies-style syntactic annotation, which makes it a useful companion to UD parsers.


6.4.4 Analysers for Other Turkic Languages
Kazakh has published work on morphological disambiguation, including a voted-perceptron approach (Tolegen, Toleu, and Mussabayev 2020). Check tool availability against a dated resource inventory; a language’s size is a poor guide. Apertium and TurkicNLP provide useful starting points, but this overview is not an exhaustive list of analysers.

title: 6  Finite-State Morphology: The Rule-Based Approach
text:
6.5 Morphological Generation and Data Augmentation

6.5.1 Generation Mode
The FST analysers described above are bidirectional: Apertium builds a generator transducer from the same sources as the analyser, mapping an analysis string (lemma plus Apertium tags) to surface forms. TurkicNLP uses these generators internally (Hakimov 2026); the example below calls the Turkish generator directly through HFST, reusing load() and tur_dir from Section 6.3, which makes the mechanism visible.
gen = load(tur_dir / "tur.autogen.hfst")          # Apertium Turkish generator

def generate(analysis: str) -> list[str]:
    return sorted({form for form, _ in gen.lookup(analysis)})

for case in ["nom", "acc", "dat", "loc", "abl", "gen"]:
    print(case, generate(f"ev<n><{case}>"))
Output:
nom ['ev']
acc ['evi']
dat ['eve']
loc ['evde']
abl ['evden']
gen ['evin']
TurkicNLP exposes the same generator through its Apertium processor, which also converts the script where the transducer expects a different one:
from turkicnlp.processors.morphology import ApertiumMorphProcessor

kaz_dir = ModelRegistry.get_model_path("kaz", "morph", "apertium", script="Cyrl")
kaz = ApertiumMorphProcessor(lang="kaz")
kaz.load(kaz_dir)
print([kaz.generate("мектеп", ["n", case]) for case in ["nom", "acc", "dat", "loc", "abl", "gen"]])
# ['мектеп', 'мектепті', 'мектепке', 'мектепте', 'мектептен', 'мектептің']


6.5.2 Data Augmentation via Morphological Generation
One practically useful application of generation is morphological data augmentation. For low-resource Turkic languages where labelled training data is scarce, generating inflected forms of known lemmas expands the variety of surface forms a model sees.
Changing an entity’s case can change its role or make a sentence ungrammatical. Мен Алматыдан келдім means ‘I came from Almaty’; replacing Алматыдан with Алматыға gives ‘I came to Almaty’, a grammatical sentence with a different meaning. For entity substitution, keep the original case and number and generate a different entity of the same type in that form. The resulting sentence still needs contextual checking:
gen_kaz = load(kaz_dir / "kaz.autogen.hfst")      # Apertium Kazakh generator
ana_kaz = load(kaz_dir / "kaz.automorf.hfst")

def substitute_entity(tokens, labels, idx, new_lemma, allowed_lemmas, ana=None, gen=None):
    """Conservative single-token B-LOC replacement; None means abstain."""
    ana, gen = ana or ana_kaz, gen or gen_kaz       # Kazakh transducers by default
    if len(tokens) != len(labels) or not 0 <= idx < len(tokens):
        raise ValueError("unaligned tokens/labels or invalid index")
    if labels[idx] != "B-LOC" or (idx + 1 < len(labels) and labels[idx + 1] == "I-LOC"):
        return None                                  # no partial replacement of an entity
    if new_lemma not in allowed_lemmas or any(c.isspace() for c in new_lemma):
        return None                                  # require an independently checked gazetteer
    readings = {a for a, _ in ana.lookup(tokens[idx]) if "<np><top>" in a and "+" not in a}
    if len(readings) != 1:
        return None
    _, tags = readings.pop().split("<", 1)
    requested = f"{new_lemma}<{tags}"
    forms = {f for f, _ in gen.lookup(requested)}
    if len(forms) != 1:
        return None
    form = forms.pop()
    if not form or any(c.isspace() for c in form):
        return None
    if requested not in {a for a, _ in ana.lookup(form)}:
        return None                                  # generator/analyser round-trip check
    new_tokens = list(tokens); new_tokens[idx] = form
    return new_tokens, list(labels)

tokens = ["Мен", "Алматыдан", "келдім", "."]
labels = ["O", "B-LOC", "O", "O"]
# Demonstration candidates; a production gazetteer needs independent validation.
cities = {"Астана", "Шымкент", "Тараз"}
for city in ["Астана", "Шымкент", "Тараз", "Париж"]:
    print(substitute_entity(tokens, labels, 1, city, cities))
# Inspect the accepted forms; Париж is rejected because it is not in cities.
The same function works for Turkmen with the Apertium Turkmen transducers (beta quality):
tuk_dir = ModelRegistry.get_model_path("tuk", "morph", "apertium", script="Latn")
gen_tuk = load(tuk_dir / "tuk.autogen.hfst")
ana_tuk = load(tuk_dir / "tuk.automorf.hfst")

tokens = ["Men", "Aşgabatdan", "geldim", "."]     # 'I came from Ashgabat'
labels = ["O", "B-LOC", "O", "O"]
cities = {"Mary", "Daşoguz", "Türkmenabat"}
for city in ["Mary", "Daşoguz", "Türkmenabat", "Parij"]:
    print(substitute_entity(tokens, labels, 1, city, cities, ana=ana_tuk, gen=gen_tuk))
Output (18 October 2026):
(['Men', 'Marydan', 'geldim', '.'], ['O', 'B-LOC', 'O', 'O'])
(['Men', 'Daşoguzdan', 'geldim', '.'], ['O', 'B-LOC', 'O', 'O'])
(['Men', 'Türkmenabatdan', 'geldim', '.'], ['O', 'B-LOC', 'O', 'O'])
None
Parij ‘Paris’ is rejected because it is not in the vetted list (the transducer does not know it either). The Turkmen transducer is incomplete in other places: asked for the past participle of oka- ‘read’, it produces okaen where the standard form is okan, which is exactly why generated forms need checking.
A well-formed request can still yield a questionable word. Re-analysis tests consistency with the generator’s own grammar. Independent linguistic checks are needed to judge that grammar.
Keep the original analyser’s tag sequence, reject ambiguity and require a vetted replacement lexicon. This example handles pretokenised, single-token location entities only. If converting the result back to raw text, rebuild character offsets and verify tokenisation before attaching spans; equal token counts do not preserve character offsets. Split source documents into train, development and test sets before augmenting, and augment training data only. Report manual grammaticality checks and performance on unchanged held-out text. Enumerating a lemma’s cases demonstrates the paradigm. It does not produce training sentences that can stand in for one another.


6.5.3 Back-Off Strategies
FST analysers fail to recognise words that are not in their lexicon: loanwords, proper nouns not in the gazetteer, neologisms, and misspellings. Three back-off strategies are used in practice:
Heuristic morphological guessing. When the analyser returns no analysis, one can strip final characters and re-analyse the remainder, guessing that the stripped characters are suffixes. Such heuristics can produce wrong guesses and need evaluation on the target language; mark their output as low-confidence and allow the system to abstain. Guesser transducers, below, are a more principled version of the same idea.
Morphological guesser FSTs. A guesser transducer matches unknown words against suffix patterns without a lexicon entry and returns the identified suffixes with an unknown stem. TRmorph ships such a guesser (Çöltekin 2010); for Apertium languages, check whether the module provides one.
Neural fall-back. For words the FST cannot analyse, a neural analyser can be used as a fall-back. TurkicNLP’s morpheme segmenter takes this hybrid approach: the Apertium reading that accounts for the whole word is preferred, and the neural analyser breaks ties and handles unknown words. On a constructed 483-word set covering 20 Turkic languages and 13 morphological categories, the hybrid reaches 89% exact segmentation, versus 79% for Apertium alone and 68% for the neural analyser alone (Hakimov 2026, Appendix E). These are diagnostic results: the gold segmentations are rated high, medium or low confidence by language, and the words are constructed test items, not an independent natural-text benchmark.


6.5.4 Generation for Machine Translation
Translation into Turkish requires both a suitable lemma and its inflected form. Case, number and the appropriate accusative allomorph all depend on the sentence. Morphological generation can supply the surface form once those choices have been made.
This morphological realisation step can be decomposed into two sub-tasks: (1) determine the required feature bundle from the source-side and target-side context; (2) generate the correct surface form from the lemma and features using the FST generator. This decomposition is used in the Apertium rule-based MT system (Forcada et al. 2011). For neural MT, Tamchyna, Weller-Di Marco, and Fraser (2017) train a system to output lemmas and morphological tags and generate the inflected forms in a separate deterministic step, for Czech and German targets.

title: 6  Finite-State Morphology: The Rule-Based Approach
text:
6.6 Limitations of the Finite-State Approach
The finite-state approach is powerful but has known limitations that motivate the neural methods in Chapter 7.
Lexicon coverage. A lexicon-based FST without guessing generally requires a licensed stem; productive compound rules and unknown-word guessers can extend that coverage. Loanwords, proper nouns, neologisms, and highly technical vocabulary are frequently unrecognised, and lexicon size varies greatly across the Turkic modules. A low feature-fill rate in Table 6.1 could also reflect tag mapping or annotation choices, so diagnose failures before attributing them to lexicon size.
Lexicon maintenance. Keeping the lexicon current requires ongoing manual effort, since new loanwords and names keep entering the written language. A static FST lexicon becomes increasingly incomplete over time without active maintenance.
Disambiguation is separate. The FST returns the analyses licensed by its implemented grammar for an ambiguous form; it does not choose among them. Disambiguation requires additional components (constraint-grammar rules, statistical taggers or neural rerankers) and, for the learned ones, training data. TurkicNLP falls back on transducer weights and heuristic scores (syntactic position, part-of-speech priority, question particles) where no trained disambiguator exists (Hakimov 2026).
Limited contextual information. The morphological grammars described here do not by themselves model sentence-level semantic plausibility. A statistical or neural disambiguator can use context to choose among their analyses.
Cross-lingual reuse is partial. While the suffix template is shared, each language still requires a new lexicon file and careful adjustment of phonological rules. For a completely new, undocumented language, building an FST requires substantial linguistic fieldwork.
Despite these limitations, finite-state morphology remains a foundation of Turkic morphological processing, particularly for languages with no annotated data. The two approaches can be combined, as in the TurkicNLP segmenter described above, where the transducer and the neural analyser cover different failures.

section: 6.7 Hands-On: A Procedure for Comparing Rule-Based and Neural Analysis
text:
6.7 Hands-On: A Procedure for Comparing Rule-Based and Neural Analysis
Question. How do rule-based and neural analyses differ on the same input?
Inputs. The three sentences below, both morphological backends and the Turkish generator.
Compute. CPU inference is possible; the neural checkpoint requires a separate model download and more memory than the FST.
Output. Side-by-side analyses and generated Turkish forms.
Interpretation. Check disagreements against a linguistic analysis; use generated paradigms to inspect alternations.
This example analyses the same sentence in Turkish, Kazakh, and Kyrgyz with both of TurkicNLP’s morphological backends, the Apertium transducers (morph) and the multilingual neural analyser (morph_neural). It then generates Turkish forms with the Apertium generator.
# pip install "turkicnlp[hfst,transformers]==0.5.0"   # Apertium and neural backends
import turkicnlp

sentences = {
    "tur": "Kitaplarımızdan birini okuyamadı.",
    "kaz": "Кітаптарымыздың бірін оқи алмады.",
    "kir": "Китептерибизден бирин окуй алган жок.",
}

for lang, sentence in sentences.items():
    turkicnlp.download(lang, processors=["tokenize", "morph", "morph_neural"])
    for proc in ["morph", "morph_neural"]:
        nlp = turkicnlp.Pipeline(lang, processors=["tokenize", proc], tokenize_backend="rule")
        doc = nlp(sentence)
        print(f"\n--- {lang} / {proc} ---")
        for w in doc.words:
            print(f"  {w.text:<28} {w.lemma or '_':<14} {w.upos or '_':<6} {w.feats or '_'}")
Compare the two backends word by word. Where do they agree? Which words does the transducer leave unanalysed, and which features does the neural analyser assign that are wrong? Repeat with a language that has only a prototype transducer (e.g., alt or kjh) and relate what you see to Table 6.1.
Then generate with the Turkish generator, using generate() from Section 6.5:
for tags in ["<n><nom>", "<n><acc>", "<n><px1sg><nom>", "<n><px1sg><abl>"]:
    print(tags, generate("kitap" + tags))
# <n><nom> ['kitap']
# <n><acc> ['kitabı']
# <n><px1sg><nom> ['kitabım']
# <n><px1sg><abl> ['kitabımdan']
Note the consonant alternation: kitap (bare) vs. kitab- before the vowel-initial suffixes shown here. (Tag names follow Apertium conventions; inspect the analyser’s output for a word to see the exact tag sequence the generator expects.)
Status: procedure only. The full three-language comparison is not reported here. Exercises 4 and 5 record related generation and backend comparisons.

title: 6  Finite-State Morphology: The Rule-Based Approach
text:
What to Take Forward
A finite-state analyser combines a lexicon, allowed morph sequences and spelling rules. Inverting the relation supports generation. On the TurkicNLP diagnostic, transducers detect the target feature more often than the neural analyser (74% against 67%), while supplying non-empty feature bundles less often (65% against 88%). Coverage and correctness need separate measures: use lookup failures to find gaps, annotated examples to assess readings, and regression tests after rule changes. Chapter 7 turns to neural tokenisation and tagging.
