title: 8  Syntactic Structure and Universal Dependencies
text:
8.5 Cross-Lingual Parsing

8.5.1 Zero-Shot and Proxy-Language Transfer
In zero-shot parsing, a model trained on one or more Turkic treebanks is applied to a language absent from that training. A multilingual encoder supports this setup. The ten-language parser in Table 8.7 reaches conditional LAS in the mid-40s on small Karakalpak, Kumyk and Sakha samples, using a related language’s proxy embedding (Hakimov 2026). Exercise 4 tests a single-source baseline on gold words: the Stanza Turkish (IMST) parser scores LAS 43.2 on Azerbaijani TueCL and 64.3 on the Turkish versions of those sentences. Both experiments show transfer, but their different test sets and conditions prevent a direct comparison of the approaches.
The principal failure modes are:
Label conventions. Even when the parser finds the right head, it often assigns a label according to the source treebanks’ conventions. Language-specific annotation decisions (light verbs, copulas, compound nouns) differ between Turkic treebanks, and the parser cannot infer the target language’s conventions without target data.
Unseen function words and constructions. Postpositions, particles and auxiliaries can differ between related languages. Check their attachment errors separately rather than assuming that familiar suffix patterns are enough for transfer.
Script mismatch. An unfamiliar script can reduce the lexical information available to an encoder. Shared syntactic patterns may still transfer, but script coverage and parsing accuracy each need their own check.


8.5.2 Script Normalisation
A Turkish-only encoder may represent Cyrillic Kazakh or Arabic-script Uyghur poorly. A multilingual encoder can already know both scripts even if its parsing fine-tuning used only Turkish. Two options are worth comparing: convert input to the model’s script and map predictions back, or train across scripts with script-specific adapters. TurkicNLP supports input-to-model script bridging within a language (Section 3.4); applying a Turkish model to another language still needs an explicit mapping and evaluation.
Shared-script conversion can increase cognate overlap (Section 3.6). Exercise 4 tests its effect on the Stanza Turkish parser with gold words. On Kyrgyz TueCL, LAS rises from 6.2 with Cyrillic input to 22.4 with word-by-word CTS conversion. On Kazakh KTB, it rises from 9.1 to 18.1 with the 2021 Kazakh Latin alphabet and to 27.2 with CTS. Conversion helps in these runs, though the in-language Kyrgyz KTMU model still scores 29.1 on the same Kyrgyz sentences.


8.5.3 Silver Treebanks and Annotation Projection
When a language has no treebank, training data can be created automatically.
Silver treebanks by translation. Translate sentences from an existing treebank (e.g., a Turkish training split) into the target language with an MT system or an LLM, and annotate the translations automatically with the best available analysers and parsers, followed by automatic validation. TurkicNLP’s Turkmen and Bashkir models were trained this way (Hakimov 2026). Silver data is noisy and inherits the source treebank’s sentence types and annotation decisions. A test set built the same way (the ‡ rows in Table 8.7) mainly measures agreement with the process that produced it, so it gives only indicative scores.
Two rules prevent leakage. Split the source material by sentence or document before translating, projecting or producing silver labels, so that no translation of a test sentence ends up in training data. And never train on translations of the sentences used for evaluation, including published parallel test sets such as UD-Turkic or PUD. FLORES-200 is an evaluation resource: use only its designated development split, if any, for tuning, and keep its test split untouched.
Annotation projection uses an existing parallel corpus instead:

Parse the source side (e.g., Turkish) with a high-quality parser.
Align source and target words with a word aligner (e.g., awesome-align or fast_align).
Project dependency arcs through the alignment: if source words \(i\) and \(j\) are aligned to target words \(i'\) and \(j'\), and there is an arc \((i, j)\) in the source parse, propose the arc \((i', j')\) in the target, then repair the result into a valid tree.

The quality of projection depends heavily on alignment precision and coverage, which must be measured for the pair and domain; related vocabulary and similar constituent order can help but do not ensure one-to-one alignment. Exercise 5 projects the Turkish TueCL gold trees onto the Azerbaijani versions of the same 148 sentences with a simple string-similarity aligner. Only 39.4% of the Azerbaijani words receive the right head and label overall, but 83.5% do among the words whose own link and whose head’s link both exist; with Stanza parses instead of gold trees the figures fall to 30.9% and 65.6%. In this experiment, restricting evaluation to aligned words hides much of the projection failure. Report the all-word score alongside the conditional one. Parallel training text is available, for example, from the TIL corpus (Mirzakhalov et al. 2021) and OPUS; FLORES-200 should be reserved for evaluation.

title: 8  Syntactic Structure and Universal Dependencies
section: 8.6 Building a Treebank for a New Turkic Language
text:
8.6 Building a Treebank for a New Turkic Language
A manually checked treebank provides a reference for evaluating transfer and, if it includes training data, for adaptation. Plan its purpose, genres and annotation conventions before collecting sentences. One possible workflow is:

Choose the sentences. Start with the UD-Turkic parallel sentences (Akhundjanova et al. 2025): they come with annotated counterparts in related languages, so every decision can be compared, and they immediately yield a parallel test set. Then add natural text (news, Wikipedia, fiction) with a clear licence, ideally a few hundred sentences from at least two genres.
Document the guidelines. Write down the decisions for the constructions where Turkic treebanks diverge: light verb constructions (compound:lvc or not), copular clauses and the copula clitics, multi-word token splitting of clitics and suffixed particles, converb chains and coordination, and the treatment of possessive compounds (dil reform-u). Start from the UD guidelines and the target language’s grammar. Compare nearby treebanks, document the chosen conventions and explain departures.
Pre-annotate automatically. Run the best available pipeline (the multilingual parser with a suitable proxy language, a related language’s model after transliteration, or projected annotation) and correct its output rather than annotating from scratch. Record which tool produced the pre-annotation.
Annotate with a UD tool such as Arborator-Grew or ConlluEditor, which validate the format as you go.
Double-annotate a sample. Have two annotators annotate the same 50–100 sentences independently and report agreement (UAS/LAS between annotators and agreement on UPOS and features); discuss disagreements and update the guidelines.
Validate and release. Run the official UD validation script, write the README and metadata (sources, licence, annotators, pre-annotation tools), and submit to Universal Dependencies so the treebank appears in the regular releases.

Case study: a Turkmen treebank. Turkmen has a mature Latin orthography, an Apertium transducer and a silver Stanza model, but no released treebank in the UD 2.17 inventory. One approach would translate Turkish TueCL and IMST sentences into Turkmen, using NLLB drafts corrected by native speakers. The Apertium morphological analyser alone cannot translate Turkish into Turkmen.
Next, pre-annotate the translations with the silver model and multilingual parser, and project the Turkish gold annotation for comparison. Trained speakers would correct the results using documented Turkmen guidelines aligned with UD. Fix the split by source sentence before starting: TueCL and IMST test translations belong in test data, and IMST training translations in training data. This would yield a manually checked parallel test set alongside corrected training material.

section: 8.7 Hands-On: Parsing Turkish Text with TurkicNLP
text:
8.7 Hands-On: Parsing Turkish Text with TurkicNLP
Question. Which dependencies does a pretrained parser recover, and how does it transfer?
Inputs. The example sentences, Turkish PUD and Azerbaijani TueCL, with the declared parser resources.
Compute. CPU inference; download the relevant Stanza/toolkit models.
Output. CoNLL-U predictions and attachment scores under a stated alignment policy.
Interpretation. Inspect roots, relative clauses and cross-language lexical errors alongside aggregate scores.
This tutorial parses Turkish with the Stanza biaffine parser (Qi et al. 2020) through TurkicNLP, reads and writes CoNLL-U, and evaluates on the Turkish PUD test set. It then applies the Turkish parser to Azerbaijani text as a zero-shot experiment and compares it with the Azerbaijani and multilingual parsers in TurkicNLP.

8.7.1 Parsing a Turkish Sentence
# pip install "turkicnlp[stanza]==0.5.0"   # Stanza backend; models download from the Hugging Face Hub
import turkicnlp

turkicnlp.download("tur", processors=["tokenize", "pos", "lemma", "depparse"])
nlp_tr = turkicnlp.Pipeline("tur", processors=["tokenize", "pos", "lemma", "depparse"],
                            pos_backend="stanza", lemma_backend="stanza", depparse_backend="stanza")

sentence = "Atatürk'ün 1928'de başlattığı dil reformu Türkiye'yi kökten değiştirdi."
doc = nlp_tr(sentence)

print(f"{'ID':<4} {'FORM':<14} {'LEMMA':<10} {'UPOS':<6} {'HEAD':<5} DEPREL")
for word in doc.words:
    print(f"{word.id:<4} {word.text:<14} {word.lemma:<10} {word.upos:<6} {word.head:<5} {word.deprel}")
Output (TurkicNLP 0.5.0 with the Stanza IMST models):
ID   FORM           LEMMA      UPOS   HEAD  DEPREL
1    Atatürk'ün     Atatürk    PROPN  3     nsubj
2    1928'de        1928       NUM    3     obl
3    başlattığı     başla      VERB   5     acl
4    dil            dil        NOUN   5     nmod:poss
5    reformu        reform     NOUN   7     nsubj
6    Türkiye'yi     Türkiye    PROPN  7     obj
7    kökten         kök        NOUN   0     root
8    değiştirdi     değiş      VERB   7     compound
9    .              .          PUNCT  7     punct
The relative-clause attachment matches the intended analysis. The participle başlattığı (word 3) takes Atatürk’ün and 1928’de as dependents. It attaches as acl to reformu (word 5), with dil between them.
The main-clause analysis is wrong. The parser treats kökten değiştirdi ‘changed radically’ as a noun-plus-verb predicate: it makes kökten the root and attaches the verb with compound. The intended root is değiştirdi, with kökten as an adverbial modifier. This resembles IMST’s nominal-headed complex-predicate convention (Table 8.3), although a single example is too little to identify the cause.
The output was reproduced exactly on 19 October 2026 with Stanza 1.11.0 and the same IMST checkpoints. Its lemmas also reduce the causative stems başlat- and değiştir- to başla- and değiş-. Check the treebank’s lemma convention before counting those reductions as errors.


8.7.2 Reading and Writing CoNLL-U
Every TurkicNLP document can be written as CoNLL-U, and CoNLL-U files can be read back into documents:
from turkicnlp.utils.conllu import read_conllu, write_conllu

write_conllu(doc, "output.conllu")            # or: print(doc.to_conllu())

for sent in read_conllu("output.conllu")[0].sentences:
    roots = [w for w in sent.words if w.head == 0]
    if len(roots) != 1:
        raise ValueError("expected exactly one root")
    root = roots[0]
    by_id = {w.id: w for w in sent.words if isinstance(w.id, int)}
    print(f"Root: {root.text!r}  ({root.deprel})")
    print(f"Sentence length: {len(sent.words)} words")
    # ordinary words only: integer IDs with a non-root head
    # (multiword-token ranges and empty nodes are not Word objects with integer IDs)
    arcs = [(abs(w.id - w.head), w) for w in sent.words
            if isinstance(w.id, int) and isinstance(w.head, int) and w.head > 0]
    max_arc = max((span for span, _ in arcs), default=0)
    longest = [f"{by_id[w.head].text}->{w.text}" for span, w in arcs if span == max_arc]
    print(f"Longest non-root arc span: {max_arc} ({', '.join(longest)})")
    for head, rel, dep in sent.dependencies:     # (head word, relation, dependent)
        print(f"  {head.text if head else 'ROOT':<12} --{rel}--> {dep.text}")
Computed from the printed tree (nine words including the final punctuation), the longest non-root arc spans two words, and four arcs tie: başlattığı → Atatürk’ün (3→1), reformu → başlattığı (5→3), kökten → reformu (7→5) and kökten → . (7→9). It is that short partly because the parser wrongly made kökten the root and attached the subject reformu to it. With the intended analysis, the arc değiştirdi → reformu (8→5) would span three words. Arc lengths are a quick check on where a parser has placed the long dependencies, but in short sentences like this one they are small whatever the analysis.


8.7.3 Evaluating on the Turkish PUD Test Set
The pinned Turkish PUD file contains 1,000 gold-annotated sentences (Table 8.5). Record the parser package/model hashes, UD release and scorer revision with the output. Parse the raw text of the test set, write CoNLL-U, and score it with the official CoNLL 2018 shared task evaluation script (conll18_ud_eval.py), which handles tokenisation mismatches between gold and predicted files:
import subprocess
import sys
from turkicnlp.utils.conllu import write_conllu

# raw text of tr_pud-ud-test.conllu (the "# text =" lines)
from pathlib import Path
blocks = Path("tr_pud-ud-test.conllu").read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip().split("\n\n")
texts = [[line[9:] for line in block.splitlines() if line.startswith("# text = ")]
         for block in blocks]
if not texts or any(len(lines) != 1 for lines in texts):
    raise ValueError("expected one original text per gold sentence")
raw = "\n".join(lines[0] for lines in texts)
write_conllu(nlp_tr(raw), "tr_pud_predicted.conllu")

try:
    result = subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, "conll18_ud_eval.py", "-v",      # same Python as this session
         "tr_pud-ud-test.conllu", "tr_pud_predicted.conllu"],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True,
    )
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as err:
    print(err.stderr)                                    # e.g. text mismatch between files
    raise
print(result.stdout)
# Reports tokenisation F1, UPOS, UFeats, AllTags, Lemmas, UAS, LAS, MLAS, BLEX


8.7.4 Zero-Shot Application to Azerbaijani
Azerbaijani uses the Latin alphabet, the same script as Turkish, so a Turkish parser can be applied directly. Compare it with the Azerbaijani-specific and multilingual parsers in TurkicNLP:
az_sentence = "Əhməd dünən aldığı kitabı bu gün oxudu."
# "Today Ahmad read the book he bought yesterday."

parsers = {
    "Turkish Stanza (zero-shot)": nlp_tr,
    "Azerbaijani (custom Stanza)": turkicnlp.Pipeline(
        "aze", processors=["tokenize", "pos", "depparse"], pos_backend="stanza",
        depparse_backend="stanza"),
    "Multilingual (Glot500)": turkicnlp.Pipeline(
        "aze", processors=["tokenize", "pos", "depparse"],
        pos_backend="multilingual_glot500_model",
        depparse_backend="multilingual_glot500_model"),
}
for name, nlp in parsers.items():
    print(name)
    for w in nlp(az_sentence).words:
        print(f"  {w.text:<14} {w.upos:<6} {w.head} {w.deprel}")
For the Turkish parser, the Stanza IMST models (Stanza 1.11.0, run directly rather than through TurkicNLP) give:
Turkish Stanza (zero-shot)
  Əhməd          PROPN  3 nsubj
  dünən          NOUN   3 obj
  aldığı         VERB   4 acl
  kitabı         NOUN   0 root
  bu             DET    6 det
  gün            NOUN   7 obl
  oxudu          NOUN   4 conj
  .              PUNCT  7 punct
The participial clause dünən aldığı kitabı is found, but the Azerbaijani words that differ from Turkish fail: dünən ‘yesterday’ (Turkish dün) becomes an object, and the main verb oxudu ‘read’ (Turkish okudu) is tagged as a noun and attached as a conjunct of kitabı, which becomes the root. Running the same loop prints the Azerbaijani and multilingual parsers’ analyses for comparison.
Scoring the three parsers on the Azerbaijani TueCL test set (Akhundjanova et al. 2025) with conll18_ud_eval.py turns this comparison into an experiment (Exercise 4).






NoteExtending to Cyrillic Turkic Languages



To parse Kazakh or Kyrgyz text with the Turkish model, first convert the input to a Latin-based script with the toolkit’s transliteration mapping (Kazakh has several published Latin designs, so record which mapping is used; or use CTS for both languages; Chapter 3), apply the Turkish pipeline, and map the analyses back to the original word forms. Whether transliteration helps for a given language pair is an empirical question: compare the native-script multilingual parser, the transliterated Turkish parser and, where available, an in-language model on the same test set (Exercise 4). For Kazakh, turkicnlp.Pipeline("kaz", processors=["tokenize", "pos", "lemma", "depparse"]) uses the Stanza model trained on the Kazakh KTB treebank, and the multilingual Glot500 parser covers Kazakh, Kyrgyz and the zero-shot languages Karakalpak, Kumyk, Sakha, Karachay-Balkar and Nogai.


Status: demonstration. The sentence analyses above are recorded output. Exercise 4 records the separate scored transfer comparison.

title: 8  Syntactic Structure and Universal Dependencies
text:
What to Take Forward
Dependency parsing recovers sentence structure from morphology, position and context, and UD makes the labels comparable while leaving language-specific choices visible. The measured patterns are clear: among BOUN training sentences with an overt subject and object, 87.1% are SOV, and the Stanza Turkish parser’s attachment score falls from 83.3% for adjacent words to 43.9% at distances of eight or more. Choose training and test treebanks from the named release inventory, and report alignment and scoring conventions with every score. Chapter 9 applies the same care to word-level labels and entity spans.

title: 8  Syntactic Structure and Universal Dependencies
text:
Further Reading
For the linguistic foundations of Turkic syntax, Johanson (2021) (Chapters 51–56, from p. 788; especially §54.7, §55 and §§56.3–56.4) discusses pro-drop, scrambling, participial clauses, converbs, postpositions, and coordination. The computational consequences of SOV order and participial subordination for parsing are discussed in the context of Turkish NLP by Oflazer and Saraçlar (2018); Eryiğit, Nivre, and Oflazer (2008) studies Turkish dependency parsing over inflectional groups, and Hoffman (1994) relates Turkish word orders to topic and focus.
The Universal Dependencies framework is defined in Marneffe et al. (2021), which covers the annotation philosophy, the design of UD relation types, and cross-linguistic consistency. The original multilingual treebank collection is described in Nivre et al. (2016). The Turkish BOUN treebank, a multi-genre treebank widely used for Turkish parser training, is described in detail in Türk et al. (2022). The Kazakh UD treebank and its annotation principles are described in Tyers and Washington (2015). The UD-Turkic parallel treebanks enabling cross-language annotation comparison are described in Akhundjanova et al. (2025). Per-language and multilingual parsing on twelve Turkic languages, including three zero-shot languages and two silver test sets, is evaluated in Hakimov (2026).
The biaffine dependency parser, one of the most widely used graph-based architectures, is introduced in Dozat and Manning (2017). McDonald and Nivre (2007) compare the error profiles of graph-based and transition-based parsers, and Kulmizev et al. (2019) revisit the comparison with contextual embeddings. Stanza, which provides accessible biaffine parsers for multiple Turkic languages, is described in Qi et al. (2020). TurkishDelightNLP (Alecakir, Bölücü, and Can 2022) uses LSTM-based joint morphology and syntax modelling for Turkish; check its reported scores against the UD release and metric you use.
Chapter 16 of this book extends the cross-lingual parsing discussion to a full treatment of transfer strategies by resource level.

title: 8  Syntactic Structure and Universal Dependencies
text:
Exercises

Scrambling and case. Write a Python function that takes a Turkish sentence in CoNLL-U format, identifies the subject (nsubj), object (obj), and root verb, and reports their relative positions (subject-before-verb? object-before-verb?). Apply it to the first 100 sentences of the TR-BOUN training split that contain an overt subject and an overt object of the root (report how many sentences you had to skip). What percentage of sentences have canonical SOV order? What order variants appear, and how often?
Participial arc length. First inspect how the treebank you choose labels relative clauses: some Turkish treebanks use plain acl for participial modifiers, so an empty acl:relcl query does not mean there are no relative clauses. Using TR-BOUN gold data read with read_conllu (and, separately, the TurkicNLP Turkish pipeline), compute for each participial modifier the three quantities of Section 8.1: clause width, the longest dependent-to-participle distance, and the participle-to-noun distance. Compare the participle-to-noun distance with the distance of acl:relcl arcs in English UD (EN-EWT). Plot the distributions and report the median and 90th percentile of each. Which of the three quantities differs most between the languages?
Pro-drop counting. Read the Turkish IMST training set with turkicnlp.utils.conllu.read_conllu (gold annotation). Select eligible predicates: finite verbs (VerbForm=Fin or no VerbForm with Person/Number agreement) that are not imperatives and not passive. A missing nsubj is not proof of pro-drop: also count nsubj:pass, csubj and other subject relations, and treat nonfinite clauses separately. For eligible predicates, compute the proportion with an overt subject per tense-mood combination (e.g., Tense=Past|Mood=Ind). Manually adjudicate a random sample of 50 “subjectless” cases and report how many are genuine pro-drop versus annotation errors or other constructions. Then parse the same text with the TurkicNLP Turkish pipeline: does the parser reproduce the gold proportions?
Cross-lingual parser evaluation. Apply the Turkish parser (turkicnlp.Pipeline("tur", processors=["tokenize", "pos", "depparse"])) to the Kyrgyz TueCL and Kazakh KTB test sets and compute UAS and LAS. Repeat after conversion to the 2021 Kazakh Latin alphabet or CTS for Kazakh, and CTS for Kyrgyz, which has no toolkit Latin mapping.
Keep a verified word-by-word map to the original. Restore FORM values only for one-to-one alignments before scoring: conll18_ud_eval.py aligns text characters, so converted strings cannot be scored against the original gold file directly. If tokenisation changes, reconstruct the original character spans explicitly; list position alone is insufficient.
Compare with Kyrgyz KTMU on Kyrgyz TueCL and Kazakh KTB on KTB. Treat the latter as an exposure-risk diagnostic because historical training membership remains unknown (Section 8.4). Also test the multilingual parser (depparse_backend="multilingual_glot500_model") on original Cyrillic input and the three hands-on parsers on Azerbaijani TueCL. How does LAS change, and which dependency relations cause the most errors?
Annotation projection experiment. Projected arcs can only be scored against gold annotation of the same target sentences. The Turkish and Azerbaijani TueCL treebanks (Akhundjanova et al. 2025) annotate the same sentences, so they provide such pairs. Parse the Turkish side with the TurkicNLP Turkish pipeline (and, as a separate comparison, use the Turkish gold trees), align words with fast_align or awesome-align, project the arcs to Azerbaijani, repair the result into a tree, and score it against the Azerbaijani gold. What fraction of arcs project correctly? Which dependency types project most reliably? How much of the error comes from alignment rather than from the Turkish parse?

title: 9  Sequence Labelling: POS Tagging, NER, and Chunking
text:
9.1 POS Tagging and Morphological Analysis
Sequence labelling assigns labels to tokens or spans. This chapter focuses on named entity recognition (NER): finding mentions such as people, organisations and places. It also covers POS tagging, phrase chunking and semantic role labelling.
These tasks use different labels. POS tagging assigns grammatical categories to words. NER marks mention boundaries and types. Chunking groups words into shallow phrases. Semantic role labelling identifies a predicate’s arguments and their roles.
Morphology matters in each task. Names can carry case suffixes, POS tags depend on the chosen word analysis, and omitted arguments require a separate treatment in semantic analysis. The examples below distinguish these linguistic issues from dataset-specific annotation rules.
crumbs: 9  Sequence Labelling: POS Tagging, NER, and Chunking

title: 9  Sequence Labelling: POS Tagging, NER, and Chunking
text:
9.1.1 POS Tagging and Morphological Disambiguation
POS tags capture some grammatical distinctions; morphological features supply others. This division applies to English as well as Turkic languages, and its details depend on the annotation scheme.
Choosing a full analysis also chooses a POS tag: selecting yüz+Num assigns UPOS=NUM. The reverse does not hold. Turkish evi can mean ‘his/her house’ or ‘the house (ACC)’; both readings are nouns. Joint models such as TurkishDelightNLP (Alecakir, Bölücü, and Can 2022) share information between POS and morphological prediction.
Compare joint prediction with a POS-only baseline on the same data. The neural morphology tutorial provides one joint tagging design (Section 7.6).


9.1.2 The UPOS Set for Turkic
UD uses 17 universal POS categories. The following distinctions need attention in Turkic annotation.
VERB vs. AUX. Turkish light verb constructions include yardım etmek “to help”, literally “to do help”. The status of verbs such as et-, yap- and ol- depends on the construction and the treebank’s annotation policy. Inspect those guidelines before combining datasets (Section 8.2). A disagreement between VERB and AUX can reflect an annotation mismatch; it can also be a model error within a consistently annotated dataset.
ADP. Postpositions are common in Turkic languages; both prepositions and postpositions are tagged ADP in UPOS. The postposition follows its complement nominal, so a strictly left-to-right model sees the postposition only after the nominal it relates to, the reverse of English order. Bidirectional encoders see both, so this matters mainly for incremental (left-to-right) taggers.
NOUN vs. PROPN. Proper names can take the same suffixes as common nouns, and a common noun can also be used as a name. Context helps distinguish them. Capitalisation and gazetteers provide additional evidence, but neither is required to be correct or complete.
PART. “Particle” is a linguistic description, not a guarantee of UPOS=PART. Turkish question mı/mi/mu/mü and additive da/de are written separately in standard orthography. Treebanks may assign different categories to them, including AUX for the question marker; inspect the selected treebank’s UPOS and dependency conventions rather than inferring them from a suffix-like pronunciation.


9.1.3 Evaluation Results Across Turkic Languages
Table 8.7 compares per-language Stanza models with a multilingual tagger. Its frozen manuscript snapshot reports higher UPOS for the multilingual system on Uzbek (71.8 → 87.6) and Kyrgyz (71.1 → 79.0). The scores cover matched words only, and the table includes gold and silver reference sets. Differences beyond multilingual training may contribute to the results; Section 8.4 gives the source and scoring conditions.


9.1.4 Cross-Lingual POS Tagging
Zero-shot POS tagging applies a model to a language without task-specific training on that language. The small Karakalpak and Kumyk samples in Table 8.7 illustrate this setup with proxy-language embeddings. Report per-tag errors as well as the overall score; shared suffix patterns cannot predict which POS categories will transfer best.

section: 9.2 Named Entity Recognition in Agglutinative Languages
text:
9.2 Named Entity Recognition in Agglutinative Languages

9.2.1 The Case Suffix Problem
Inflected names raise two separate questions: can a system recognise an unfamiliar surface form, and where should the annotated mention end? The first concerns generalisation; the second depends on the dataset’s boundary policy.
Capitalisation helps, but entities need not be capitalised. Informal Latin- and Cyrillic-script text may omit capitals. Perso-Arabic writing, including Ottoman Turkish, has no upper/lowercase distinction. NER therefore also needs contextual and lexical evidence.
Entities inflect. Names take suffixes, but not every mention has an overt case marker. An unmarked form is not necessarily a subject. The Kazakh city name Алматы (Almaty) illustrates the surface variation:



Table 9.1: The Kazakh city name Алматы in six cases (the instrumental Алматымен ‘with Almaty’ is a seventh). A recogniser needs to detect mentions in these inflected forms; resolving their identity is a separate task. In Turkish, the apostrophe (Almatı’ya, Almatı’dan) separates the name from its suffix in formal writing, but is often omitted in informal text (Almatıya, Almatıdan).

A dictionary that matches only Алматы misses Алматыдан. A learned model may also struggle with inflected forms that are rare in its training data. Exercise 1 tests this by measuring the distribution of case forms and recall for each case.
Mention boundaries depend on annotation. Turkish Ankara’da contains the name Ankara and a locative suffix. A dataset may label the whole token or only the name. The apostrophe helps locate the suffix in formal Turkish, but informal Ankarada lacks it. Kazakh Алматыдан likewise has no separator. Follow the chosen annotation policy rather than assuming that every NER span must stop at the stem. The recurring Uzbek sentence (Table 1.4) has the same choice to make for Toshkentda ‘in Tashkent’, while Kazakh Қазақстан appears unmarked.


9.2.2 BIO Tagging Strategies
The standard BIO (Begin, Inside, Outside) tagging scheme labels each token as either the beginning of an entity span (B-TYPE), the continuation of a span (I-TYPE), or outside any span (O). Two possible labelling units are words and morphological segments:
Word-level BIO. Tag each word token with a BIO label, including the case suffix. Алматыдан → B-LOC. The entity boundary is the word boundary. This matches datasets whose mention spans include the suffix.
Morpheme-level BIO. Segment words into morphemes before tagging, then tag each morpheme. Алматы-дан → B-LOC, O. This example assumes a stem-only boundary policy. Possessive and derivational forms (Алматылық ‘from Almaty, Almaty-an’) need explicit rules. The cost is a morphological segmenter as a required upstream component, and the segmenter’s errors can affect mention boundaries (Chapter 6 and Chapter 7).
Neither strategy by itself produces a canonical name or an entity identity. Three outputs should be kept apart, as in this example:



Table 9.2: Three different outputs for one Kazakh mention. A stem-only span is not necessarily the canonical name (multiword names, aliases and inflected modifiers inside names need their own rules), and a canonical name is not yet an identity: ambiguous names need linking.










Output
Example for Алматыдан келдім ‘I came from Almaty’
Task




Mention span in the original text
zero-based span [0, 9), Алматыдан, LOC
NER (what datasets annotate)


Normalised name
Алматы
name normalisation (lemmatisation, rules for multiword and possessive names)


Linked entity
the city of Almaty, represented by an identifier in the chosen knowledge base, or unresolved
entity linking






Score mention spans against each dataset’s own boundary policy, and evaluate normalisation and linking as separate tasks.
KazNERD (Yeshpanov, Khassanov, and Varol 2022) and WikiANN (Pan et al. 2017) supply token-level labels, so the tutorial uses word-level BIO. Yeniterzi’s Turkish CRF study represents a word as a root state followed by morphological-feature states, while constraining those states to preserve the word’s entity label. This is different from excluding suffixes from mention spans. Its morpheme-level and word-level scores were 88.94 and 88.71 F1; the difference was not significant (Yeniterzi 2011, 107–9).

It separates human annotation from weak supervision and automatic projection, because they support different conclusions. KazNERD (Yeshpanov, Khassanov, and Varol 2022) is a human-annotated Kazakh NER dataset. Built from transcripts of Kazakh television news, it contains 112,702 sentences with 136,333 entity annotations in 25 classes (the pinned release has 136,337 B- tags). The best model in the original paper, a fine-tuned XLM-R-large, reached an exact-match F1 of 97.22% on the test set, ahead of BERT (96.24), a BiLSTM-CNN-CRF (93.51) and a CRF (92.41). Table 9.4 lists the classes with mention counts computed from the authors’ release.



Table 9.4: The 25 KazNERD entity classes (Yeshpanov, Khassanov, and Varol 2022), grouped for readability, with mention counts computed from the authors’ release (IOB2; 90,228 / 11,167 / 11,307 training / validation / test sentences; 109,346 / 13,483 / 13,508 mentions). Rare classes such as NON_HUMAN have too few test mentions for a meaningful per-class F1.

TurkicNLP ships a Stanza NER model trained on KazNERD for Kazakh and one trained on the Starlang NER corpus for Turkish; these are the two pretrained NER models described for toolkit version 0.5.0 (Hakimov 2026).
Turkish NER. Several Turkish NER datasets exist, among them MilliyetNER and the Turkish part of WikiANN, which Mukayese uses for its NER benchmark (Safaya et al. 2022), and those surveyed in Çöltekin, Doğruöz, and Çetinoğlu (2023). Check each dataset’s label inventory and boundary rules before combining it with another.
A practical challenge in Turkish NER is the apostrophe: formal Turkish writing separates proper names from their suffixes with an apostrophe (İstanbul’a “to Istanbul”), but informal text often omits it (İstanbula). A model trained on edited text may have lower recall on the apostrophe-less form; to check this, evaluate separately on mentions with and without the apostrophe.
Other languages. KyrgyzNER (Turatali et al. 2025) is a human-annotated news dataset with a 27-class scheme; 25 classes occur in the release. It provides training and test splits, with no development split. The paper’s count of 39,075 “entity mentions” counts entity-tagged tokens (B- plus I-); the release contains 16,819 spans. PERSON spans can include titles and positions, as in a whole … орун басары Тожибек Норов ‘deputy head … Tozhibek Norov’. KazNERD instead gives POSITION its own type.
An Uzbek legal dataset combines semi-automatic candidates, staged human review and synthetic records for rare labels. Its authors call it human-reviewed, with further work needed for a final gold standard (Saidov et al. 2026). A large Azerbaijani dataset on the Hugging Face Hub has a non-commercial licence, but its card leaves the annotation method unspecified (LocalDoc, n.d.). For Uyghur, Azmat et al. (2020) projected training labels from Chinese through machine translation. Comparisons across these resources need a declared label mapping and an account of their different domains, boundaries and annotation methods.
WikiANN / PAN-X (Pan et al. 2017) derives NER labels from Wikipedia links in 282 languages, using PER, ORG and LOC. Its Turkic splits vary greatly in size (Table 9.3). Turkish has 20,000 training sentences; Kyrgyz, Uyghur, Turkmen, Sakha, Bashkir, Chuvash and Crimean Tatar have 100 sentences per split. Link-derived labels can omit mentions or include noisy boundaries, and their coverage reflects Wikipedia’s entities. Scores describe performance on this automatically labelled material; evaluate on the intended domain before drawing conclusions about practical NER quality.
The gap. The October 2026 survey found human-annotated fine-grained datasets for Turkish, Kazakh and Kyrgyz, and human-reviewed legal data for Uzbek. It found no human-annotated NER resource for the other languages in the inventory, including Tatar, Bashkir, Turkmen and the Siberian Turkic languages. WikiANN supplies automatic labels for some of them. Check for newer or overlooked resources before starting an annotation project.


9.2.4 Neural NER Architectures
Character embedding + BiLSTM-CRF (Lample et al. 2016; Jurafsky and Martin 2024, chapter “Sequence Labelling for Parts of Speech and Named Entities”) was widely used before pretrained transformers. The character-level BiLSTM is useful for Turkic: it encodes the surface form of each word, including its suffix pattern, which can help with unseen inflections of known entity stems: a model that has seen Алматы in training shares the character prefix with Алматыдан at test time.
Transformer token classification is the architecture used in the tutorial. A pretrained encoder produces a contextual embedding for each subword; a linear head predicts the BIO label. The encoder may be monolingual (BERTurk for Turkish) or multilingual (XLM-R, which was pretrained on text in many languages including several Turkic ones). Self-attention uses context within the model’s input window; the tutorial checks that each sentence fits.
Span-based NER predicts entity boundaries and types directly. It can represent nested mentions, such as Алматы inside Алматы облысының әкімдігі ‘the Almaty Region administration’. A single BIO sequence can encode only one non-overlapping layer. The datasets in Table 9.3 use flat annotation, so they do not test this ability. Computation depends on the number of candidate spans and how the model selects them.
For practical work on Turkic languages, XLM-R + token classification is a reasonable starting point: it starts from a multilingual encoder and is the architecture behind the best KazNERD result (Yeshpanov, Khassanov, and Varol 2022). How many annotated sentences a useful system needs depends on the label set, domain and acceptance criteria; measure it with a learning curve on a fixed test set rather than assuming a number. Exercise 3 draws one for Kyrgyz.

title: 9  Sequence Labelling: POS Tagging, NER, and Chunking
text:
9.3 Cross-Lingual NER Transfer

9.3.1 Encoder Coverage, Task Language and Script
Separate pretraining coverage, NER training data and input script. XLM-R was pretrained on Kazakh and Kyrgyz Cyrillic text (Conneau et al. 2020), so Turkish-only NER fine-tuning does not make Cyrillic input unknown to its encoder. But pretraining coverage does not guarantee accurate entity recognition: local names, context and label conventions still differ.
A fair comparison uses the same annotated target sentences under three conditions:

Native script: a multilingual model fine-tuned on source-language NER applied to the target text as written.
Transliterated: the same model applied to text converted to the source script (or to CTS), with predicted spans mapped back to the original string through a character-offset map. One-to-many letter changes shift offsets, so spans cannot be copied by position.
Target-language fine-tuning: the model fine-tuned on a small amount of annotated target-language data.

Script conversion may help or hurt, and recognising the script is not the same as recognising the entities.


9.3.2 Entity Distribution Shift
The entity distribution can also differ: people, organisations and places in one corpus need not appear in another. Measure this overlap instead of inferring it from language relatedness.
The recorded Exercise 4 compares PERSON name-token types in KazNERD training data and Starlang Turkish NER data. After the documented stem extraction, CTS conversion and lowercasing, their Jaccard overlap is 0.016; character-trigram overlap is 0.315. The figures describe two corpora under one normalisation method. Kazakh and Turkish names in general may behave differently. Analyse errors separately for names seen and unseen during training.


9.3.3 Label Schemes and Domains
KazNERD, WikiANN and KyrgyzNER use different label inventories and mention boundaries. Define a shared mapping before scoring. For example, collapsing GPE and LOCATION to LOC removes a distinction; mapping unsupported types to O excludes them from the task. Apply the same rules to gold and predictions, retain all tokens, and report the resulting label inventory and support. A label mapping does not fix boundary differences, such as whether a person’s title belongs inside the mention. Use one target test set for all systems and record its domain.


9.3.4 Zero-Shot vs. Few-Shot NER
The recorded Exercise 3 compares a pretrained Stanza KazNERD model with CRFs trained on KyrgyzNER, after mapping both datasets to PER, LOC and ORG. With gold words, zero-shot Stanza reaches 39.9 micro F1. The CRF averages 38.6 at 200 training sentences and 48.0 at 500 over three sampling seeds; one 200-sentence run reaches 42.1, above the zero-shot score. Training on all 7,033 sentences gives 62.6 in one run.
The mean first exceeds the zero-shot score at the tested 500-sentence setting. No general annotation budget follows from it, since the systems, training data and domains differ. KyrgyzNER’s inclusion of titles in PERSON spans also affects exact-match scoring. The comparison does not isolate the cause of the gap. The results describe the released test split. For a new tuned experiment, reserve development data from the training split, fix the sampling sizes and model settings there, and evaluate the fixed learning curve on test without further adjustment.

title: 9  Sequence Labelling: POS Tagging, NER, and Chunking
text:
9.4 Other Sequence Labelling Tasks

9.4.1 Chunking
Noun phrase chunking labels the beginning, continuation and outside of a phrase, for example B-NP, I-NP and O. Define the chunk first: a base noun phrase and a full phrase containing a relative clause are different targets.
Turkish constituent chunking has been studied with CRFs (Aslan, Gunal, and Dincer 2018). That study proposes an OE scheme that marks the final token of a chunk. Its reported advantage concerns the tested constituent-chunking setup; it would be a stretch to conclude that all Turkish phrase boundaries are easy to find. Prenominal modifiers and flexible word order still require explicit annotation rules (Section 8.1).


9.4.2 Semantic Role Labelling
Semantic role labelling (SRL) assigns predicate-argument roles to the participants of each event: who did what to whom, where, when, and how. In PropBank-style SRL, numbered roles are defined per predicate sense. ARG0 is typically the proto-agent and ARG1 the proto-patient; higher numbers depend on the frame. Roles do not map directly to grammatical relations: a passive subject need not be ARG0. Modifier roles such as ARGM-LOC (location) and ARGM-TMP (time) are shared across predicates.
Turkish SRL resources follow the PropBank convention: each verb sense has a frame with numbered argument roles. A first Turkish PropBank annotated sentences of a Turkish dependency treebank, using framesets of root verbs (Şahin and Adalı 2018); TRopBank extended the frame inventory to Turkish verb senses linked to the Turkish WordNet: its released frame file has 17,531 framesets (Kara et al. 2020).
Two issues from Chapter 2 matter for the task definition and evaluation:
Pro-drop. Subjects are often unexpressed (Section 8.1). Most SRL tasks annotate overt arguments only, so an unexpressed ARG0 should remain unlabelled under that policy. Recovering it requires a separate task definition and evaluation. Agreement can constrain person and number; identifying the referent also needs discourse evidence. In either task, follow the selected predicate frame’s role definitions.
Flexible word order. In a canonical English active transitive clause, the subject precedes the verb and the object follows it; their numbered roles still depend on the predicate frame. Turkic arguments can be reordered for discourse reasons. An SRL system therefore needs case, agreement and frame information as well as position. This is the same combination of signals as in dependency parsing (Section 8.1).
For languages other than Turkish, this survey identified no PropBank-style resource (searched October 2026; check for newer releases). Transfer from Turkish is one option, alongside multilingual models and target-language annotation. Cognate verbs may have similar frames, but light verbs and causative chains differ between languages, so transferred frames need language-specific checking.

section: 9.5 Pretrained Taggers and Recognisers in TurkicNLP
text:
9.5 Pretrained Taggers and Recognisers in TurkicNLP
TurkicNLP 0.5.0 provides Stanza and multilingual Glot500 POS backends, plus pretrained NER models for Turkish and Kazakh. Check the available processors and backends for each language rather than treating support as uniform across the toolkit.
# pip install "turkicnlp[stanza]==0.5.0"   # Stanza POS/NER backend
import turkicnlp

for lang, text in [("tur", "Ali dün Ankara'ya gitti."),
                   ("kaz", "Қасым-Жомарт Тоқаев кеше Астанада инвесторлармен кездесті.")]:
    nlp = turkicnlp.Pipeline(lang, processors=["tokenize", "pos", "ner"])
    doc = nlp(text)
    print([(w.text, w.upos, w.ner) for w in doc.words])
    print([(e.text, e.type) for e in doc.entities])
Output (TurkicNLP 0.5.0, Stanza backend):
[('Ali', 'PROPN', 'O'), ('dün', 'NOUN', 'O'), ("Ankara'ya", 'PROPN', 'B-LOCATION'), ('gitti', 'VERB', 'O'), ('.', 'PUNCT', 'O')]
[("Ankara'ya", 'LOCATION')]
[('Қасым-Жомарт', 'PROPN', 'B-PERSON'), ('Тоқаев', 'PROPN', 'I-PERSON'), ('кеше', 'ADV', 'B-DATE'), ('Астанада', 'PROPN', 'B-GPE'), ('инвесторлармен', 'NOUN', 'O'), ('кездесті', 'VERB', 'O'), ('.', 'PUNCT', 'O')]
[('Қасым-Жомарт Тоқаев', 'PERSON'), ('кеше', 'DATE'), ('Астанада', 'GPE')]
The outputs illustrate both annotation conventions and errors. Turkish uses Starlang labels such as LOCATION; Kazakh uses KazNERD’s finer inventory, including GPE and DATE. Both outputs include case suffixes in the mention. The Turkish model misses the person name Ali; its NOUN tag for dün ‘yesterday’ reflects a treebank choice for temporal words rather than a clear error, since treebanks differ on NOUN or ADV for such forms. The Kazakh model includes кеше ‘yesterday’ as DATE, following KazNERD’s inventory. Keep the printed predictions distinct from a manually checked reference.
Lemmas may help normalise a name, but they do not solve multiword-name normalisation or entity linking (Table 9.2). The example does not request the lemma processor; add it if the application needs lemmas.
For other languages, toolkit version 0.5.0 does not ship a pretrained NER model; this is not a claim that no model exists elsewhere. The toolkit can instead ask a large language model, through an OpenAI-compatible server (vLLM, Ollama), OpenAI, Claude, or a local Hugging Face model. The model labels the toolkit’s own tokens, and the toolkit checks its returned structure before storing it. A well-formed response can still carry wrong entity labels:
nlp = turkicnlp.Pipeline(
    "kir", processors=["tokenize", "ner"], ner_backend="llm",
    ner_labels=["PER", "LOC", "ORG"],
    llm_model="qwen2.5:7b", llm_base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", llm_api_key="ollama",
)
doc = nlp("Бишкекте Алмазбек Атамбаев менен жолугушуу өттү.")
print([(e.text, e.type) for e in doc.entities], doc._processor_log)
Measure exact span-and-type performance on an annotated sample before relying on the LLM backend (Exercise 6).

9.5.1 Measured pretrained KazNERD baseline
The cached Stanza KazNERD checkpoint was evaluated on all 11,307 sentences and 129,824 words in the pinned KazNERD test split (Yeshpanov, Khassanov, and Varol 2022). Gold sentence and word boundaries are supplied. An entity is correct only when its complete span and type match; all 25 types contribute to micro-averaged precision, recall and F1. Stanza BIOES predictions are decoded to strict spans, and an independent rescore with Stanza’s own entity decoder reproduces the totals.



Table 9.5: Measured cached Stanza KazNERD checkpoint on the complete pinned test split, with gold word/sentence boundaries and exact entity spans and types. No fine-tuning was performed. Source: run_ner.py; Yeshpanov, Khassanov, and Varol (2022).

Figure 9.1: Measured exact span-and-type F1 for the pretrained Stanza KazNERD checkpoint. Each label shows the number of gold test entities for that type; small-support categories should not be interpreted as equally precise estimates.



The pretrained Stanza checkpoint reaches 94.94% F1 with gold tokenisation on this test set. This baseline measures exact entity spans and types under those conditions; raw-text performance and cross-language transfer require separate evaluations. No independent contamination audit was performed. Predictions, per-type counts and model/input hashes accompany run_ner.py. The exercises use this checkpoint to measure case-stratified recall (Exercise 1) and zero-shot transfer to Kyrgyz (Exercise 3).

title: 9  Sequence Labelling: POS Tagging, NER, and Chunking
section: 9.6 Hands-On: A Fine-Tuning Procedure for Kazakh NER with XLM-R
text:
9.6 Hands-On: A Fine-Tuning Procedure for Kazakh NER with XLM-R
Question. How can a reproducible NER recipe align subwords and entity labels?
Inputs. KazNERD splits, XLM-R and the training script linked below.
Compute. A large checkpoint and substantial training memory; choose hardware and batch settings before the full run.
Output. A saved model, predictions and entity-level micro and macro F1.
Interpretation. Inspect suffix boundaries and label mappings, then compare a target-language transfer condition.
This tutorial fine-tunes xlm-roberta-large for named entity recognition on KazNERD (Yeshpanov, Khassanov, and Varol 2022) and then applies the model to Kyrgyz text as a zero-shot experiment. The code provides a training recipe; the book reports no fine-tuned score from it, and the measured pretrained Stanza baseline above is the reference point.

9.6.1 Setup
# Tested mechanics: transformers==5.3.0 datasets==4.6.1 seqeval==1.2.2
# torch==2.10.0 accelerate==1.12.0; install sentencepiece for the tokenizer.
# Run from the book root, with the pinned KazNERD clone at KazNERD/.
# Record the versions you used: they are saved with the model below.
import json, random, sys, hashlib
from importlib.metadata import version
from pathlib import Path
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path("code/ch09-ner").resolve()))
from ner_utils import read_iob2, valid_iob2, repair_training_iob2, align_batch, tag_sequences

import numpy as np
import torch
import transformers
from datasets import Dataset, DatasetDict
from transformers import (
    AutoTokenizer,
    AutoModelForTokenClassification,
    TrainingArguments,
    Trainer,
    DataCollatorForTokenClassification,
)
from seqeval.metrics import classification_report, f1_score
from seqeval.scheme import IOB2

SEED = 42
random.seed(SEED); np.random.seed(SEED); torch.manual_seed(SEED)


9.6.2 Loading KazNERD
The authoritative release is the authors’ repository (github.com/IS2AI/KazNERD, CC BY 4.0), which stores the three splits as two-column CoNLL files in IOB2. A Hugging Face copy also exists (issai/kaznerd, with the same 90,228 / 11,167 / 11,307 split sizes); if you use it, pin a revision with load_dataset("issai/kaznerd", revision=...) and check that the label list and counts below are reproduced. Here we read the release directly, validate it, and build the label map from the training split:
ROOT = Path("KazNERD/KazNERD")      # git clone https://github.com/IS2AI/KazNERD then git checkout bd4333d0f5952b9fafb2ef2ac2fefa0ad3c0333f
raw = {split: read_iob2(ROOT / f"IOB2_{name}.txt")
       for split, name in [("train", "train"), ("validation", "valid"), ("test", "test")]}

label_names = ["O"] + sorted({t for _, tags in raw["train"] for t in tags} - {"O"})
label2id = {label: i for i, label in enumerate(label_names)}
id2label = {i: label for label, i in label2id.items()}

for split, sents in raw.items():
    unseen = {t for _, tags in sents for t in tags} - set(label_names)
    invalid = sum(not valid_iob2(tags) for _, tags in sents)
    assert not unseen, (split, unseen)          # every tag must be known from training
    print(f"{split:<10} {len(sents):>6} sentences  longest {max(len(t) for t, _ in sents)} words"
          f"  invalid IOB2: {invalid}")
print(len(label_names), "labels:", label_names[:5], "...")

if any(not valid_iob2(tags) for split in ("validation", "test") for _, tags in raw[split]):
    raise ValueError("malformed evaluation gold; resolve the source before scoring")
raw["train"], training_repairs = repair_training_iob2(raw["train"])

dataset = DatasetDict({
    split: Dataset.from_dict({"tokens": [t for t, _ in sents],
                              "ner_tags": [[label2id[x] for x in g] for _, g in sents]})
    for split, sents in raw.items()
})
Output (release commit bd4333d):
train       90228 sentences  longest 71 words  invalid IOB2: 14
validation  11167 sentences  longest 51 words  invalid IOB2: 0
test        11307 sentences  longest 70 words  invalid IOB2: 0
51 labels: ['O', 'B-ADAGE', 'B-ART', 'B-CARDINAL', 'B-CONTACT'] ...
The 51 labels are B- and I- tags for the 25 types of Table 9.4 plus O. The release audit found 16 orphan I- tags across 14 training sentences. No malformed IOB2 sequences were found in the evaluation splits; this does not certify every annotation. This tutorial repairs orphan training tags (I-X → B-X) and saves each changed position; evaluation labels remain unchanged. The class-count table counts the original release’s B-tags, so its training total precedes this repair.


9.6.3 Tokenising with Word Alignment
The same word-alignment strategy from Chapter 7 applies: only the first subword token of each word receives the NER label; subsequent tokens receive -100 (ignored by the loss). A word count does not bound subword length. The code tokenises every sentence without truncation and rejects any that exceed the model window, because truncation would drop trailing entities from both training and scoring. For longer documents, split them into overlapping windows, keep the original word index of every subword, and merge the per-word predictions before scoring.
MODEL_NAME = "FacebookAI/xlm-roberta-large"
MODEL_REVISION = "c23d21b0620b635a76227c604d44e43a9f0ee389"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME, revision=MODEL_REVISION)
MAX_LEN = 512


def tokenise_and_align(examples):
    return align_batch(examples, tokenizer, MAX_LEN)


tokenised_dataset = dataset.map(tokenise_and_align, batched=True,
                                remove_columns=dataset["train"].column_names)
The complete tokeniser audit retained all 1,302,352 words. Maximum encoded lengths, including special tokens, were 139 / 91 / 108 for train / validation / test. These are measured values from code/ch09-ner/audit_release.py; they do not follow from the longest sentence’s word count.


9.6.4 Defining the Evaluation Metric
NER scoring requires both the predicted span and its type to match the gold annotation. With seqeval, specify the averaging method and treatment of malformed tag sequences. Its f1_score defaults to micro averaging, which gives every mention equal weight and lets frequent types dominate. Macro F1 averages the per-type scores. Report both and state which selects the checkpoint. For strict IOB2 scoring, set mode="strict", scheme=IOB2; the default mode accepts some ill-formed sequences.
def to_tag_sequences(predictions, labels):
    return tag_sequences(predictions, labels, id2label)


def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    logits, labels = eval_pred
    true_tags, pred_tags = to_tag_sequences(np.argmax(logits, axis=-1), labels)
    return {
        "micro_f1": float(f1_score(true_tags, pred_tags, average="micro", mode="strict", scheme=IOB2, zero_division=0)),
        "macro_f1": float(f1_score(true_tags, pred_tags, average="macro", mode="strict", scheme=IOB2, zero_division=0)),
    }


9.6.5 Fine-Tuning
model = AutoModelForTokenClassification.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_NAME, revision=MODEL_REVISION, num_labels=len(label_names), id2label=id2label, label2id=label2id)

use_bf16 = torch.cuda.is_available() and torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported()
use_fp16 = torch.cuda.is_available() and not use_bf16     # mixed precision only where supported

training_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="xlmr-kaznerd",
    num_train_epochs=5,
    per_device_train_batch_size=8,
    per_device_eval_batch_size=16,
    learning_rate=1e-5,
    warmup_ratio=0.1,
    eval_strategy="epoch",
    save_strategy="epoch",
    load_best_model_at_end=True,
    metric_for_best_model="micro_f1",       # the named development metric
    bf16=use_bf16,
    fp16=use_fp16,
    seed=SEED,
    report_to="none",
)

trainer = Trainer(
    model=model,
    args=training_args,
    train_dataset=tokenised_dataset["train"],
    eval_dataset=tokenised_dataset["validation"],
    processing_class=tokenizer,             # `tokenizer=` in transformers < 4.46
    data_collator=DataCollatorForTokenClassification(tokenizer),
    compute_metrics=compute_metrics,
)
trainer.train()

# Save everything needed to reproduce the predictions
out = Path("xlmr-kaznerd/best")
trainer.save_model(out)
tokenizer.save_pretrained(out)
(out / "run_info.json").write_text(json.dumps({
    "labels": label_names, "seed": SEED, "kaznerd_commit": "bd4333d0f5952b9fafb2ef2ac2fefa0ad3c0333f",
    "model_revision": MODEL_REVISION, "training_repairs": training_repairs,
    "data_sha256": {p.name: hashlib.sha256(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest() for p in ROOT.glob("IOB2_*.txt")},
    "scorer": {"mode": "strict", "scheme": "IOB2", "seqeval": version("seqeval")},
    "dependencies": {name: version(name) for name in ("datasets", "accelerate", "numpy", "sentencepiece")},
    "versions": {"transformers": transformers.__version__, "torch": torch.__version__},
}, indent=2))
Record the development scores and wall time from this experiment, together with the GPU type; no target score is guaranteed.


9.6.6 Evaluating on the Test Set
Evaluate the selected checkpoint once on the test set, with the same strict IOB2 scoring. Predicted orphan I-tags are left unchanged and scored under strict IOB2; report that policy rather than silently repairing predictions. Macro F1 averages entity types present in the gold/predicted span union, not a fixed inventory of 25 types. The report lists precision, recall, F1 and support (number of gold mentions) for each type:
pred = trainer.predict(tokenised_dataset["test"])
true_tags, pred_tags = to_tag_sequences(np.argmax(pred.predictions, axis=-1), pred.label_ids)
print(compute_metrics((pred.predictions, pred.label_ids)))
print(classification_report(true_tags, pred_tags, mode="strict", scheme=IOB2, digits=3))
Every word of every test sentence is scored, because no sentence was truncated. Per-type scores for types with few test mentions are unstable: NON_HUMAN has a single test mention, and ADAGE and CONTACT have about twenty each (Table 9.4). The original paper’s 97.22 is an exact-match F1 (Yeshpanov, Khassanov, and Varol 2022); compare with it only after confirming that its scorer and averaging match yours, and with the pretrained Stanza baseline (94.94, micro F1, strict spans) on the same test split.


9.6.7 Zero-Shot Application to Kyrgyz
The multilingual tokeniser accepts Kyrgyz text directly. The standard Kyrgyz and Kazakh scripts are both Cyrillic, but a shared script does not guarantee useful NER predictions:
# pip install "turkicnlp[stanza]==0.5.0"
import turkicnlp

kir_tokenizer = turkicnlp.Pipeline("kir", processors=["tokenize"])   # Kyrgyz tokenizer
model.eval()


def ner_predict(text: str) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    """Run NER on a string; return one (word, label) pair per word."""
    words = [w.text for w in kir_tokenizer(text).words]
    if not words:
        return []
    inputs = tokenizer(words, is_split_into_words=True, return_tensors="pt")
    if inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] > MAX_LEN:
        raise ValueError("text too long for one window; split it into sentences first")
    word_ids = inputs.word_ids()
    inputs = {k: v.to(model.device) for k, v in inputs.items()}
    with torch.inference_mode():
        preds = model(**inputs).logits.argmax(-1)[0].tolist()

    results, seen = [], set()
    for wid, lid in zip(word_ids, preds):
        if wid is not None and wid not in seen:       # first subword of each word
            results.append((words[wid], id2label[lid]))
            seen.add(wid)
    assert len(results) == len(words)
    return results


# "A meeting with Almazbek Atambayev took place in Bishkek."
for token, label in ner_predict("Бишкекте Алмазбек Атамбаев менен жолугушуу өттү."):
    print(f"{token:<25} {label}")
For comparison, the pretrained Stanza KazNERD model recognises the person and place in this sentence when given the same seven words (Stanza 1.11.0). The output below comes from Stanza; the XLM-R model trained by the recipe would give its own:
Бишкекте                  B-GPE
Алмазбек                  B-PERSON
Атамбаев                  I-PERSON
менен                     O
жолугушуу                 O
өттү                      O
.                         O
(Stanza’s BIOES tags S-GPE and E-PERSON are shown as their IOB2 equivalents.) One sentence does not estimate transfer accuracy; Exercise 3 evaluates the same model on the KyrgyzNER test set.
For a controlled script-conversion experiment, use the three conditions in Section 9.3 and preserve offsets when mapping predictions back to the original text. The single-sentence illustration in Chapter 16 does not measure a transfer gain.
Status: procedure only. The XLM-R fine-tuning run is not reported here. The pretrained baseline and the exercise experiments are separate results.

title: 9  Sequence Labelling: POS Tagging, NER, and Chunking
text:
What to Take Forward
Sequence labelling starts with a label definition and an alignment policy. In Exercise 3, the CRF trained on 500 Kyrgyz sentences outperforms zero-shot transfer from the Kazakh model on average across three sampling seeds. This result suggests measuring a small learning curve before choosing between transfer and annotation; it does not set a general annotation budget. Preserve the label mappings and compare systems on the same evaluation items. Chapter 10 turns from labelling words to translating sentences between Turkic languages.

title: 9  Sequence Labelling: POS Tagging, NER, and Chunking
text:
Further Reading
The Kazakh NER dataset KazNERD, with its 25-entity-type scheme, is described in detail in Yeshpanov, Khassanov, and Varol (2022). For Turkish NER and the wider body of Turkish NLP work, including POS tagging, chunking, and semantic role labelling, Oflazer and Saraçlar (2018) is the standard reference, and Çöltekin, Doğruöz, and Çetinoğlu (2023) provides a critical survey of available resources through 2022. Mukayese (Safaya et al. 2022) is the primary multi-task Turkish NLP benchmark, covering NER among its eight tasks.
WikiANN, which provides automatically derived NER data for several Turkic languages, is described in Pan et al. (2017); KyrgyzNER is described in Turatali et al. (2025). Yeniterzi (2011) compares word- and morpheme-level NER for Turkish, and Aslan, Gunal, and Dincer (2018) studies Turkish chunking schemes. Multilingual POS tagging across the Turkic family, including zero-shot languages, is evaluated in Hakimov (2026).
For the algorithmic foundations of sequence labelling (CRF, BiLSTM-CRF and BERT-based token classification), Jurafsky and Martin (2024) (chapter “Sequence Labelling for Parts of Speech and Named Entities”) provides an accessible treatment, and Lample et al. (2016) introduced the BiLSTM-CRF tagger for NER. The XLM-R encoder used in this chapter’s hands-on is described in Conneau et al. (2020); TurkishDelightNLP (Alecakir, Bölücü, and Can 2022) provides a unified Turkish POS tagging, NER, and dependency parsing system. The seqeval documentation explains its averaging options and strict IOB2 mode.

title: 9  Sequence Labelling: POS Tagging, NER, and Chunking
text:
Exercises

Case suffix analysis in NER. Take the KazNERD test set. For every GPE, LOCATION and PERSON mention, analyse the final word with the Apertium analyser in TurkicNLP and record its case. Keep three outcomes apart: a non-nominative case, nominative, and unknown (no analysis, or several readings with different cases). Do not count analyser failures as nominative. Manually check a random sample of 50 mentions and report the analyser’s error rate on it. What proportion of mentions of each type is inflected? Is a trained model’s recall (for example that of the pretrained Stanza KazNERD model) lower for some cases?
Vocabulary overlap and NER. Fine-tune two models on KazNERD: one using xlm-roberta-base and one using dbmdz/bert-base-turkish-cased (BERTurk). Compare their micro and macro F1 (strict IOB2) on the KazNERD test set. Then measure BERTurk’s tokeniser coverage on a declared Cyrillic Kazakh word list. Report both the fraction of words containing an unknown token and mean subwords per word; a fragmented word is not an unknown word. Is the vocabulary gap a plausible explanation for the F1 difference, and what experiment would test it beyond this single pair of models?
Few-shot NER for Kyrgyz. Use KyrgyzNER (Turatali et al. 2025), after checking its splits and licence; WikiANN Kyrgyz has only 100 training sentences. Reserve a fixed development subset before drawing nested training samples, such as 50, 200, 500 and 2,000 sentences where the release permits. Train XLM-R or a CPU-based CRF with three seeds per size. Choose hyperparameters and checkpoints on development data. Once the recipe and sizes are fixed, plot test F1 without using the curve to retune.
Compare with zero-shot transfer from the pretrained Stanza KazNERD model or your fine-tuned XLM-R. Before examining scores, map the 25 KazNERD and 27 KyrgyzNER types to a shared inventory. Map unsupported types to O in both gold and predictions, retain all tokens and score both systems on the same mapped test set.
Document unresolved mention-boundary differences and the domain difference between TV news and a news portal. At what sampled training size does the Kyrgyz model overtake zero-shot transfer?
Entity distribution shift measurement. Extract all PERSON entity spans from the KazNERD training set and a Turkish NER training set (for example the Starlang Turkish NER data or MilliyetNER). Normalise both sets (lemmatise or strip case suffixes, and transliterate to a common script with a documented mapping), then compute the Jaccard overlap of the name tokens and of their character trigrams. Which normalised strings are shared and which are not? Do not infer a name’s etymology from string overlap alone. Stratify Exercise 3’s PERSON mentions by whether their normalised name strings occur in the source training data: are unseen names the main source of cross-lingual PERSON errors?
PropBank argument detection. Use sense-annotated Turkish PropBank sentences (Şahin and Adalı 2018) and read the selected predicates’ role definitions. Measure the position of overt ARG0 spans relative to the predicate. For examples without an overt ARG0, inspect the annotation policy and context before treating the argument as omitted. What does agreement tell you, and what discourse evidence is needed to recover a referent? If you use TRopBank frames with a UD treebank instead, treat subjects as syntactic observations: nsubj is not a gold ARG0 label. Manually establish predicate senses and roles before making an SRL claim. Evaluate overt-argument labelling and implicit-argument recovery separately.
An LLM as a recogniser. Annotate 50 Kyrgyz (or Tatar) news sentences with PER, LOC and ORG by hand. Run TurkicNLP with ner_backend="llm" and two models of different sizes, and compute entity-level F1 with seqeval. Then run the same LLM backend on 50 sentences of the KazNERD test set, where you can compare it with the trained Stanza model. Declare a mapping from KazNERD types to PER/LOC/ORG before scoring, use the same mention boundaries, and apply that mapping to both systems and gold. How large is the gap, and which entity types does the LLM miss?

title: 10  Machine Translation: Within and Beyond the Family
text:
10.1 The Challenges of Turkic MT
Machine translation brings together morphological generation, syntactic reordering, lexical choice and discourse interpretation. English→Turkish translation must interpret the English source and generate Turkish with appropriate inflection and constituent order. Translation between Turkic languages can exploit related vocabulary and constructions, but must still handle language-specific meanings, scripts and unequal resources.
The chapter covers Apertium’s rule-based pipeline (Section 10.2), multilingual neural models and evaluation (Section 10.3), direct and pivot translation (Section 10.4), and low-resource adaptation (Section 10.5). The hands-on provides a Kazakh→Kyrgyz fine-tuning recipe.
crumbs: 10  Machine Translation: Within and Beyond the Family

title: 10  Machine Translation: Within and Beyond the Family
text:
10.1.1 Target-Side Morphological Richness
Translation maps between different grammatical distinctions. English “she came” can be translated as Turkish geldi: the verb marks past tense and third-person singular agreement, while the subject’s gender is not encoded. Related forms such as gelmedi “did not come”, gelmiş (an indirect/evidential reading in context), gelecek “will come”, and geldiler “they came” illustrate choices a translator must make. Features need not each have an independent overt suffix.
Russian also has rich inflection. Translation must map between grammatical systems with different distinctions and forms. An incorrect case or agreement marker can change the meaning even when most characters match the reference.


10.1.2 SOV–SVO Reordering
English has a relatively fixed SVO order, while Russian permits substantial reordering. Turkic languages commonly have SOV order, prenominal modifiers and postpositions, with variation across constructions and languages (Johanson 2021, secs. 56.3–56.4). English→Turkish translation may therefore require moving whole constituents.
Relative clauses illustrate the reordering. English commonly places them after the noun, sometimes with an overt marker: the book that I read yesterday. Turkish places a participial clause before it: dün okuduğum kitap, literally “yesterday-read-my book”. Translation must produce the correct participial form and make the clause modify the intended noun. Both deserve checking even when the output reads fluently.


10.1.3 Data Scarcity
The TIL corpus (Mirzakhalov, Babu, Ataman, et al. 2021) contains sharply unequal amounts of training data across pairs. The following table is generated from a frozen release README; its counts are training sentence pairs, not the aggregate language totals in the paper.

English–Turkish has about 370 times more training data than English–Uyghur. Karachay-Balkar, Khakas and Tuvan are covered, but with small pair sizes; Nogai is not covered.

Corpus size alone cannot define a universal threshold for usable MT: domain, duplication, alignment quality, pretraining and the evaluation criterion all matter. The TIL paper reports merging the original Tatoeba training, development and test portions during corpus construction (Mirzakhalov, Babu, Ataman, et al. 2021, sec. 3.1). Audit overlap with any intended evaluation set before using the corpus for training.


10.1.4 Script Mismatch Within the Family
Intra-family MT must identify the scripts actually present in each corpus. Uzbek occurs in both Latin and Cyrillic; Kazakh script reform does not imply that a corpus has already switched scripts. Uyghur also has more than one writing tradition (Chapter 3). Compare native-script training with a documented conversion if useful, retain the original text, and audit lossy mappings. Translation does not require script conversion. Whether to convert is an experimental choice.

title: 10  Machine Translation: Within and Beyond the Family
text:
10.2 Rule-Based MT: Apertium

10.2.1 Architecture
Apertium is an open-source rule-based machine translation platform originally designed for related language pairs (Forcada et al. 2011; Khanna et al. 2021). Its pipeline for a Turkic source–target pair can be understood through five stages (the precise modules depend on the pair):

Morphological analysis: the source-side text is processed by the source language’s FST analyser (Chapter 6), producing candidate lemma and morphological-feature analyses for each recognised word.
Disambiguation and selection: choose among competing source morphological readings in context; pair-specific lexical-selection modules may also select among translation candidates.
Lexical transfer: the source lemma is mapped to the corresponding target lemma using a bilingual dictionary. Morphological features are passed through unchanged where they apply; category-specific transfer rules handle feature mismatches between languages.
Structural transfer: chunk-level reordering rules handle systematic constituent order differences. For a Turkish–English system, relative-clause placement and verb order are examples of differences that transfer rules would need to address; coverage depends on the implemented pair.
Morphological generation: the target lemma and morphological feature bundle are passed to the target language’s FST generator, which produces a surface form licensed by the grammar.

The generator restricts output to forms licensed by its transducer. Errors can still enter through an incomplete lexicon or grammar, a wrong source analysis or a mistaken target choice. Define how the system handles unknown words and failed generation.


10.2.2 Turkic Pairs in Apertium
Apertium has released Turkic pairs as well as development repositories (Khanna et al. 2021). The wiki groups pairs by development stage; this is not a quality ranking:

Shared vocabulary and morphology can reduce dictionary and transfer-rule work, while leaving ambiguity to resolve. Evaluate translation in the intended domain for both within-branch and cross-branch pairs; genealogy is no guarantee of quality.


10.2.3 Strengths and Limitations
Apertium provides inspectable intermediate analyses and can be built without a sentence-aligned training corpus, though it requires dictionaries, rules and linguistic work. Errors may arise in analysis, disambiguation, lexical selection, transfer or generation. Trace the entire pipeline before deciding which component to repair.
Missing lexical entries require unknown-word handling: depending on the pipeline, a word may be copied or marked rather than translated. Even a well-formed generated word can have the wrong meaning if the chosen analysis or target lemma is wrong. Domain-specific accuracy claims require a held-out comparison.
Apertium output can also supply synthetic parallel data for a neural system; Section 10.5 discusses how to test its contribution.

title: 10  Machine Translation: Within and Beyond the Family
text:
10.3 Neural MT for Turkic Languages

10.3.1 The TIL Corpus
The Turkic Interlingua (TIL) corpus (Mirzakhalov, Babu, Ataman, et al. 2021) is a broad parallel resource for the Turkic family. It covers 22 Turkic languages and more than 400 translation directions, with English and Russian included as hub languages (Table 10.1). The corpus was assembled from publicly available parallel data and cleaned and deduplicated for each language pair.
The TIL release includes the X-WMT evaluation sets: human-post-edited test sets of at least 300 sentences for 88 translation directions among eight Turkic languages (Azerbaijani, Bashkir, Karakalpak, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Sakha, Turkish and Uzbek) plus English and Russian. X-WMT supports comparison on common sentence content. The corpus paper reports bilingual baselines (Mirzakhalov, Babu, Ataman, et al. 2021); the separate multilingual study evaluates multiway systems (Mirzakhalov, Babu, Kunafin, et al. 2021). Do not attribute the multilingual experiment to the corpus paper or treat every release split as independent of every training collection.


10.3.2 NLLB-200
Meta’s No Language Left Behind (NLLB-200) model (NLLB Team et al. 2024) is a multilingual sequence-to-sequence model covering 200 languages and built with both human-translated and automatically constructed parallel data. It covers eleven Turkic language/script varieties, including separate North and South Azerbaijani entries. FLORES-200 codes combine an ISO 639-3 code with a script subtag:

For supported varieties, specify the full language code, including its script subtag. The target-language token controls what the model generates: a wrong valid code requests a different language, while an unsupported code can fail during tokenisation or generation. Test quality for each direction and domain. TurkicNLP’s translate and embeddings processors wrap the distilled 600M-parameter model (Hakimov 2026), whose model card specifies a CC BY-NC 4.0 licence.


10.3.3 Evaluation Metrics
Use complementary metrics, state their configurations and inspect linguistic errors. BLEU (Papineni et al. 2002) measures word n-gram overlap with references and is sensitive to tokenisation and alternative word forms. A correct paraphrase can receive less credit, but a wrong case or tense can also change meaning: it should not automatically be excused as a morphological variant.
chrF (Popović 2015) measures character n-gram overlap. It gives partial credit to shared stems and suffixes, but can also reward a fluent or closely spelled mistranslation. chrF++ (Popović 2017) adds word n-grams; the tutorial uses CHRF(word_order=2). Its score is not numerically comparable with BLEU even though both are conventionally reported on a 0–100 scale.
COMET (Rei et al. 2020) is a learned metric; reference-based checkpoints use the source, hypothesis and reference. Reliability depends on the checkpoint, training distribution, language and domain. That a language is covered by the encoder tells us nothing about how well the metric correlates with human judgements in it. Record the exact checkpoint and validate it against human judgements when using it to support quality claims.
