The suite saves exact SacreBLEU signatures, every translation, input/model hashes and end-of-sequence audits. One output in each direction reaches the generation ceiling without a terminating EOS token; none is empty. Those outputs remain in the corpus scores and are not silently excluded. These automatic scores do not substitute for a human adequacy and morphology review. There is no fine-tuning or independent pretraining-overlap audit.


10.3.5 ISSAI Tilmash
The ISSAI Tilmash model card describes a system fine-tuned from NLLB-200 (distilled 1.3B) for Kazakh, Russian, English and Turkish, using Kazakh-centred parallel data including KazParC (Yeshpanov, Polonskaya, and Varol 2024). The model is gated: access requires agreeing to share contact information. The page lists FLORES in its dataset metadata and reports FLORES test scores, but does not identify the training split there. This leaves overlap unresolved; verify the training records before treating those scores as an independent comparison with NLLB. The existence of a release is not a benchmark result for every direction.


10.3.6 General-Purpose LLMs as Translators
General-purpose LLMs can also be tested as translators. Evaluate the intended language and domain, and check whether the output is in the requested language. Unrestricted language-ID predictions (Section 3.7) can flag possible mistakes, but need manual checking. A classifier restricted to Turkic labels cannot reject an English answer. Higher token fertility increases token usage for a fixed text; runtime and cost also depend on the model and output length (Section 7.1).
TurkicNLP puts both kinds of system behind the same translate processor: NLLB-200 for the varieties above, and an LLM backend that accepts all 24 toolkit language labels. A label that the model accepts may still produce poor translations. The following example compares outputs and language-ID predictions:
import turkicnlp

lid = turkicnlp.LanguageDetection()
text = "Алматы — Қазақстанның ең ірі қаласы."

nllb = turkicnlp.Pipeline("kaz", processors=["translate"], translate_tgt_lang="kir")
llm = turkicnlp.Pipeline("kaz", processors=["tokenize", "translate"], translate_backend="llm",
                         translate_tgt_lang="kir",
                         llm_model="qwen2.5:7b", llm_base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1",
                         llm_api_key="ollama")
for name, nlp in [("NLLB", nllb), ("LLM", llm)]:
    out = nlp(text).translation
    print(name, out, lid.model.predict(out.replace("\n", " "), k=3))  # unrestricted labels
    # Expected language is kir_Cyrl; these scores are diagnostics, not proof of correctness.
translate_tgt_lang accepts an ISO 639-3 code (kir), a FLORES-200 code (kir_Cyrl), or, for the LLM backend, a language name; with translate_tgt_script the LLM backend can also be asked for a specific script (e.g. Uzbek in Cyrillic).

title: 10  Machine Translation: Within and Beyond the Family
text:
10.4 Intra-Family Translation

10.4.1 Closely Related Pairs
Related languages share vocabulary and constructions that a model may exploit. Whether this improves translation over an equally resourced cross-family pair is a controlled empirical question. False cognates, different loanwords, language-specific auxiliary constructions and suffix allomorphy can still prevent correct copying or transfer.
An exploratory all-pairs comparison is available in the recorded Exercise 6. NLLB-200 600M with greedy decoding was applied to the first 15 X-WMT sentences per direction for six languages. chrF ranges from 31.3 (Turkish→Bashkir) to 56.6 (Bashkir→Kyrgyz). The mean is 44.3 for eight same-branch, same-script directions, 43.5 for four cross-branch, same-script directions, and 40.3 for eighteen cross-branch, cross-script directions. There are no same-branch, cross-script directions in this sample. Directions also use different sentence content. The groups are small and unbalanced. They cannot isolate script or genealogical effects, let alone rank language pairs.


10.4.2 Pivot Strategies
When direct parallel data is limited, pivot translation routes the translation through an intermediate language. How limited depends on the pair: the TIL release has 12,216 Kazakh–Kyrgyz training pairs but 119,946 Uzbek–Kyrgyz ones, and NLLB-200 was trained on its own collection. Two possible routes for Uzbek→Kyrgyz are illustrated below.
Turkish pivot: Uzbek→Turkish→Kyrgyz. A larger English–Turkish corpus is no evidence that both legs of this route beat direct Uzbek→Kyrgyz translation. Inspect pair-specific data and compare outputs on the same held-out sentences.
Russian pivot: Uzbek→Russian→Kyrgyz provides another route. Shared terminology may help in some domains, but each decoding step can introduce errors. Exercise 4 compares both pivots with direct NLLB-200 translation on the same 50 X-WMT Uzbek–Kyrgyz sentences. Direct translation scores chrF++ 41.2, the Russian pivot 40.3 and the Turkish pivot 36.5. The Turkish route takes about twice as long in that run. In one sentence, its first leg enters a repetition loop and the second translates the repetitions. Record such error propagation alongside scores and latency, using fixed decoding settings.


10.4.3 Multilingual NMT
A multilingual model shares parameters across directions and uses language tags to specify the requested output. The multiway TIL study evaluates this approach (Mirzakhalov, Babu, Kunafin, et al. 2021). Results depend on the directions, sampling strategy, model capacity and domains; parameter sharing does not guarantee an improvement for every pair.
A useful experiment compares bilingual and multilingual systems with matched architectures, evaluation data and reported training budgets. Target-language tags must follow the model’s own convention: an illustrative <2kaz> prefix is not interchangeable with NLLB’s kaz_Cyrl token.


10.4.4 Zero-Shot Intra-Family Transfer
Zero-shot translation means evaluating a direction without its task-specific parallel training data. A multilingual model that represents both languages is a different starting point from a Turkish–Kazakh-only model fed Azerbaijani input. Related vocabulary may permit some transfer, but neither genealogy nor transliteration guarantees it. Compare native-script and converted input on the same held-out set, and check output language as well as adequacy.

title: 10  Machine Translation: Within and Beyond the Family
text:
10.5 Low-Resource Neural MT Strategies

10.5.1 Back-Translation
Back-translation is a widely used data augmentation strategy for low-resource MT (Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch 2016). Given a monolingual corpus in the target language (e.g., Kyrgyz news articles), an existing MT system translates this corpus in the reverse direction (Kyrgyz→Turkish) to produce synthetic source sentences. The resulting synthetic parallel corpus (synthetic Turkish, real Kyrgyz) is then combined with real parallel data to train the final system.
Back-translation depends on the backward system’s output. A Kyrgyz→Turkish Apertium system or small TIL baseline may generate noisy synthetic source sentences; test whether adding them helps. Source-side perplexity can flag some disfluency but can miss fluent mistranslations. Also inspect a sample for language, alignment, duplication and adequacy.
For Uyghur and other very low-resource Turkic languages, back-translation from a monolingual corpus offers a way to bootstrap: a reverse-direction system, where one exists, can generate candidate training pairs whose usefulness must be evaluated.


10.5.2 Fine-Tuning NLLB-200
NLLB-200 (NLLB Team et al. 2024) provides a pretrained starting point for the varieties in Table 10.3. Compare fine-tuning on a language pair or domain with the unadapted model and a bilingual system trained from scratch. Adaptation may improve the target task, but can also overfit or reduce performance elsewhere.
The tutorial uses facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M. Memory requirements depend on sequence length, batch size, optimiser and precision; a single GPU is not guaranteed to suffice. The model card describes research use and a CC BY-NC 4.0 licence. Check suitability and licence terms before deployment; a large model is not automatically ready for production.


10.5.3 Transfer Learning from Turkish
Turkish-trained weights are one possible initialisation for an under-resourced language. Their value relative to a multilingual checkpoint must be tested. Kyrgyz and Tatar already have NLLB language codes, so they are not examples of missing NLLB coverage.
Adapting NLLB to a language outside its inventory requires training data and a policy for language tokens and vocabulary. For Karakalpak, Mamasaidov and Shopulatov (2024) trained a SentencePiece model, added 13,195 tokens to the distilled 600M model and initialised them from their subword embeddings. They used 100,000 sentence pairs each with Uzbek, Russian and English. Their baselines assigned Karakalpak the Kazakh or Uzbek code; that code substitution alone leaves the model without language-specific adaptation.


10.5.4 Synthetic Data from Apertium
For a supported translation direction, an Apertium system can generate synthetic parallel sentences from monolingual data (Section 10.2). A neural system can then train on a mixture of these sentence pairs and genuine parallel data. Evaluate whether the synthetic pairs help on held-out data from the intended domain.

title: 10  Machine Translation: Within and Beyond the Family
section: 10.6 Hands-On: A Fine-Tuning Procedure for Kazakh–Kyrgyz Translation with NLLB-200
text:
10.6 Hands-On: A Fine-Tuning Procedure for Kazakh–Kyrgyz Translation with NLLB-200
Question. Does adaptation improve Kazakh–Kyrgyz translation over the original checkpoint?
Inputs. Prepared disjoint parallel splits and the pinned NLLB checkpoint.
Compute. Model downloads and fine-tuning resources; record the actual hardware and elapsed time.
Output. Baseline and adapted predictions, BLEU/chrF++ signatures and split manifests.
Interpretation. Compare both systems on the same reserved sentences and inspect incomplete outputs.
The executable tutorial is code/ch10-mt/train.py, with its input contract in code/ch10-mt/README.md. It adapts facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M from Kazakh (kaz_Cyrl) to Kyrgyz (kir_Cyrl). The code mechanics have been checked with a tiny random model. The book reports no fine-tuned score; the Turkish–Kazakh greedy scores above illustrate baseline reporting but are not a Kazakh–Kyrgyz baseline. The runner evaluates the unadapted model on the prepared Kazakh–Kyrgyz data under the same four-beam decoding policy as the adapted model.

10.6.1 Prepare independent splits
Prepare train.tsv, validation.tsv and test.tsv, each with the header document_id, src, tgt (tab-separated). Keep original source-document groups together across all corpora and synthetic translations. Use validation for checkpoint selection and reserve the test set for the final fixed comparison. The loader rejects malformed or empty records, duplicate pairs, and cross-split document or normalised source/target text overlap. Unknown source-document provenance is a limitation to resolve, not a reason to invent independent IDs.
The TIL release lists 12,216 Kazakh–Kyrgyz training pairs (Table 10.1); an arbitrary tail of that file is not necessarily an independent validation set. Record upstream corpus revisions, licences, grouping and split rules alongside the prepared files. The runner saves their hashes and actual sizes.


10.6.2 Set and verify both language tokens
The runner uses the explicit NllbTokenizer class and pins the model and tokeniser revision. This matters because an automatic tokeniser loader may not preserve language-specific behaviour across library versions. The source encoding must begin with the Kazakh token and target labels with the Kyrgyz token; both must terminate in EOS.
from transformers import NllbTokenizer

MODEL_NAME = "facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M"
REVISION = "f8d333a098d19b4fd9a8b18f94170487ad3f821d"
tokenizer = NllbTokenizer.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_NAME, revision=REVISION,
    src_lang="kaz_Cyrl", tgt_lang="kir_Cyrl", legacy_behaviour=False,
)
source_ids = tokenizer("Алматы")["input_ids"]
target_ids = tokenizer(text_target="Бишкек")["input_ids"]
assert source_ids[0] == tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids("kaz_Cyrl")
assert target_ids[0] == tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids("kir_Cyrl")
assert source_ids[-1] == target_ids[-1] == tokenizer.eos_token_id
All training and evaluation sentences are encoded without truncation. Examples above the declared token budgets stop the run so that segmentation and reconstruction can be addressed explicitly. Dynamic padding masks target padding with -100 for the loss.


10.6.3 Use the same decoding policy throughout
The target token must be set before development evaluation, not only during later interactive inference. The runner applies this configuration to both the original and adapted model:
model.generation_config.forced_bos_token_id = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids("kir_Cyrl")
model.generation_config.max_length = 256
model.generation_config.max_new_tokens = None
model.generation_config.num_beams = 4
model.generation_config.do_sample = False
The corresponding Seq2SeqTrainingArguments use predict_with_generate=True, generation_max_length=256 and generation_num_beams=4. They were chosen for the tutorial and have not been tuned. The model is selected by validation chrF++ (metric_for_best_model="chrfpp"), with epoch evaluation and checkpoint saving. Batch size and precision must be chosen for the available hardware.


10.6.4 Score original references and retain outputs
The metric callback decodes generated token IDs but compares them with the original reference strings, avoiding changes caused by decoding tokenised labels. It checks equal sentence counts and reports corpus BLEU (tokenize="13a") and chrF++ (word_order=2). The 13a tokeniser gives a reproducible baseline; it knows nothing about Turkic morphology.
Run from the book root in an environment with the versions listed in the companion README:
python code/ch10-mt/train.py path/to/prepared-splits --output nllb-kaz-kir
The script first measures the original model’s development performance. It then trains, restores and saves the checkpoint with the best development score. Once training choices are fixed, it evaluates both checkpoints on the same test data with identical decoding.
Saved outputs include predictions, SacreBLEU signatures, versions, language-token IDs, split hashes and counts of outputs that reach the generation limit. Inspect those outputs for incomplete translations. Report development and test BLEU and chrF++ for both models, hardware, wall time and a paired analysis of their errors. The adapted model may improve or worsen the baseline.
Status: procedure only. The full adaptation run is not reported here. The exercise comparisons use their own declared model configurations.

title: 10  Machine Translation: Within and Beyond the Family
text:
What to Take Forward
Translation experiments need supported language directions, documented parallel data and a reserved test set. Performance varies across the tested directions, but the small all-pairs comparison cannot attribute those differences to relatedness or script. In a separate comparison on 50 Uzbek–Kyrgyz sentences, direct translation outperforms both tested pivots (Exercise 4). Establish the pretrained direct baseline first, then test pivoting, back-translation or adaptation under the same decoding and scoring settings. Chapter 11 extends the pipeline from written text to speech.

title: 10  Machine Translation: Within and Beyond the Family
text:
Further Reading
The TIL corpus and bilingual baselines are described in Mirzakhalov, Babu, Ataman, et al. (2021); multiway multilingual experiments are reported separately in Mirzakhalov, Babu, Kunafin, et al. (2021). NLLB Team et al. (2024) describes the NLLB-200 model architecture, training data, and evaluation methodology; its supplementary materials include coverage statistics for all 200 languages, including the eleven Turkic varieties.
For Apertium’s rule-based approach, Forcada et al. (2011) provides the architectural overview, while Khanna et al. (2021) documents Apertium as of that publication. Washington, Salimzyanov, and Tyers (2014) describes the finite-state morphological transducers for three Kipchak languages (Kazakh, Tatar and Kumyk) on which Apertium’s analysis and generation stages for these languages are built.
MT evaluation metrics are introduced in the “Machine Translation” chapter of Jurafsky and Martin (2024). Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch (2016) describes back-translation for neural MT. For using NLLB-200 inside a Turkic pipeline (translation and sentence embeddings for the covered Turkic varieties), see Hakimov (2026).

title: 10  Machine Translation: Within and Beyond the Family
text:
Exercises

Data scarcity analysis. Using Table 10.1 as a reference, compute the ratio between English–Turkish and English–Uyghur sentence pair counts. Choose two differently resourced pairs and design a learning-curve experiment. Specify domain, metric and acceptance criteria; do not assume a universal sentence-count threshold.
Metric comparison. Take 20 English sentences and translate them into Turkish using facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M, with two decoding settings (for example greedy and beam search) as competing systems. Use references written or checked by a competent speaker, such as the human-post-edited X-WMT test sets. Compute corpus BLEU and chrF++, retaining metric signatures. For sentence-level diagnostics, state the BLEU smoothing and effective-order settings. Inspect examples where the two metrics rank competing outputs differently; their raw score magnitudes are not directly comparable. Distinguish legitimate variants from meaning-changing suffix errors.
Apertium pipeline trace. Install Apertium and the Kazakh–Tatar language pair (or, without an Apertium installation, run its stages by hand with the Kazakh analyser, the pair’s bilingual dictionary and the Tatar generator). Translate the Kazakh sentence Бүгін ауа райы өте жақсы. (“The weather is very nice today.”) and trace each stage of the pipeline: morphological analysis output, lexical transfer output, structural transfer output, and morphological generation output. What does the trace reveal about how each stage handles this sentence?
Pivot translation comparison. For the language pair Uzbek→Kyrgyz, implement two translation strategies using NLLB-200: (a) direct translation with codes uzn_Latn → kir_Cyrl; (b) pivot through Turkish (uzn_Latn → tur_Latn, then tur_Latn → kir_Cyrl). With TurkicNLP, (a) is Pipeline("uzb", processors=["translate"], translate_tgt_lang="kir") and (b) chains a uzb→tur and a tur→kir pipeline. Translate the same 50 held-out sentences (for example from the X-WMT Uzbek–Kyrgyz test set) under matched decoding settings; evaluate each strategy with chrF++, record added latency and inspect error propagation. Which approach scores higher on this sample? Use paired examples to investigate possible causes rather than treating the score difference as an explanation.
Back-translation experiment. Configure a separate Kyrgyz→Kazakh NLLB model (src_lang="kir_Cyrl", tgt_lang="kaz_Cyrl", forced target token kaz_Cyrl) to back-translate a small training-only monolingual Kyrgyz corpus (1,000 sentences from Wikipedia or news, disjoint from development/test source documents) into Kazakh, producing synthetic Kazakh. Combine this synthetic data with the available real training pairs and retrain the model. Tune the synthetic-data amount on validation, then compare fixed systems on the same untouched test set. Does adding back-translated data improve chrF++? How sensitive is the gain to the size of the back-translated corpus?
An intra-Turkic quality matrix. Load the FLORES-200 devtest sentences for the eleven NLLB Turkic varieties (Table 10.3), or the X-WMT test sets for the six languages that X-WMT and NLLB share. Align by documented sentence IDs or verify correspondence from the release; do not assume that independently filtered files remain row-aligned. For an exploratory subset, select and record the sentence IDs (for example 200) and translate between distinct-language pairs with facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M (one TurkicNLP translate pipeline per source language, with translate_tgt_lang set to each target) and compute chrF against the references. Plot the matrix as a heatmap. Label the matrix as a subset experiment, exclude identity directions, and tune choices only on development data. Do within-branch pairs score higher than cross-branch pairs? Do same-script pairs score higher than cross-script pairs with similar genealogical distance?
Beyond NLLB’s languages. NLLB-200 does not cover Nogai, Kumyk or Sakha, but TurkicNLP’s LLM backend accepts all 24 toolkit language labels. Take 20 Nogai (or Sakha) sentences with reference translations into Russian, written or checked by a native speaker. Translate them with Pipeline("nog", processors=["tokenize", "translate"], translate_backend="llm", translate_tgt_lang="rus", ...) using two models of different sizes, and compute chrF against the references. Then reverse the task with a short prompt to the same models (Russian → Nogai) and use the unrestricted lid.model.predict(...) method of turkicnlp.LanguageDetection() on the outputs. How often does it assign another language label (Section 3.7)? Have a competent speaker check those cases: an LID label is not a verified language annotation.

title: 11  Speech Technologies
text:
11.1 Phonological Sketch of Turkic Languages
Speech systems connect recordings with written text. They must handle the target language’s sounds, spelling and pronunciation. Related languages may offer useful training data, but performance also depends on speakers, recording conditions and domain.
This chapter covers the phonological foundations relevant to speech processing (Section 11.1), automatic speech recognition (Section 11.2), text-to-speech synthesis (Section 11.3), and the specific low-resource strategies applicable to Turkic speech (Section 11.4). The hands-on provides a Whisper fine-tuning recipe for Kazakh ASR using the Hugging Face ecosystem.

title: 11  Speech Technologies
text:
11.1.1 Vowel Systems and Orthography
The grammar-based inventory in Table 2.4 distinguishes phoneme analyses from alphabet letters. Use that inventory and the harmony discussion in Chapter 5 when designing a pronunciation lexicon; a single family-wide vowel count is inappropriate. Johanson treats sound types and vowel systems in Chapters 12–18 and word accents in Chapter 50 (Johanson 2021). Standard Uzbek and harmony-preserving Uzbek varieties must be distinguished.
A speech system maps between acoustic realisations and a particular transcription convention. Surface suffix vowels are normally already written: the abstract morphophoneme A in a morphological rule is not an unspecified vowel in ordinary Turkish input. Pronunciation modelling must still handle allophony, loans, abbreviations and variety-specific spelling–sound correspondences.


11.1.2 Consonants and Transfer
Transliteration can obscure sound differences. Standard Turkish ğ usually lengthens the preceding vowel or surfaces as a glide; Kazakh ғ is a voiced back fricative. An acoustic encoder may nevertheless transfer useful features to sounds absent from its source language. Evaluate that transfer on held-out target speech and inspect the confusions, rather than predicting accuracy from shared letters.


11.1.3 Prosody
Stress, phrase boundaries, duration and intonation depend on the language, variety and construction. A blanket final-stress rule is insufficient. A morphological analyser can supply candidate features, but selecting the reading and predicting prosody require contextual modelling. Evaluate an analyser-assisted front end against the same model without those features, with fluent listeners and matched recordings.
A Turkmen example. Turkmen retains primary long vowels (Gökçür 2016). Its spelling usually leaves length unmarked. The exception is ‹üý› for /yː/ (Johanson’s /üː/), as in süýt ‘milk’ and güýç ‘strength’ (Johanson 2021, 257–58). Thus at can represent /at/ ‘horse’ or /aːt/ ‘name’, and ot /ot/ ‘grass’ or /oːt/ ‘fire’ (Johanson 2021, 248, 258). Before a vowel-initial suffix, the consonant following the long vowel becomes voiced: compare ady ‘his/her name’ with aty ‘his/her horse’.
The Apertium analyser gives both at nouns the same at<n> analysis, alongside a verb reading, and both ot nouns the same ot<n>. A TTS front end therefore needs lexical and contextual information beyond these analyses to choose a pronunciation.
Turkmen also differs from Turkish in its consonants. In native words, ‹s› and ‹z› represent /θ/ and /ð/: süýt /θyːt/ ‘milk’, duz /duːð/ ‘salt’. Plain /s/ and /z/ occur in loans (Johanson 2021, 258, 262). Turkish letter-to-sound rules would miss this distinction. These transcriptions use IPA; Johanson writes the same sounds as /üː/, /θ/ and /δ/ in Turkological notation.

title: 11  Speech Technologies
text:
11.2 Automatic Speech Recognition

11.2.1 End-to-End Architectures
Three widely used end-to-end ASR architectures provide the background for the Turkic systems discussed here. For algorithmic details see the chapter on automatic speech recognition in Jurafsky and Martin (2024).
CTC (Connectionist Temporal Classification) (Graves et al. 2006) trains an encoder to predict a probability distribution over output units (such as characters or subwords) and a blank symbol at each encoder time step, then uses the CTC loss to align the predicted sequence with the target text without requiring explicit frame-to-phoneme alignment. Its frame-level predictions are conditionally independent given the encoded audio. Greedy decoding needs no autoregressive decoder, while beam search may incorporate an external language model; MMS and the Omnilingual CTC models below use this design.
Attention encoder-decoder uses an encoder (typically a convolutional front-end followed by transformer layers) to produce a sequence of audio representations, and a decoder that attends over these representations to generate output tokens autoregressively. This architecture is the basis of Whisper (Radford et al. 2023). The decoder uses preceding output tokens as well as the audio.
RNN-T (Recurrent Neural Network Transducer) (Graves 2012) combines an acoustic encoder with a prediction network that encodes the preceding output labels. A joint network uses both representations to predict the next label or blank. RNN-T supports streaming when the acoustic encoder and decoding policy are causal. Compare latency and recognition error on the intended workload; architecture by itself decides little about suitability for deployment.


11.2.2 Whisper
The original Whisper models (Radford et al. 2023) were trained by OpenAI on 680,000 hours of weakly supervised web audio; 117,000 of those hours cover 96 languages other than English. Their tokeniser has 99 language tokens. The later large-v3 model added Cantonese, bringing the count to 100 in its generation configuration. Whisper uses an attention encoder-decoder architecture with a log-mel spectrogram front end and a transformer encoder and decoder. The original release had five sizes (tiny, base, small, medium, large), with the large model having 1,550 million parameters.
Whisper has dedicated tokens for seven Turkic languages: Turkish (tr), Azerbaijani (az), Uzbek (uz), Kazakh (kk), Tatar (tt), Turkmen (tk) and Bashkir (ba). Kyrgyz and Uyghur have no dedicated Whisper language tokens. Training audio varies widely by language; the paper notes that most languages have less than 1,000 hours. Its FLEURS and Common Voice word error rates provide per-language reference baselines.
Exercise 4 tests an int8 ONNX export of Whisper small with greedy decoding on Piper-synthesised speech: 20 Turkish items from one voice and 30 Kazakh items from six voices. Normalised CER is 5.9% and 54.4%, respectively. Different texts and voices prevent attributing this gap to language alone. Within the Kazakh sample, the Kazakh token outperforms each tested alternative language token and automatic language detection. These synthetic-audio diagnostics leave performance on real recordings unmeasured.
Evaluate Whisper on the intended domain for every language, including Turkish; for Kyrgyz and Uyghur, start from a model that covers them (TurkicASR, Söyle, MMS, or Omnilingual ASR) instead. The whisper-small (244 million parameters) and whisper-medium (769 million) checkpoints are common starting points for fine-tuning; measure memory and runtime on the hardware at hand.


11.2.3 TurkicASR
TurkicASR (Mussakhojayeva et al. 2023) is a multilingual ASR system developed at ISSAI that covers 10 Turkic languages: Azerbaijani, Bashkir, Chuvash, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Sakha, Turkish, Tatar, Uzbek, and Uyghur. A single model is trained jointly on data from all ten languages; the work also released a 218.2-hour Turkish speech corpus.
Kazakh Speech Corpus 2 (KSC2) contains over a thousand hours of transcribed Kazakh speech, combining the earlier KSC and KazakhTTS2 recordings with television and radio, parliamentary speeches and podcasts, and including Kazakh–Russian code-switching (Mussakhojayeva, Khassanov, and Varol 2022a).
TurkicASR’s best jointly trained model reduced character and word error rates by 56.7% and 54.3% relative, on average, compared with monolingual models. Adding related Turkic language data helped more than adding English or Russian (Mussakhojayeva et al. 2023). These results support the tested multilingual recipe. A controlled comparison would be needed to separate the contributions of shared phonology, vocabulary and other factors, or to assess the benefit for another language.
Söyle (Mussakhojayeva et al. 2024) is a Whisper-based system from ISSAI covering 11 Turkic languages and the official languages of the United Nations, released together with the Tatar speech corpus TatSC. It is designed for noisy recording conditions and fine-tunes Whisper on noise-augmented speech, with improvements reported on the paper’s evaluation conditions. Deployment on a new microphone, domain or speaker population still requires a separate test.


11.2.4 Open Speech Datasets: Common Voice and FLEURS
Mozilla Common Voice (Ardila et al. 2020) is a crowd-sourced speech dataset collected through volunteer recording. Several Turkic languages have Common Voice datasets, and their sizes do not follow the general resource hierarchy. In the release statistics for Common Voice 27.0 (11 September 2026), Uyghur has 462 validated hours and Bashkir 259, against 130 for Turkish, 102 for Uzbek, 39 for Kyrgyz, 33 for Tatar, 25 for Chuvash, 16 for Sakha, 3 each for Kazakh and Turkmen and 1 for Azerbaijani (datasets/scripted-speech/cv-corpus-27.0-2026-09-11.json in the common-voice/cv-dataset repository, commit 65ca246). These counts describe validated audio, not all submitted recordings. Check the current release statistics for each language before planning an experiment. Mozilla’s distribution notice directs downloads to Mozilla Data Collective from October 2025, so older loading code may no longer work.
FLEURS (Conneau et al. 2023) provides about 12 hours of read speech per language for 102 languages, recorded for FLORES sentences, with fixed train/dev/test splits; its Turkic languages are Turkish, Azerbaijani, Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Uzbek. Its shared source-sentence design supports comparisons, but recordings, retained items and speakers differ across languages. Check prompt IDs and split contents when constructing a matched comparison; the approximate hours describe the whole dataset per language, not the training split alone.

title: 11  Speech Technologies
text:
11.3 Text-to-Speech

11.3.1 Text and Pronunciation in Turkic TTS
A grapheme-based TTS system receives the written surface form, including the selected suffix vowels. A phoneme-based system needs a pronunciation front end that respects the target variety. Suffix vowels use the language’s vowel inventory; each grammatical suffix does not need its own phoneme symbol. Morphological features may help disambiguation or prosody, but their benefit is an experimental question.
Keep text normalisation (numbers, abbreviations and names), grapheme-to-phoneme conversion and prosodic prediction separate in error analysis. Test both frequent forms and productive unseen inflections. For synthesis, report intelligibility separately from naturalness and speaker similarity.


11.3.2 KazakhTTS2 and TurkicTTS
KazakhTTS2 (Mussakhojayeva, Khassanov, and Varol 2022b) contains 271 hours of studio-recorded Kazakh speech from five speakers (three female, two male), up from 93 hours and two speakers in the first release, with subjective mean opinion scores of 3.6 to 4.2 across the speakers. Its repository releases Tacotron 2 models with Parallel WaveGAN vocoders for each speaker. Emotional speech is covered by the separate KazEmoTTS dataset: 74.85 hours from three narrators in six emotions (Abilbekov et al. 2024). The open Piper voice kk_KZ-issai-high, a VITS model trained on the ISSAI data with six speakers, is used in this chapter’s exercises.
TurkicTTS (Yeshpanov, Mussakhojayeva, and Khassanov 2023) tests transliteration-based synthesis for ten languages, including Kazakh, its training language. The other nine are zero-shot targets. Letters are mapped through IPA to Kazakh letters before a Kazakh-trained Tacotron 2 model synthesises the text. The authors report subjective evaluations of this procedure. Mapping target sounds to Kazakh letters can approximate or merge distinctions, so a shared representation does not guarantee faithful target-language pronunciation.


11.3.3 Neural TTS Architectures
The released systems discussed here use Tacotron 2 and VITS. Codec language modelling provides a further architectural comparison:
Tacotron 2 (Shen et al. 2018) uses a sequence-to-sequence architecture with attention to convert grapheme or phoneme sequences to mel spectrogram frames, followed by a separate neural vocoder (WaveNet in the original paper, Parallel WaveGAN in the KazakhTTS2 release) to convert spectrograms to audio. KazakhTTS2 and TurkicTTS both use it.
VITS (Variational Inference with adversarial learning for end-to-end TTS) (Kim, Kong, and Son 2021) is an end-to-end architecture that combines the acoustic model and vocoder in a single network trained with a generative adversarial loss. Its inference procedure can sample durations and latent variables. Repeated output therefore depends on the random seed and noise settings (Exercise 3 measures this for the selected Piper implementation). The MMS and Piper Turkic voices are VITS models. Its relative quality depends on data, training and the listener evaluation.
VALL-E style codec language modelling (Chen et al. 2025) treats TTS as a language modelling problem over discrete speech codec tokens. The cited work studies voice-conditioned synthesis; its quality on Turkic languages is untested. Data and compute requirements depend on the checkpoint and adaptation protocol. Voice-cloning experiments additionally require explicit permission for the intended voice use.


11.3.4 Availability and Evaluated Quality
Public VITS checkpoints exist for MMS Chuvash TTS and MMS Crimean Tatar TTS, both under CC BY-NC 4.0. The pinned entries in Table B.6 document their availability. Assess naturalness, dialect coverage and suitability for the intended use separately.
For each candidate, check its tokeniser’s expected script, training domain, speaker coverage and licence, then run a shared prompt set. Use blinded, counterbalanced listener judgements with the same prompts, listening conditions and evaluation scale for competing systems. Do not compare a new MOS directly with a historical score collected from different listeners.

title: 11  Speech Technologies
text:
11.4 Speech for Low-Resource Languages

11.4.1 Cross-Lingual Acoustic Model Transfer
Start with a checkpoint whose input/output conventions and language coverage fit the task. Compare its unadapted output with full fine-tuning and a declared partial-freezing policy. Build learning curves by increasing training hours while keeping validation speakers and transcripts fixed; select the recipe on validation, then evaluate once on the reserved test set. No universal number of hours guarantees useful ASR. Shared phonetic structure motivates transfer but does not identify its cause without controlled comparisons (Mussakhojayeva et al. 2023).


11.4.2 Data Augmentation
Apply augmentation to training recordings only, recording its algorithm, probability, seed and parameter distribution. Resampling-based speed perturbation changes pitch and duration together (Ko et al. 2015). Pitch-preserving time stretching changes duration separately. Pitch shifting varies a recording’s pitch while retaining the same speaker.
Exercise 2 checks these operations on synthetic Kazakh speech. Duration and median fundamental-frequency ratios use six items; ASR errors use 30. A speed factor of 0.9 produces about 1.11 times the duration and 0.90 times the fundamental frequency. The other operations approximately preserve the quantity they are designed to leave fixed.
On this sample, time stretching and pitch shifting increase CER more than the tested speed perturbations or 20 dB noise. This tests recogniser sensitivity at inference. An experiment that trains with augmentation is needed to measure its benefit.
SpecAugment (Park et al. 2019) masks time and frequency regions of the acoustic representation. Additive noise is mixed at a declared signal-to-noise ratio; reverberation is produced by convolving audio with a room impulse response. These are separate interventions. Preserve intelligibility and transcript alignment, and compare each intervention at the same update budget before combining them.


11.4.3 Massively Multilingual Speech Models
Meta’s Massively Multilingual Speech (MMS) project covers recognition and synthesis in over 1,100 languages, and language identification in about 4,000 (Pratap et al. 2024). It uses separate systems: wav2vec 2.0-based models for recognition and identification, and VITS for synthesis. Recordings of religious texts supply much of the data for small languages, limiting domain coverage; recording conditions also need checking.
The later Omnilingual ASR system covers more than 1,600 languages with CTC models and models using an LLM-inspired decoder, ranging from about 300 million to 7 billion parameters (Omnilingual ASR Team et al. 2025). TurkicNLP accepts 20 Turkic languages for this backend. Tuvan, Khalaj, Ottoman Turkish and Old Turkic lack an Omnilingual language code (TurkicNLP 0.5.0 README).
MMS and Omnilingual ASR offer further candidates where the earlier systems lack coverage. Compare an unadapted model with fine-tuning on target-domain speech. Evaluate on FLEURS where available, or on held-out recordings from the intended domain.


11.4.4 Speech Recognition with TurkicNLP
TurkicNLP wraps Omnilingual ASR as SpeechRecognizer. The wrapper takes TurkicNLP language codes, checks that the model supports them, splits recordings longer than the model’s 40-second limit at pauses, and returns transcripts in the language’s TurkicNLP script. Where the model writes another script, the toolkit transliterates: Karakalpak and Crimean Tatar come out of the model in Cyrillic and are returned in Latin. Speech recognition needs its own Python environment (pip install "turkicnlp[all,asr]" in a fresh environment, because the ASR dependencies pin older versions of PyTorch and NumPy).
import turkicnlp

print(turkicnlp.list_asr_languages(check_model=True))   # e.g. {'kaz': {'Cyrl': 'kaz_Cyrl'}, ...}

asr = turkicnlp.SpeechRecognizer(model_card="omniASR_LLM_1B", device="cpu")
texts = asr.transcribe(["kaz_sample.wav", "tat_sample.wav"], lang=["kaz", "tat"], batch_size=2)

res = asr.transcribe("kaz_sample.wav", lang="kaz", return_details=True)
for seg in res.segments:                       # time-aligned pieces of long recordings
    print(f"[{seg.start:.2f}-{seg.end:.2f}] {seg.text}")
print(asr.transcribe("kaz_sample.wav", lang="kaz", script="Latn"))   # 2021 Latin alphabet
The transcript can go straight into the text pipeline:
nlp = turkicnlp.Pipeline("kaz", processors=["asr", "tokenize", "pos", "lemma", "depparse"],
                         asr_model_card="omniASR_LLM_1B", asr_device="cpu")
doc = nlp.from_audio("kaz_sample.wav")
print(doc.text, doc.audio_segments)
for w in doc.words:
    print(w.text, w.upos, w.lemma, w.head, w.deprel)
The wrapper’s documented Omnilingual output is lower-case and unpunctuated. This differs from edited training text and can affect tagging and parsing; measure downstream accuracy on checked transcripts rather than assuming the size or direction of the change. Memory use depends on the checkpoint, precision, loader and recording length; measure it in the intended environment.

title: 11  Speech Technologies
section: 11.5 Hands-On: A Fine-Tuning Procedure for Kazakh ASR with Whisper
text:
11.5 Hands-On: A Fine-Tuning Procedure for Kazakh ASR with Whisper
Question. Does Whisper adaptation improve recognition on held-out Kazakh recordings?
Inputs. The pinned FLEURS Kazakh release and Whisper-small checkpoint below.
Compute. Audio decoding, checkpoint downloads and training memory; a GPU is useful for fine-tuning.
Output. Saved predictions, raw and normalised WER/CER, and an experiment manifest.
Interpretation. Compare real-recording baseline and adapted output under the same scoring policy.
The executable implementation is speech.py. It uses google/fleurs, configuration kk_kz, at revision 70bb2e84b976b7e960aa89f1c648e09c59f894dd, and the pinned openai/whisper-small checkpoint in Table B.6. The current dataset release has Parquet files; the loader requests undecoded audio and uses SoundFile explicitly rather than assuming an older datasets.Audio array interface.
python code/ch11-speech/speech.py runs/kazakh-asr --epochs 3 --seed 42
The script keeps official train, validation and test splits separate. It rejects duplicate recording paths and cross-split identical transcripts, reports retained duration per split, and relies on the dataset card’s speaker separation because speaker IDs are not exposed in this schema. If these checks fail, investigate the release rather than silently redistributing benchmark items.
Only finite mono 16 kHz recordings of at most 30 seconds enter this short-utterance recipe. Longer audio must be segmented with aligned transcripts in a separately documented experiment. Truncating a recording while retaining its whole transcript teaches the wrong alignment. Overlength decoder targets are also rejected.
The collator removes the leading decoder-start token exactly once; Whisper inserts it during label shifting. It retains language/task tokens, supplies the acoustic attention mask, and masks label padding with -100. Checkpoint selection uses validation WER. After selection, the baseline and adapted checkpoint are decoded on the same complete test items with the same language, task and generation limit.
The scorer compares predictions with the original reference strings. It reports corpus-level raw and conservatively normalised WER/CER, empty-reference counts, recording-ID hashes and per-item transcripts. Its normalisation preserves alphabet distinctions and apostrophes; state that policy when comparing scores. Reference words or characters form the denominator, while insertions against empty references still contribute to the numerator.
The implementation checks exercise the collator, audio guards, metric arithmetic and a tiny randomly initialised Whisper forward/backward pass. The recorded Exercise 1 uses the same scoring functions on synthetic speech, but a different int8 ONNX export and runtime. Its error rates are not the unadapted FLEURS baseline for this training recipe.
For long-recording inference, use a separately validated chunking/stitching procedure. For short recordings, call model.eval() and torch.inference_mode() and enforce the same sample-rate and duration checks.
Status: procedure only. The fine-tuning run on real recordings is not reported here.

title: 11  Speech Technologies
text:
What to Take Forward
Speech systems connect written conventions with sounds, timing and speakers. The synthetic-audio probes illustrate recogniser behaviour on specific texts and voices; ranking languages by quality on this basis would overreach. Evaluate ASR on real recordings under a stated normalisation policy and TTS with listeners. Compare cross-language training and augmentation on held-out speech. Chapter 12 returns to text and pretrained models.

title: 11  Speech Technologies
text:
Further Reading
The TurkicASR system is described in Mussakhojayeva et al. (2023), the primary reference for ISSAI’s multilingual Turkic ASR. Mussakhojayeva, Khassanov, and Varol (2022b) describes KazakhTTS2, and Yeshpanov, Mussakhojayeva, and Khassanov (2023) the zero-shot TurkicTTS approach.
The Whisper paper (Radford et al. 2023) describes the training procedure, data filtering methodology, and language coverage of the Whisper model series; its supplementary materials include per-language WER breakdowns that are the primary source for Turkic ASR baselines. For speech processing fundamentals including CTC, attention-based encoder-decoders, and the RNN-T architecture, the speech chapters of Jurafsky and Martin (2024) provide a thorough treatment.
For Turkic phonology, Johanson (2021) (chapters 12–18 and 50) covers vowel systems, consonant inventories, and prosodic patterns with systematic comparison across the family. Use these descriptions when checking pronunciation assumptions in a speech system.

title: 11  Speech Technologies
text:
Exercises

Measure the unadapted Whisper baseline on a frozen Kazakh test set: raw and normalised WER and CER, total duration, results per speaker where identifiers are available, and error examples. FLEURS does not expose speaker IDs in the schema used here, so do not invent a speaker breakdown from recording paths. With the Hands-On script, compare it with the adapted checkpoint on the same items, choosing all decoding settings on validation.
Apply resampling speed perturbation, pitch-preserving time stretching, pitch shifting and additive noise separately. Verify what each operation changes (duration, fundamental frequency, signal-to-noise ratio) and measure the recogniser’s sensitivity to each before using any of them in training, where they are compared at matched updates and seeds and kept in their source split.
Compare TTS voices with an ASR-based transcription-error diagnostic, measure how much repeated sampling of the same text changes it, and distinguish recogniser errors from synthesis errors. This diagnostic alone cannot rank human intelligibility or naturalness. Use the same prompts for every voice and design a blinded, counterbalanced listening test for fluent, compensated listeners. Obtain permission for any cloned voice.
Decode Kazakh and Turkish speech with the Whisper tokens of related languages and with automatic language detection. Check which Turkic language tokens the model accepts; for Kyrgyz or Uyghur, compare related-language and multilingual initialisations by fine-tuning instead of forcing an unsupported token.

title: 12  Pretrained Language Models for Turkic
text:
12.1 Encoder-Only Models for Turkic Languages
Chapter 7 introduced neural morphology and tokenisation. This chapter builds on that foundation: selecting pretrained encoders, adapting generative models and evaluating the results. It separates language coverage, tokenisation and task accuracy.
The chapter covers encoders (Section 12.1), generative models (Section 12.2), adaptation (Section 12.3) and context budgeting (Section 12.4). The hands-on provides an XLM-R classification recipe with LoRA. The exercises report separate experiments with Glot500 on SIB-200.
crumbs: 12  Pretrained Language Models for Turkic

title: 12  Pretrained Language Models for Turkic
text:
12.1.1 The BERT Architecture as Infrastructure
BERT-style encoders (Devlin et al. 2019) learn contextual token representations through masked language modelling: predict selected tokens from their surrounding text. A task-specific head then maps those representations to labels or answer spans.
For POS tagging and NER, a classification head predicts labels from token representations. Sequence classifiers use a pooled representation, often the first special token. Extractive question-answering heads predict answer boundaries in the supplied context. Token alignment and label conventions still need task-specific handling, as in Section 9.6.
The training pattern is reusable across languages, but changing the model name and dataset is not enough. Check the tokeniser, input length, annotation scheme and evaluation procedure for each model and task.


12.1.2 BERTurk
BERTurk has four main BERT variants: cased and uncased models, each with a 32K or 128K vocabulary (Schweter 2020). The release README reports a 35 GB, 4.4-billion-token training corpus drawn from Turkish OSCAR, Wikipedia, OPUS and material supplied by Kemal Oflazer. Cased models preserve capitalisation; uncased models lowercase the input. Check how each normaliser handles Turkish dotted and dotless letters (Chapter 3).
A larger vocabulary increases the embedding matrix and may shorten token sequences (Section 7.2). Exercise 1 compares published BERTurk task scores. Its recorded run did not measure the BERTurk tokenisers, which were unavailable locally.



Table 12.1: The main BERTurk variants. The family also includes DistilBERTurk, ConvBERTurk, ELECTRA and T5 models, some trained on the Turkish part of mC4 (242 GB).

The 32K and 128K vocabularies require different-sized embedding matrices, so the models also differ in parameter count. To compare monolingual and multilingual encoders, use the same splits, preprocessing and search budget.
The BERTurk repository’s five-run evaluations show that the preferred model depends on the task. On WikiANN NER, cased BERTurk 128K has the best BERTurk test F1: 93.90, compared with 92.96 for XLM-R base. On BOUN POS tagging, XLM-R base scores highest at 91.86% accuracy, followed by cased BERTurk 32K at 91.49 and cased 128K at 91.02 (OLD_EVALUATIONS.md in stefan-it/turkish-bert, commit 0ab49e2).


12.1.3 Multilingual Models: mBERT and XLM-R
Multilingual BERT (mBERT) (Devlin et al. 2019) uses a shared WordPiece vocabulary and multilingual masked-language pretraining. Current Wikipedia article counts cannot reconstruct the training distribution of a historical checkpoint. Record the checkpoint and its documented training coverage, then measure tokenisation on the actual target corpus.
XLM-R (Conneau et al. 2020) is trained on 2.5 terabytes of filtered CommonCrawl data in 100 languages and reported large gains over mBERT on cross-lingual benchmarks such as XNLI, which includes Turkish. The model is available in two sizes: xlm-roberta-base and xlm-roberta-large (approximately 270M and 550M parameters in the original paper; exact counts depend on the loaded task head).
XLM-R’s CC-100 training corpus includes Turkish, Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Uyghur. It excludes Tatar, Bashkir, Turkmen, Chuvash, Sakha and the smaller Turkic languages. Related languages and shared scripts may still support transfer to them; measure the resulting representation quality.
Glot500 extends XLM-R to 500+ languages and expands its vocabulary from 250,002 to 401,145 entries (Imani et al. 2023). All but one of XLM-R’s pieces retain their IDs (Exercise 1). It covers many more Turkic languages and supplies the frozen encoder for TurkicNLP’s multilingual POS tagger and dependency parser (Chapter 8).
For cross-lingual work, include a multilingual encoder as a baseline. Kardeş-NLU reports gains from Turkish intermediate training and fine-tuning on its tested NLU tasks in Azerbaijani, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Uyghur (Senel et al. 2024). The parsing results in Chapter 8 use different tasks and reference sets; they should be interpreted separately.


12.1.4 Language-Specific Models and Model Selection
BERTbek (Kuriyozov, Vilares, and Gómez-Rodríguez 2024) is a set of three Uzbek BERT models trained on different text sources and corpus sizes; the authors report that they outperform mBERT on sentiment analysis, multi-label topic classification and NER. Script, casing, training domain and released weights must be checked for each model separately; “Uzbek” alone does not specify its input conventions. The catalogue is selective; many more models have been released.
For within-language work, compare a suitable monolingual encoder with a multilingual baseline. For transfer, include a multilingual model whose language coverage and tokeniser fit the target. Keep mBERT where it is relevant to a historical comparison or deployment constraint. Neither monolingual specialisation nor a larger corpus guarantees superiority on every task. Table B.6 records exact configurations used in the book’s experiments.

title: 12  Pretrained Language Models for Turkic
text:
12.2 Generative Language Models for Turkic

12.2.1 Turkish Generative Models
TURNA is a Turkish encoder-decoder model pretrained with UL2 on a corpus curated for the project (Uludoğan et al. 2024). The authors evaluate three generation and five understanding tasks. They report gains over several multilingual models and competitive understanding results against monolingual Turkish models. Those comparisons support conclusions about the tested datasets and baselines; they leave broader comparisons with decoder-only models open.
For any additional academic, community or commercial checkpoint, record its exact model card, base revision, tokeniser, adaptation data and licence before adding it to an experiment. A name without a verified release is not a reproducible baseline.


12.2.2 Kazakh: KAZ-LLM and Sherkala
KAZ-LLM (Institute of Smart Systems and Artificial Intelligence (ISSAI) 2024), released by ISSAI in December 2024, comes in 8-billion and 70-billion-parameter versions built on Llama 3.1. ISSAI reports training on more than 150 billion tokens of Kazakh, Russian and English text, with additional support for Turkish; the weights are licensed CC BY-NC 4.0. Its evaluation code (the IS2AI/KazLLM_Benchmark repository) runs MMLU, Winogrande, HellaSwag, ARC, GSM8K and DROP in Kazakh, Russian and English.
Sherkala-Chat (Koto et al. 2025) is an 8-billion-parameter Kazakh chat model built by adapting Llama 3.1 8B in a “moderately resourced” setting: continued pretraining on 45.3 billion tokens of Kazakh, English, Russian and Turkish text, instruction tuning on translated data plus an automatically built, manually checked Kazakhstan-specific instruction set, and Kazakh safety data. Its paper is a documented recipe for adapting an existing LLM to a Turkic language.


12.2.3 Other Generative Models and the Multilingual Fallback
Other languages. This catalogue is selective. A missing entry means that a release has not been verified here, not that no dedicated model exists.
Multilingual models. Where no dedicated model fits the task, evaluate a multilingual model. TUMLU (Isbarov et al. 2025) tests multiple-choice performance on native questions in the listed Turkic languages (Chapter 15). It does not directly measure grammaticality, generation quality or cultural adequacy.
Exercise 4 gives a narrower comparison: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (Qwen Team et al. 2024) scores 84.2% on 500 English COPA test items and 52.2% on their Kazakh translations from Kardeş-NLU (Ponti et al. 2020; Senel et al. 2024). The Kazakh score’s 95% interval, 47.8–56.5%, includes the 50% random-choice baseline. This result concerns one model and scoring protocol; it does not identify the cause of the language gap.
Combining an LLM with toolkit analyses. TurkicNLP offers LLM backends for morphology, NER, translation, sentiment and spelling correction (Section 9.5, Section 10.3). With morph_backend="apertium_llm", the LLM selects among the analyser’s candidate readings for ambiguous words. This constrains the selection, but the candidates may be incomplete and the chosen reading may be wrong. A free-form explanation from llm.ask is a separate output and needs checking:
import turkicnlp

llm = dict(llm_model="qwen2.5:7b", llm_base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", llm_api_key="ollama")

nlp = turkicnlp.Pipeline("kaz", processors=["tokenize", "morph"], morph_backend="apertium_llm", **llm)
doc = nlp("Ол кітабымды оқып жатыр.")
print([(w.text, w.lemma, w.upos, w.feats) for w in doc.words])

print(turkicnlp.llm.ask("Explain the verb form in this sentence.", doc=doc, **llm))
The same llm_* options work with an OpenAI-compatible server (vLLM, Ollama), OpenAI, Claude (llm_provider="anthropic") or an in-process Hugging Face model (llm_provider="hf"). doc._processor_log records the model and prompt version used, which you need when reporting results.

title: 12  Pretrained Language Models for Turkic
text:
12.3 Building Turkic Language Models

12.3.1 Continued Pretraining
Continued pretraining updates a pretrained model on additional text. For BERT-style encoders, it continues masked language modelling. Decoder LLMs instead continue their next-token prediction objective. Compare the adapted checkpoint with the original on the intended tasks.
Continued pretraining can adapt a model even when the target language was absent from its documented training data. Glot500 is an example of extending multilingual coverage. Gains, forgetting and preservation of cross-lingual alignment must be measured; compare downstream validation performance before and after adaptation, including a retained source-language task.
Use audited, deduplicated target-language text and document the effective token count. Section 4.1 provides dated corpus measurements with their units; raw web totals are not a guarantee of clean usable training data.


12.3.2 Vocabulary Extension
Measure full-text fertility, unknown-token behaviour and downstream performance before adding tokens. Adding an already representable word can shorten sequences; byte fallback means missing whole words need not be unrepresentable. Tokeniser add_tokens adds matching rules and entries; it does not train new BPE merges.
Keep existing token IDs when adding vocabulary entries. Resize the input and output embeddings as needed, check weight tying and initialise each new row from its old-token decomposition or another documented method.
Make sure the new rows receive gradients. If every base parameter is frozen, attention LoRA alone leaves them untrained. Either train and save the full embedding module, including its parameters in the count, or use a tested method that updates selected rows. Save the tokeniser, resized embeddings/output head and adapter together. After reloading, compare logits and token IDs. Renumbering old IDs to merge independently trained vocabularies breaks their association with the learned embeddings.
Exercise 5 carries out these checks for 300 Kazakh words added to Glot500: the old IDs survive, only the new rows receive gradients when PEFT’s trainable_token_indices is used, and the checked logits match after reload. In that recorded PEFT version and configuration, saving also writes the whole resized embedding matrix, producing a 1.2 GB adapter file. The extension shortened the Kazakh test text by 2.5% and gave a lower mean classification score (mean macro-F1 0.818 against 0.837 without it, over three seeds).


12.3.3 Training from Scratch
Decide between training from scratch and adaptation using the cleaned data volume, compute budget and deployment requirements. Compare adaptation with a smaller model trained from scratch on the same held-out tasks. Keep benchmark text out of tokeniser training and pretraining as well as supervised fine-tuning.


12.3.4 Adapting a Decoder LLM to a Turkic Language
Adapting an existing open-weight LLM is one route; KAZ-LLM and Sherkala are documented examples. The following workflow separates the main decisions:

Tokeniser extension. Measure the base tokeniser’s fertility on your language (Table 7.1). If extension is justified, follow the ID, embedding and reload checks above and measure the resulting full-text token counts.
Continued pretraining. Continue training on target-language text mixed with a share of the base model’s original languages (often English, and for Central Asian languages Russian) and test whether the mixture reduces forgetting. Turkish is another candidate to compare, although Kardeş-NLU’s NLU results say little about the best mixture for decoder pretraining.
Instruction tuning. Audit the available native, translated and generated instruction data. Check meaning, language and relevance to the intended users. Compare data sources at matched training budgets; the Sherkala recipe above provides one documented example.
Preference tuning and safety. Check what preference data and evaluations exist for the selected language. Test both appropriate assistance and refusal behaviour with target-language prompts; behaviour in English may not carry over.
Evaluation. Use native benchmarks (TUMLU, KazMMLU, and others in Chapter 15), measure retention on any source languages the application needs, and use unrestricted language identification to flag outputs for manual review (Section 3.7).



12.3.5 LoRA: Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning
For an adapted projection \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}}\), standard LoRA uses
\[W'=W+\frac{\alpha}{r}BA,\qquad A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}},\quad B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}.\]
The added parameter count is \(r(d_{in}+d_{out})\) per projection, not per transformer layer. Count every adapted projection plus any trainable classifier, embedding or bias parameters. Target module names depend on the architecture: XLM-R uses query and value, unlike models whose projections are named q_proj and v_proj (Hu et al. 2022). For an XLM-R-base-sized model with rank 8 on query and value, that is 12 × 2 × 8 × (768 + 768) = 294,912 adapter weights; the seven-class classification head adds 595,975.
In Exercise 2, LoRA with ranks 2, 8 and 32 on Glot500 gave Kazakh SIB-200 test macro-F1 between 0.807 and 0.861; a comparator with frozen word embeddings gave 0.792. Although the saved output calls it full, only the other encoder weights and classifier were updated: 86,047,495 parameters. It is partial fine-tuning. Only rank 8 has three seeds, so the runs are too few to rank training methods or ranks reliably.
QLoRA quantises frozen base weights. Ideal four-bit weight storage is one quarter of sixteen-bit storage, but scales, unquantised modules, gradients, optimiser states and activations also occupy memory. Measure peak memory and throughput for the actual batch and sequence lengths; a nominal GPU capacity does not guarantee a configuration will fit.

section: 12.4 The Tokeniser Problem for Large Language Models
text:
12.4 The Tokeniser Problem for Large Language Models

12.4.1 Estimating Context Use
Section 7.1 defines fertility. For context budgeting, the relevant quantity is the token count of the complete prompt, including formatting and special tokens. This applies to encoders as well as decoder LLMs.
A model’s context limit is measured in tokens. How much text fits depends on the language, tokeniser and text itself. A larger limit also does not guarantee that the model uses all parts of a long input effectively.
The table below estimates word counts by dividing a token budget by the isolated-word fertility values in Table 7.1. This arithmetic describes token consumption; evaluating long-context reasoning requires a separate task.

Autoregressive models generate tokens sequentially. For a fixed text, higher fertility can increase decoding work, though elapsed time also depends on architecture, batching, hardware, prompt processing and output length. The estimates above use isolated words, omit chat-template and special tokens, and leave no response space. Treat them as rough capacity calculations.
Running-text counts can differ. In Exercise 1’s SIB-200 sentence sample, including punctuation, the Llama 3 tokeniser uses 4.77 tokens per Kazakh whitespace word and 2.15 per Turkish one. The isolated-word figures in Table 7.1 are 3.51 and 2.03, measured on a different sample.
You can measure fertility for your own text and tokeniser in a few lines, in the native script and after conversion to the toolkit’s Common Turkic Script (CTS):
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
import turkicnlp
from turkicnlp.scripts import Script
from turkicnlp.scripts.transliterator import Transliterator

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("FacebookAI/xlm-roberta-base",
    revision="e73636d4f797dec63c3081bb6ed5c7b0bb3f2089")  # public encoder tokenizer diagnostic
words = [w.text for w in turkicnlp.Pipeline("kaz", processors=["tokenize"], tokenize_backend="rule")(
             "Мен мектептерімізде оқыдым. Алматы — Қазақстанның ең үлкен қаласы.").words
         if w.text.isalpha()]
to_cts = Transliterator("kaz", Script.CYRILLIC, Script.COMMON_TURKIC)

def fertility(ws):
    if not ws:
        raise ValueError("no words to measure")
    return sum(len(tok.encode(w, add_special_tokens=False)) for w in ws) / len(ws)

print(f"native {fertility(words):.2f}   CTS {fertility([to_cts.transliterate(w) for w in words]):.2f}")
Use add_special_tokens=False for this isolated-word diagnostic. Context budgeting requires encoding the complete prompt with the actual model tokeniser and template, including any required access to gated checkpoints.


12.4.2 The Vocabulary Overlap Problem
A shared vocabulary reuses character sequences across languages, but context determines their meaning. Models can also learn relationships between forms with different token IDs.
Different scripts reduce literal overlap, but do not prevent a multilingual encoder from learning aligned representations. The overlap study in Figure 3.3 is a diagnostic on its stated sample, not proof that all cross-script trigrams are absent or that Turkish knowledge cannot transfer to Kazakh.
Script conversion can increase literal overlap while changing the input distribution (Section 3.6, Section 16.2). Exercise 3 illustrates why the task result must be measured: Glot500 fine-tuned on Turkish SIB-200 topic classification (Adelani et al. 2024) reaches a Kazakh macro-F1 of 0.838 on Cyrillic test sentences but 0.694 on the same sentences in CTS (means over three seeds), although conversion raises the share of Kazakh subword pieces seen in the Turkish training text from 9% to 52%.


12.4.3 LoRA for Vocabulary and Script Adaptation
Treat script conversion, vocabulary extension and LoRA as separate factors. Compare the native-script baseline, conversion alone, extension alone and their combinations under a matched update budget. Follow the embedding-saving contract above whenever the vocabulary changes. Evaluate task accuracy alongside fertility (Section 15.1).

section: 12.5 Hands-On: A LoRA Fine-Tuning Procedure for Kazakh Text Classification with XLM-R
text:
12.5 Hands-On: A LoRA Fine-Tuning Procedure for Kazakh Text Classification with XLM-R
Question. Does LoRA improve Kazakh text classification on source-disjoint data?
Inputs. Licensed JSONL train/dev/test files in the documented schema and XLM-R.
Compute. Checkpoint download and training memory; record the selected trainable modules and hardware.
Output. Saved adapters and task head, label mappings, predictions and scores.
Interpretation. Select the checkpoint on development data and compare the reserved test predictions with a baseline.
The complete runner is classify.py. Supply train.jsonl, dev.jsonl and test.jsonl with id, group_id, text and a string label; group_id identifies the original article or source group across excerpts and variants. The runner rejects cross-split IDs, source groups and exact normalised texts, unknown evaluation labels and overlength examples. Define document chunking before using long articles.
python code/ch12-classify/classify.py data/kazakh-news runs/kazakh-lora --lora
The tokeniser and base model share a pinned revision. LoRA adapts XLM-R’s query and value projections with rank 8 and scaling 16/8. The randomly initialised classifier is explicitly trainable and saved using modules_to_save=["classifier"]. The run manifest counts actual trainable and total parameters rather than printing a fixed percentage.
Development macro-F1 selects the checkpoint. The runner saves the model/adapter and tokeniser, reloads onto a fresh base model, and checks evaluation logits before scoring the reserved test split. It saves per-item predictions, label mappings, input hashes and seed. The inference checkpoint includes the classifier; loading the base encoder alone creates an untrained task head.
The local mechanics checks use a tiny randomly initialised encoder and balanced synthetic labels to test loss, gradients and adapter reload. They provide no evidence of classification accuracy. The exercises instead use Glot500 on SIB-200, selecting checkpoints on development data. Their separate runner truncates at 256 tokens, while this hands-on rejects overlength inputs. Record affected items when interpreting those exercise scores.
Status: procedure only. No licensed news corpus with source-disjoint splits was prepared for this run, so no Kazakh news-classification score is reported.

title: 12  Pretrained Language Models for Turkic
text:
What to Take Forward
Choose a pretrained model for the task, then test whether adaptation improves task performance or meets a justified cost, latency or deployment requirement. Exercise 4 shows why evaluation matters: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct scores 52.2% on the Kazakh COPA translations, with a 95% interval of 47.8–56.5% that includes the 50% chance baseline. Use token counts to plan context and cost, and task scores to assess an adaptation. Chapter 13 applies these models to representations and search.

title: 12  Pretrained Language Models for Turkic
text:
Further Reading
The BERTurk model family is documented in its release (Schweter 2020), whose repository describes the training corpora and compares the BERTurk variants with mBERT and XLM-R on Turkish POS tagging, NER and question answering; no variant wins every task. For multilingual encoders more generally, Conneau et al. (2020) describes the training data, language coverage and cross-lingual transfer properties of XLM-R, including its XNLI results for Turkish.
Hu et al. (2022) introduces LoRA and compares it with full fine-tuning on the paper’s tasks. Use those results as motivation for a matched comparison on the target task. For Turkic-specific LLM evaluation, Isbarov et al. (2025) is a primary reference for native multiple-choice evaluation, with results by language, subject and script. See Chapter 15 for the release-count caveat.
The fertility analysis underlying the context window calculations in Section 12.4 is from Hakimov (2026), which provides measurements across 20 Turkic languages and four LLM tokenisers. The same paper shows the effect of a common script on fertility and lexical overlap (Section 12.4). Senel et al. (2024) shows how a high-resource relative improves sentence-level transfer within the family; Koto et al. (2025) documents the adaptation of an open LLM to Kazakh.

title: 12  Pretrained Language Models for Turkic
text:
Exercises

Compare vocabulary variants of one model family on the same documents. For BERTurk’s 32K and 128K models, use the scores published in its repository; measure full-text tokens per word and embedding parameters for XLM-R and Glot500 (whose vocabulary extends XLM-R’s), and compare them with LLM tokenisers.
Compare classifier-only training, full fine-tuning and several LoRA ranks; report any frozen modules explicitly. Use the same real train/dev/test splits and training budget. Report macro-F1, class support, trainable parameters, peak memory and measured time.
Test native script and CTS as separate treatments for zero-shot transfer from Turkish to Kazakh and Kyrgyz. Keep original IDs and labels, and freeze the protocol on development data.
Evaluate Kazakh multiple-choice items with a conditional scorer, as in Section 15.6, and compare it with an encoder whose multiple-choice head is randomly initialised. The latter is not a zero-shot reasoning model.
Extend a tokeniser without changing old IDs. Verify new embedding gradients and save/reload equivalence, then test whether reduced fertility improves downstream performance.

title: 13  Meaning: Embeddings, Semantic Resources, and Retrieval
text:
13.1 Lexical-Semantic Resources
Chapter 12 introduced pretrained models and adaptation. This chapter turns to semantic resources and retrieval: representing text, comparing meanings and finding relevant passages. It then connects retrieval to generation, which Chapter 14 examines in more detail.
Inflection and script variation both affect matching. Turkish ev ‘house’, evler and evimiz are related forms, but exact matching treats them as different strings. Script differences can also hide shared forms (Section 3.6). The chapter compares lexical and dense retrieval, including queries and documents in different languages.
Lexical-semantic resources describe what words mean and how they relate: synonymy and hypernymy in a WordNet, predicate–argument structure in a PropBank, relations between clauses in a discourse treebank. The selected inventory below includes several Turkish resources, WordNets for Tatar and Uzbek, and a Kyrgyz word-similarity set (Table 13.1):
Other lexical sources include Wiktionary, the Apertium bilingual dictionaries used by the translation pairs in Chapter 10, and lemma/POS outputs from Chapter 6. These supply lexical features. Sense relations, coreference and semantic roles require their own annotation.
TRopBank’s paper reports 17,673 verbs; Chapter 9 counts 17,531 framesets in the inspected release. The two figures come from different source descriptions and cannot be swapped for each other. A frame inventory also does not substitute for sense-annotated sentences.
