title: 13  Meaning: Embeddings, Semantic Resources, and Retrieval
text:
13.2 Word Embeddings and Morphology
Whole-word static embeddings assign a vector to each word form. Rare inflected forms may have little training evidence. Character n-gram embeddings share information across forms and can construct vectors for unseen words; useful task performance still needs to be tested. Lemma-based embeddings instead collapse forms to an analyser’s selected lemma, losing explicit inflectional distinctions and inheriting analysis errors.
Static embeddings for several Turkic languages can be aligned into a shared space with a bilingual dictionary. Kuriyozov, Doval, and Gómez-Rodríguez (2020) built new monolingual embeddings and bilingual dictionaries for Turkish, Uzbek, Azerbaijani, Kazakh and Kyrgyz and aligned the embedding spaces with established, weakly supervised mapping methods. In bilingual dictionary induction, the authors report that the embeddings of the lower-resourced languages benefit from alignment with a closely related, better-resourced language; in Uzbek sentiment analysis, aligned embeddings gave a slight improvement over monolingual ones.
crumbs: 13  Meaning: Embeddings, Semantic Resources, and Retrieval

title: 13  Meaning: Embeddings, Semantic Resources, and Retrieval
text:
13.3 Sentence Encoders

13.3.1 Models
Sentence encoders map text to vectors for comparison. Whether vector similarity reflects the intended meaning or relevance must be tested. Four multilingual model families are:

LaBSE (Feng et al. 2022), trained on translation pairs;
LASER3 (Heffernan, Çelebi, and Schwenk 2022), with encoders for low-resource languages;
multilingual E5 (Wang et al. 2024);
BGE-M3 (Chen et al. 2024).

TurkicNLP adds a fifth option: sentence vectors from the encoder of NLLB-200, which was trained on translation between 200 languages, including the eleven Turkic varieties of FLORES-200 (Table 10.3):
import numpy as np
import turkicnlp

def embed(lang, text):
    return np.array(turkicnlp.Pipeline(lang, processors=["embeddings"])(text).embedding)

tr = embed("tur", "Bugün hava çok güzel.")
kk = embed("kaz", "Бүгін ауа райы өте жақсы.")
print(tr @ kk / (np.linalg.norm(tr) * np.linalg.norm(kk)))   # cosine similarity
In real use, build each language’s pipeline once and reuse it.
Training coverage differs across encoders. LaBSE’s 109 languages include Turkish, Azerbaijani, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, Turkmen, Tatar and Uyghur, but exclude Bashkir, Chuvash and Sakha (Feng et al. 2022). The LASER repository lists a separate LASER3 encoder for each of the eleven Turkic varieties in FLORES-200.
Multilingual E5 starts from XLM-R and lists support for its 100 languages. Its Turkic members are Turkish, Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Uyghur (Chapter 12). BGE-M3 extends XLM-R-large to 8,192-token inputs and reports “more than 100 working languages”, without a separate Turkic list (Chen et al. 2024). Models may accept languages outside their documented coverage, but their vectors need direct evaluation. Dedicated Turkish encoders are also evaluated on TR-MTEB, the Turkish version of the MTEB embedding benchmark (Baysan and Gungor 2025).


13.3.2 Evaluation
Three kinds of evaluation are available for Turkic languages:

Semantic textual similarity. Kardeş-NLU includes an STS task for Azerbaijani, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, and Uyghur (Senel et al. 2024): 800 test pairs per language, translated from English STS pairs that keep their English gold scores. In Exercise 3, the NLLB encoder has the highest point estimates among the three tested systems for Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Uyghur (Spearman’s ρ 0.58–0.75) and the XLM-R paraphrase encoder for Azerbaijani, while the two paraphrase encoders lead on the English originals (0.83–0.84). TR-MTEB includes Turkish similarity and retrieval tasks (Baysan and Gungor 2025).
Natural language inference. Kardeş-NLU and the Turkish part of XNLI test entailment, contradiction and neutrality (Chapter 15). Evaluating an encoder on this task needs a declared classifier or scoring method; cosine similarity alone does not distinguish those relations.
Parallel-sentence retrieval. Given a sentence in one language, find its translation among all sentences in another. FLORES-200 provides the same 1,012 test sentences in eleven Turkic varieties (Table 10.3), so it supports a full matrix of language pairs within the family. What it tests is translation matching. General search relevance is a different question.



13.3.3 Measured native-script sentence retrieval
The October empirical suite evaluates two released paraphrase encoders, paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 and paraphrase-xlm-r-multilingual-v1, on original FLORES-200 devtest (NLLB Team et al. 2024). Each of thirteen varieties supplies 1,012 queries against all 1,012 sentences in each other variety: 156 directed comparisons per encoder, 312 in total. The release’s aligned row order is retained and its files are checksummed; this is separate from the FLORES+ ID-based loader in the hands-on section.
Both pinned checkpoints use attention-mask mean pooling, L2 normalisation, cosine similarity and their configured 128-token ceiling. Per-language truncation counts are saved, so this is a comparison of the complete encoder configurations rather than unlimited-context representations. Exact duplicate target strings count as additional positives; top-score ties within \(10^{-6}\) receive fractional credit instead of favouring an earlier row.

13.3.4 Script and morphology in embedding space
Compare native text with the toolkit’s common-script representation (CTS; Section 3.6) on the same retrieval task. Conversion changes tokenisation and the model’s input distribution. The direction of any benefit cannot be inferred from shared letters alone.
Exercise 1 uses 1,004 SIB-200 sentences derived from FLORES-200 (Adelani et al. 2024). For Kazakh→Kyrgyz, converting both sides to CTS reduces top-1 accuracy from 93.7% to 46.1% with the XLM-R paraphrase encoder and from 99.6% to 46.0% with NLLB. MiniLM rises from 41.7% to 45.4%. These outcomes do not identify the mechanism behind the changes.
The exercise uses 128-token limits for the paraphrase encoders and 512 for NLLB, retains the original NLLB language token after conversion, and resolves score ties by the first candidate. It sorts each language’s rows by ID but does not perform the hands-on’s explicit alignment checks. These protocol differences matter when comparing it with the full FLORES baseline. NLLB’s 98.9–100% native-script scores motivate an independent evaluation, yet high scores and FLORES’s origin together still fall short of proving contamination. LaBSE, LASER3, E5 and BGE-M3 were not run here.

title: 13  Meaning: Embeddings, Semantic Resources, and Retrieval
text:
13.4 Keyword Search in Agglutinative Languages

13.4.1 The problem
Keyword search ranks documents by the terms they share with the query, weighted by how rare each term is (BM25 is the standard formula). A query ev fiyatları ‘house prices’ should match a document containing evlerin fiyatı ‘the price of the houses’. With exact surface-word matching, neither query word matches either document word. Five representations of word forms before indexing are available:



Table 13.3: Ways to reduce Turkic word forms for keyword search.










Method
Example: evlerimizden
Needs




Surface form (lower-cased)
evlerimizden
nothing


Fixed-length prefix (first k letters)
evler (k = 5)
nothing


Stemmer
ev
a stemmer for the language

a morphological analyser


Subword units
ev ##ler ##imiz ##den (depends on the model)
a subword vocabulary






Lower-casing itself needs care: Turkish and Azerbaijani have dotted and dotless i (İ/i, I/ı), and locale-independent lowercasing may not preserve the intended distinctions (Section 3.3).
Prefix truncation is a cheap baseline motivated by Turkish retrieval work (Can et al. 2008). Choose k on development relevance judgements; truncation can merge unrelated roots as well as recover inflections. The result for one collection is not a universal adequacy guarantee.
Exercise 2 searches 825,309 Kazakh Wikipedia passages for 1,929 KazQAD test questions, using BM25 with \(k_1=1.2\) and \(b=0.75\) (Yeshpanov et al. 2024). Surface forms score 0.140 nDCG@10. Five-letter prefixes score 0.198, context-free Apertium lemmas 0.200 and Glot500 subwords 0.204. Prefix length was selected on 548 validation questions before testing.
Paired sign-flip tests compare each alternative with surface forms over the 1,929 test questions. None of 10,000 random draws reaches the observed absolute gain for any alternative. The two-sided Monte Carlo estimate is therefore \(p \le 1/10{,}001 \approx 10^{-4}\), rather than exactly zero. The comparisons remain clear after Bonferroni correction for six alternatives: four prefix lengths, lemmas and subwords. Questions are the sampling unit, so these tests support conclusions about this question set and collection.
The tests do not distinguish the three leading alternatives from one another: lemma vs. prefix, subword vs. prefix and subword vs. lemma give \(p = 0.63\), \(0.18\) and \(0.38\), respectively. Their relative performance stays unresolved, which is different from showing that they are equivalent.
Apertium returns analyses for 82.1% of the collection’s word tokens. Some queries losing retrieval accuracy contain merged or ambiguous lemma forms: жүзін and жүзіп, for example, both map to жүз. They are candidates for manual error analysis; on their own they do not explain the rank change. Dense and hybrid retrieval were not run on this collection.
import turkicnlp

# Rule-based tokenizer and Apertium lemmas: fast, no neural model. For Kazakh,
# processors=["tokenize", "lemma"] with the default backends gives Stanza lemmas instead.
nlp = turkicnlp.Pipeline("kaz", processors=["tokenize", "morph"], tokenize_backend="rule", morph_backend="apertium")

def index_terms(text: str, mode: str = "lemma", k: int = 5) -> list[str]:
    if mode not in {"surface", "prefix", "lemma"} or k < 1:
        raise ValueError("invalid mode or prefix length")
    words = [w for w in nlp(text).words if w.upos != "PUNCT"]
    if mode == "surface":
        return [w.text.lower() for w in words]
    if mode == "prefix":
        return [w.text.lower()[:k] for w in words]
    return [(w.lemma if w.lemma and w.lemma != "_" else w.text).lower() for w in words]   # unknown words keep their surface form

query = "Мектептерімізден кітаптар алдық."     # 'We took books from our schools.'
for mode in ["surface", "prefix", "lemma"]:
    print(mode, index_terms(query, mode))
# surface ['мектептерімізден', 'кітаптар', 'алдық']
# prefix ['мекте', 'кітап', 'алдық']
# lemma ['мектеп', 'кітап', 'ал']
The example shows the trade-off in miniature. The five-letter prefix happens to give the right stem for кітаптар ‘books’, cuts мектеп ‘school’ short, and leaves the short verb алдық ‘we took’ unchanged; the analyser gets all three lemmas right. For fair baselines, cache the same token boundaries once; surface/prefix indexing need not run a lemmatiser. Apply the identical normalisation to queries and documents. For Turkish and Azerbaijani, lower-case with turkicnlp.utils.unicode_utils.normalize_turkish_i(text).lower() so that İ and I are handled correctly.


13.4.2 Measured passage-recovery baseline
Belebele supplies questions and translated source passages (Bandarkar et al. 2024). Here it is repurposed as source-passage retrieval, not the benchmark’s multiple-choice task: each of seven languages contributes 900 questions and 488 candidate passages. The gold candidate is the passage attached to that question. Passage links and question numbers are checked for uniqueness and joined across languages. Other potentially relevant passages are not exhaustively judged.

title: 13  Meaning: Embeddings, Semantic Resources, and Retrieval
text:
13.5 Retrieval across Scripts and Languages

13.5.1 Across scripts
A Kazakh user may type a query in Cyrillic while some documents are in Latin; an Uzbek user may search in Cyrillic over a collection in Latin. Literal keyword overlap may fall sharply, though names, numbers, shared symbols and mixed-script text can still match. Dense retrieval may partly bridge the gap if the encoder has seen both scripts. Query transliteration is one condition to test (Section 3.4); preserve the original and check ambiguous mappings.


13.5.2 Across languages: Turkic queries and Russian documents
A collection may contain Russian documents that answer questions asked in Kazakh, Kyrgyz or Uzbek. Two candidate designs are:

Multilingual dense retrieval. Encode the question and the Russian documents with the same multilingual encoder.
Query translation. Translate the question into Russian (for example with NLLB, Section 10.3) and use Russian keyword or dense search.

Exercise 1 offers a translation-matching diagnostic: the XLM-R paraphrase encoder retrieves the aligned Russian sentence for 97.8% of Kazakh SIB-200 queries, compared with 93.7% for Kyrgyz candidates. MiniLM scores 43.9% on Kazakh→Russian. Matching translations is different from finding an answer passage in an independently collected Russian corpus. Query translation and hybrid retrieval remain untested here.


13.5.3 Measured script and language probes
The Uzbek script probe keeps the 488 Latin candidate passages fixed and transforms the same 900 questions with the recorded toolkit Latin→Cyrillic mapping. A third condition converts those generated questions back to Latin. This is a synthetic query transformation, with source hashes retained; it has not been validated by native speakers and does not represent a naturally occurring Cyrillic query collection.

title: 13  Meaning: Embeddings, Semantic Resources, and Retrieval
text:
13.6 Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Turkic Languages
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) gives a language model retrieved passages as context and asks it to answer from them. Three design decisions connect the earlier sections.
A token budget holds different amounts of text. Language variety, writing system, tokeniser and the text itself affect capacity. Isolated-word fertility (Table 7.1) and corpus characters per token (Figure 4.2) provide useful diagnostics. To estimate document capacity, measure running text directly; separating script effects requires a controlled comparison.
Table 13.7 and Figure 13.3 report the sentence-stream packing experiment on the original FLORES-200 devtest release, using 1,012 aligned sentence rows for each of 11 Turkic varieties plus English (NLLB Team et al. 2024). This release is distinct from the subsequently revised FLORES+ dataset. The tokenisers are pinned snapshots of Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-FP8, Meta-Llama-3-8B and Olmo-3-1025-7B, plus o200k_base; the experiment records their hashes and library versions. No model weights, chat templates or special tokens are used.
The packing procedure takes sentences in release order, trims outer whitespace and joins them with one space. It re-tokenises each proposed chunk as a whole. If the next sentence would push the chunk beyond 512 tokens, it closes the chunk and starts another. Every individual sentence fits; the largest takes 388 tokens.
Means cover closed chunks and exclude each language/tokeniser’s final tail. The saved audit still accounts for all 1,012 rows, including the tail. Here, “words” means nonempty whitespace-delimited units and “sentences” means aligned dataset rows.

Ranges are the minimum and maximum means across four pinned tokenisers; extrema in different columns need not come from the same tokeniser. Words are whitespace-delimited units. The final tail is excluded from means, with all rows retained in the chunk audit. Fill is the mean percentage of the 512-token budget used. Source: experiment N2-4; NLLB Team et al. (2024).

Whole-sentence packing leaves unused space: mean utilisation ranges from 84.4% to 97.4% across the 48 language/tokeniser combinations. Thus, the observed capacity reflects both tokenisation and the packing rule. The figure also reports aligned sentence counts so that differences in translated word counts are visible alongside differences in shared sentence coverage.
This experiment measures sentence-stream packing. Chunks may cross the source articles from which FLORES sampled its sentences, so retrieval relevance, chunk coherence and answer quality need separate evaluation (Section 15.1). Translations differ in length, whitespace conventions affect word counts, and the design does not vary language and script independently. In deployment, budget indexing chunks with the embedding tokeniser and final context with the generator’s tokeniser, allowing space for prompts, citations and output.
A separate probe uses the ten longest Kazakh Wikipedia articles of KazQAD (13,700–43,000 words each). A 512-token chunk holds on average 95 words with the Llama 3 tokeniser, 76 with OLMo 3 and 126 with Qwen3.6, against 203 with Glot500’s tokeniser, an encoder-side vocabulary that splits Kazakh far less (Exercise 4). A system that retrieves with one model and generates with another must therefore budget chunks for each tokeniser separately. Whether token-based or sentence-based chunking retrieves better on KazQAD has not been measured.
The answer must stay in the user’s language. Check whether Russian context changes the language of an answer requested in a Turkic language. Evaluate this separately from correctness, using the language-fidelity checks in Section 14.1.
Evaluate each stage. Measure retrieval relevance, answer correctness, citation support, language fidelity and abstention on unanswerable questions separately. Retain document provenance and permissions, remove duplicate candidates and record all judged relevant passage IDs for each query. A translated parallel sentence may have other relevant alternatives.
Tune prefix length, BM25 parameters and fusion weights on development data. Report collection size, MRR cutoff, nDCG gains and the treatment of queries without relevant items. Set evaluation sample size according to the precision the study needs.

title: 13  Meaning: Embeddings, Semantic Resources, and Retrieval
section: 13.7 Hands-On: A Procedure for Finding Translations Across the Family
text:
13.7 Hands-On: A Procedure for Finding Translations Across the Family
Question. Can an encoder retrieve the aligned translation among candidate sentences?
Inputs. An authorised FLORES+ export with stable IDs and the chosen encoder.
Compute. CPU inference is possible; model size and candidate count determine memory needs.
Output. Ranked candidates, retrieval scores and input/encoder metadata.
Interpretation. Compare native and CTS conditions with the same candidate set and explicit tie handling.
FLORES+ requires acceptance of its access conditions. Use an authorised local export and save its revision, selected language/script/variety, split and file hashes; keep it evaluation-only. The loader must preserve id, split and text rather than discarding metadata and assuming row-order alignment.
The tested helpers in retrieval.py require unique (id, split) keys, equal coverage and nonempty text, then join and sort the two varieties by those keys. They validate embedding dimensions, finite values and nonzero norms. Exact duplicate target strings count as additional positives; tied highest scores receive fractional credit across all ties. Semantically equivalent but nonidentical alternatives need separate relevance judgements.
from retrieval import align, top1  # code/ch13-retrieval on PYTHONPATH
# source_rows and target_rows are authorised exports retaining IDs and split.
source_rows, target_rows = align(source_rows, target_rows)
a = encoder.encode([r["text"] for r in source_rows], normalize_embeddings=True)
b = encoder.encode([r["text"] for r in target_rows], normalize_embeddings=True)
result = top1(source_rows, target_rows, a, b)
Build and cache each embedding matrix once per model revision, variety, condition and preprocessing hash. For larger candidate sets, score in blocks. Record truncation rate and maximum length; do not silently compare different retained subsets.
A model comparison needs its own interface specification. LaBSE uses its sentence embedding interface; multilingual E5 uses the documented query: and passage: prefixes for retrieval, including non-English text. Select a LASER language encoder explicitly. BGE-M3 dense, sparse and multi-vector modes are different systems: start with a declared dense mode. Record pooling, normalisation, similarity and training-language evidence for each checkpoint.
Test native/native, CTS/CTS and native/CTS separately. Every included variety needs an intentional supported mapping, including native Latin and Arabic inputs; do not return Latin unchanged while labelling it CTS. Unsupported mappings are missing conditions. Preserve originals, converter versions and checked examples.
Status: procedure only. The full FLORES+ protocol is not run here. Exercise 1 records a separate SIB-200 retrieval diagnostic with different alignment, tie and length policies.

title: 13  Meaning: Embeddings, Semantic Resources, and Retrieval
text:
What to Take Forward
Representation quality depends on the retrieval task, candidate set and input conventions. In Exercise 1, converting both sides of the Kazakh–Kyrgyz task to CTS sharply reduces retrieval accuracy for the XLM-R paraphrase and NLLB encoders, while MiniLM improves slightly in this sample. Test input changes, including conversion and chunking, with the same queries and candidate set. For a retrieval-augmented system, check retrieval before judging the generated answer. Chapter 14 turns to models that write Turkic text.

Further Reading

Feng et al. (2022), Heffernan, Çelebi, and Schwenk (2022), Wang et al. (2024), and Chen et al. (2024) describe the multilingual encoders surveyed in this chapter, and Artetxe and Schwenk (2019) the margin criterion for mining parallel sentences.
Baysan and Gungor (2025) describes TR-MTEB, the Turkish embedding benchmark.
Kuriyozov, Doval, and Gómez-Rodríguez (2020) builds cross-lingual word embeddings for Turkic languages.
Yeshpanov et al. (2024) describes KazQAD, the Kazakh open-domain QA dataset with a retrieval component.
Can et al. (2008) is the classic study of stemming for Turkish information retrieval.

title: 13  Meaning: Embeddings, Semantic Resources, and Retrieval
text:
Exercises

Russian documents and scripts. Extend the hands-on to SIB-200: for Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Tatar queries, retrieve the Russian translation of each sentence and compare with Turkic neighbours. Then test native/native, CTS/CTS and native→CTS conditions for four pairs.
Lemmatisation errors. On KazQAD, compare BM25 over surface forms, prefixes (choose k on validation), analyser lemmas and subwords. Inspect the test queries where lemmas lose most: how many losses come from wrong or merging lemmas?
STS. Compare encoders on the Kardeş-NLU STS test sets with Spearman’s ρ and bootstrap intervals. Then design a 50-pair STS set for a Turkic language without one: two native raters, a 0–5 scale, and quadratic-weighted κ for their agreement.
Chunking. Take the ten longest Kazakh articles in KazQAD and split them into 512-token chunks with three LLM tokenisers and one embedding tokeniser. How many words does a chunk hold on average with each? What does this mean for a RAG system’s context budget?

title: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation
text:
14.1 What Goes Wrong When Models Write Turkic Text
Chapter 13 examined how to find supporting text. This chapter asks how to evaluate the answers and conversations a model produces. Multiple-choice scores do not directly test whether an answer stays in the requested language and script, uses appropriate word forms or suits the social context.
The chapter moves from individual answers to extended interaction. Its final section uses dialogue games: structured conversations between models with explicit rules (Chalamalasetti et al. 2023). Those rules make comparisons repeatable, once the language-specific word lists and instructions have been validated.
The following seven categories organise the evaluation. They can occur in other languages too, and their order says nothing about frequency.
Exercise 2 collects examples of several types from one small open model, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (Qwen Team et al. 2024), answering everyday cultural questions:
The model did not produce clear cases of the address and evidentiality types in these answers; finding them needs prompts that require them, such as the role plays described below. Repetition loops, which affected several answers, are not specific to Turkic languages.
crumbs: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation

title: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation
text:
Drift into a neighbouring language. Kazakh output with Kyrgyz or Tatar words; Turkish words in Azerbaijani, Turkmen, or Gagauz output. Turkish has the largest token total among the listed Turkic subsets of HPLT v3 (Table 4.1); this does not reveal any particular model’s training mixture or prove the cause of drift. In Exercise 2, GlotLID (Kargaran et al. 2023) labels 20 of the 66 sentences that Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct wrote in answer to Kazakh questions as Kyrgyz.
Drift into the contact language. Russian words and phrases in Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Tatar, or Bashkir output; sometimes a switch to Russian after a few sentences. Language confusion of this kind has been documented for many languages (Marchisio et al. 2024).
Script switching. An Uzbek answer in Cyrillic to a question asked in Latin, or the reverse; Kazakh in a mixture of Cyrillic and one of the Latin alphabets.
Malformed words. Vowel-harmony violations (a back-vowel suffix on a front-vowel stem), suffixes in the wrong order, or invented suffix combinations. An annotator must distinguish genuine errors from loanword exceptions, dialectal forms and legitimate allomorphy.
Wrong level of address. Languages such as Turkish, Uzbek and Kazakh distinguish a familiar ‘you’ (Turkish and Uzbek sen, Kazakh сен) from a polite or plural one (siz, сіз). The choice depends on age, relationship, and setting, and it shows up in verb agreement and possessive suffixes as well as in the pronoun.
Evidential meaning. Some forms can convey indirect evidence or reported information: Turkish -mIş, Kazakh -ған екен. Evaluate the choice in its discourse context; a past-tense form is not universally a claim of eyewitness knowledge, and a summary need not mechanically copy every source suffix.
Cultural grounding. Names, holidays, units, place names or idioms that do not fit the requested context. A foreign name or borrowed expression is not itself an error.



Neighbouring language. Asked in Kazakh when and how Nauryz is celebrated, the model begins Наурыз - бул Кыргызстандын …, with Kyrgyz бул ‘this’ (Kazakh бұл) and the Kyrgyz genitive of Kyrgyzstan (Kazakh Қырғызстанның), and goes on to talk about Kyrgyzstan.
Contact language and script. Asked in Latin-script Uzbek about Navroʻz, it answers Navro‘z bayrami 15-16 декабря: a Russian month name in Cyrillic inside a Latin-script sentence. Asked about Alisher Navoiy, it writes literaturniy tili, a transliterated Russian adjective, instead of Uzbek adabiy til ‘literary language’.
Cultural grounding. The Kazakh answer about Abai Qunanbaiuly calls him one of Kazakhstan’s cities.
crumbs: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation

title: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation
text:
14.2 Measuring Fidelity Automatically
Three automatic signals help triage output; none establishes correctness alone:

Language, per sentence. Search the full LID label space, including Russian and English. A Turkic-restricted classifier must select a Turkic label even for Russian. Retain the top label, score and text; choose an abstention threshold on development examples from the target and competing languages, then validate it on held-out data. Audit short, mixed and ambiguous spans manually (Section 3.7). Shared words and quotations are not automatically drift.
Script, per word or letter. Declare the requested script and the denominator. Report mixed and unknown cases separately; names, quotations and code can legitimately use another script.
Raw analyser recognition. Count alphabetic word tokens with at least one finite, non-failure FST reading. Report numerator, denominator and transducer hash. A pipeline’s guessed lemma or UPOS != "X" can include heuristic fallback and is not raw transducer acceptance.

An FST can accept a grammatical word used in the wrong context, including a word shared with another language. It can also reject a valid name, loan or dialectal form missing from its lexicon. Use coverage as a diagnostic. Compare matched human-written text and validate against independent error annotations before setting a threshold.
# Run from the book root; provide a tokenizer and a pinned HFST transducer.
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "code/ch04-corpus")
from corpus import fst_coverage

def analyser_coverage(text, tokenize, transducer):
    return fst_coverage(tokenize(text), transducer.lookup)
# Returns accepted_words, eligible_words and coverage (None if no eligible words).
A handful of illustrative sentences says nothing reliable about the languages as a whole. To validate this diagnostic, measure false alarms and missed errors on held-out examples, including names, shared vocabulary and code-switching. Keep raw recognition and any normalised-lookup variant as separate measurements.
Exercise 3 compares 1,000 KazNERD news sentences (Yeshpanov, Khassanov, and Varol 2022) with 668 news-style sentences generated by Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. Apertium accepts 94.5% of the human text’s word tokens and 84.1% of the model’s. Restricting the model sample to sentences labelled Kazakh by GlotLID raises coverage to 84.7%, though such sentences can still contain mixed-language words.
Frequent rejected model tokens include the Kyrgyz forms Берилген, өзгөрүшү and Бул (Kazakh берілген, өзгеруі, бұл). Rejections in the human text include different cases: і and іі are Roman numerals typed with Cyrillic і; нші is an ordinal suffix separated from its numeral (2-нші); and көпбалалы ‘having many children’ is a valid word absent from the lexicon. These observations need systematic annotation. The samples differ in content and length, and repeated model phrases affect token counts. Independent judgements are needed to measure false alarms and missed errors.
crumbs: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation

title: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation
text:
14.3 Generation Tasks and Data
Summarisation. MLSUM includes Turkish news summaries (Scialom et al. 2020). XL-Sum’s published current repository statistics list Azerbaijani (6,478 train / 809 validation / 809 test), Kyrgyz (2,266 / 500 / 500), Turkish (27,176 / 3,397 / 3,397) and Uzbek (4,728 / 590 / 590) (Hasan et al. 2021). These are article–summary pairs from BBC; the totals differ from the repository’s legacy v1.0 release. See the maintainers’ split table. The four entries show what data exist; other Turkic summarisation resources may be missing from the list.
Instruction and chat data. Distinguish native-authored, translated, synthetic and mixed collections. Translation can introduce unsuitable names, units or contexts; native authorship alone does not guarantee factual or linguistic quality. For every selected release record provenance, revision, split sizes, language/script, licence and independent quality checks. Sherkala-Chat’s Kazakh instruction data, for example, combine translated sets with an automatically built, manually checked Kazakhstan-specific set (Chapter 12). This chapter does not inventory instruction releases, and no family-wide absence is claimed.
Dialogue data. Separate single-turn instruction pairs, open conversation, task-oriented exchanges and spoken dialogue. Their supervision and evaluation units differ. For each release, check native versus translated provenance and redistribution terms, and record what the documentation does not say. A search that finds no resource is not proof that none exists.
crumbs: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation

title: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation
text:
14.4 Evaluating Generated Text

14.4.1 Metrics against references
For summaries and translations with references, chrF adds character-level overlap to the word-level evidence from BLEU. A wrong suffix affects the whole word match in BLEU and a smaller set of character matches in chrF (Chapter 10). Neither metric directly measures morphological correctness, and their relative usefulness depends on the task. Open-ended answers, dialogue and pragmatic choices need evaluation beyond reference overlap.


14.4.2 LLMs as judges
Using a strong LLM to rate generated text is now common (Zheng et al. 2023). Validate each judge on the target language and error types. Include language confusion and morphological errors rather than assuming a general rating captures them.
Exercise 4 pairs 100 Kazakh SIB-200 sentences (Adelani et al. 2024) with automatic changes: 25 each involving vowel harmony, a Russian conjunction, a Kyrgyz cognate or a word in Latin script. Only the harmony change (қайықтар → *қайықтер) reliably creates an ungrammatical standard form. The other changes may produce acceptable variants. Russian но occurs in informal Kazakh–Russian mixing, Latin spelling need not be a grammatical error, and replacing мен with менен yields an existing Kazakh word: the ablative of мен ‘I’, meaning ‘from me’.
The pairs carry labels for the applied changes, without speaker validation of whether each result is wrong. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct chooses “A” in 91 pairs with an English prompt and 88 with a Kazakh prompt. It chooses the original sentence in 34 and 32 pairs; 5 and 12 replies are unparsable. Randomisation leaves the original first in only 37 pairs. These results reveal a strong position preference in this setup, while leaving error-detection ability unresolved.
Before comparing judges, have speakers label errors, acceptable variants and register differences. Drop or relabel substitutions that produce valid words, and present every pair in both orders.
Until such checks have been done for a language, LLM judgements of Turkic text should be validated against at least a small sample of human judgements (Section 15.4).
crumbs: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation

title: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation
text:
14.5 Interactive Evaluation with Dialogue Games

14.5.1 Why games
A dialogue game is a short, rule-governed interaction between two players. Here the players are both models, or a model and a program. clembench (Chalamalasetti et al. 2023) evaluates chat-optimised language models by having them play such games: word guessing, reference games, and others. The program that runs the game checks every move against the rules and scores the outcome. Games have three advantages for comparing Turkic languages:

The same game can be run in every language, but translation alone does not equate difficulty. Match word frequency, ambiguity, clue informativeness, alphabet rules and cultural familiarity, and report remaining differences.
Rule violations are measured, not just success. A model that wins Taboo by using a forbidden word has broken a rule.
Long interactions show drift. Language and script fidelity can be measured turn by turn.



14.5.2 Taboo needs morphology
In Taboo, one player must describe a target word without using it or a few related words, and the other player must guess the target. Exact matching can miss inflected forbidden words, in English as well as Turkic languages. If the target is ev ‘house’, the describer can write evlerimizden ‘from our houses’ and a surface-string check will not notice. Morphological analysis can identify additional candidates, but ambiguous readings and unknown words need an explicit review policy.
Use the rule checker (code/ch14-generation/turkic_taboo_checker.py) with a pinned transducer. It reports exact surface hits, lemma candidates and unresolved tokens separately. It considers all analyser readings, so an ambiguous reading can produce a candidate that needs contextual adjudication. There is no prefix fallback: a shared prefix is not evidence of a forbidden lemma, and a retrieval experiment’s best truncation length is not a validated game-rule threshold.
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "code/ch14-generation")
from turkic_taboo_checker import check_tokens

# tokens: output of the declared tokenizer; lookup: pinned HFST lookup callback.
result = check_tokens(tokens, forbidden=["үй", "пәтер", "тұр"],
                      lookup=transducer.lookup, lang="kaz")
# result contains surface_hits, lemma_candidates and unresolved.
The forbidden list must use the selected analyser’s lemma convention. Record any infinitive/stem conversion explicitly; do not strip a universal suffix across languages. Freeze whether ambiguous candidates invalidate a turn or trigger human review. Tokenisation and casing must be identical for the surface and morphological comparisons.


14.5.3 Wordle and other games
Wordle asks a player to find a five-letter word from feedback on each letter. It depends on the alphabet and on what counts as a word. Turkic alphabets differ in size and letter frequencies, and the allowed word list may contain lemmas, inflected forms or both. Specify that choice and whether length counts orthographic letters, grapheme clusters or code points; normalise Unicode and apply language-aware casing consistently. Reference games, where one player describes an item so the other can pick it out, can be localised with culturally familiar content.


14.5.4 Results
Exercise 1 uses Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct as both describer and guesser for twelve Kazakh targets, with at most three rounds. No game is won. Three opening clues contain the target itself (Кітап, Жылқы, Балық), which the surface check catches; the other nine games reach the turn limit. The lemma checker detects no additional violations and leaves the outcomes unchanged. Missed violations remain possible: 72 of the 246 clue words have no analyser reading, and the exercise allows unresolved tokens to pass. GlotLID labels four of the 30 clues Kyrgyz.
The target lists still need speaker review. All twelve targets are frequent concrete nouns, so they cover no range of frequency bands. Күн means both ‘sun’ and ‘day’, but its forbidden words address only ‘sun’. Other forbidden lemmas have homonyms: іш- ‘drink’ and іш ‘inside, belly’; жаз- ‘write’ and жаз ‘summer’; ат ‘horse’ and ‘name’; бет ‘page’ and ‘face’; мін- ‘ride’ and мін ‘fault’. A lemma-only checker can flag an allowed sense. Record part of speech as well as lemma, and adjudicate remaining ambiguity in context.
The exercise also differs from the Hands-On protocol: unresolved words pass without adjudication, and the guess matcher checks only the first word. It could therefore accept a multiword response despite the one-word instruction. Fix these policies and validate the word list before comparing systems.


14.5.5 Address and politeness
Test address with role plays written by native speakers. Each should specify a relationship and setting, such as a student speaking to a teacher or two friends talking. Ask speakers which forms are acceptable for that situation and variety. Pronouns and agreement offer clues, but pro-drop may leave the choice unexpressed. Retain ambiguous and omitted cases in the report instead of forcing them into familiar or polite categories.
crumbs: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation

title: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation
text:
14.6 Language Drift in Ordinary Chat
Ask models ordinary questions in a Turkic language and check the language and script of each answer. Short and mixed-language answers need manual review.
Exercise 2 does this for 25 culturally grounded questions each in Kazakh and Uzbek with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. Only 13 of the 25 Kazakh answers have every sentence labelled Kazakh by GlotLID; 20 of their 66 sentences are labelled Kyrgyz, and Apertium accepts only 58.7% of their words. GlotLID labels 83 of the 84 Uzbek-answer sentences Uzbek, with every sentence so labelled in 24 of the 25 answers. Yet one answer contains Cyrillic Russian month names. The labels help select passages for review; an answer that passes may still mix languages or get the facts wrong.
crumbs: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation

title: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation
text:
14.7 Spoken Dialogue
Voice assistants combine speech recognition (Chapter 11), a dialogue model, and speech synthesis. Published MMS checkpoints include Chuvash and Crimean Tatar TTS (Table B.6); checkpoint availability is not evidence of conversational quality. Audit each component’s language, licence, input/output script, latency and held-out quality, then test the combined system with speakers.

title: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation
section: 14.8 Hands-On: A Procedure for Kazakh Taboo with a Morphological Rule Checker
text:
14.8 Hands-On: A Procedure for Kazakh Taboo with a Morphological Rule Checker
Question. How well can a Kazakh Taboo game enforce morphological rules?
Inputs. Twenty speaker-reviewed targets, forbidden lemmas, two declared model roles and the bounded controller.
Compute. Inference for the selected models, plus fluent-speaker adjudication; local controller tests use scripted replies.
Output. Turn logs, rule-check outcomes, guesses and language/script diagnostics.
Interpretation. Count failed and unresolved games and compare automated checks with human decisions.
This is a protocol for a simplified Kazakh Taboo experiment. Exercise 1 illustrates a simpler version with one small model and twelve targets; the differences are described above.

Ask a speaker to select 20 target lemmas across frequency bands, with three related forbidden lemmas each. Record the variety, script and adjudication policy.
Use the bounded controller in code/ch14-generation/game.py. Supply separate describer and guesser callbacks, a clue checker and an explicit guess-matching policy. The target and forbidden list belong only in the describer’s context.
Allow at most three rounds. Stop on a rejected clue, a correct guess, an unresolved rule check or the turn limit. Save each turn and its outcome; do not drop failed games from denominators.
Record unrestricted language labels, script signals and raw FST recognition for each utterance. Have a speaker adjudicate ambiguous lemma candidates and unresolved tokens before comparing checkers.

The local scripted-reply test verifies controller flow and target secrecy; the model game requires the protocol above.
Questions to answer:

How many violations does the surface checker miss?
Do the models drift into Russian or another Turkic language during the game? In which turns?
Are the guesser’s answers in the base form, or inflected? How should the game score an inflected correct guess?

Status: procedure only. The speaker-reviewed twenty-target game is not run here. Exercise 1 records a separate twelve-target diagnostic whose target list remains unchecked.
crumbs: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation

title: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation
text:
What to Take Forward
Useful generated text needs more than fluent-looking words. The Kazakh generation exercises produce sentences labelled Kyrgyz by GlotLID and lower analyser recognition than the human news sample. These diagnostics flag passages for review; speaker judgements establish whether they contain language or grammatical errors. Validate automatic judges against human decisions before relying on their scores. Chapter 15 combines these checks with task scores, baselines and uncertainty.

title: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation
text:
Further Reading

Chalamalasetti et al. (2023) introduces clembench and the dialogue-game approach to evaluating chat models.
Marchisio et al. (2024) studies language confusion: models answering in the wrong language or mixing languages.
Zheng et al. (2023) studies strong LLMs as judges and discusses their biases.
Scialom et al. (2020) and Hasan et al. (2021) describe the multilingual summarisation datasets that include Turkic languages.

title: 14  Generation, Dialogue, and Interactive Evaluation
text:
Exercises

Port a game. Play Kazakh Taboo with a model as describer and guesser, using the controller and rule checker of the Hands-On. Compare the surface and lemma checkers, track the language of each clue by round, and decide how to score inflected guesses. Then document every language-specific decision needed to port one more clembench game: word lists, morphology in the rule checks, script and cultural content.
Error collection. Ask a model 25 culturally grounded questions each in two Turkic languages (holidays, food, place names, proverbs). Measure language, script and analyser coverage automatically, then classify the errors in the answers with the seven types of Section 14.1.
Coverage baseline. Compute analyser coverage on 1,000 sentences of human-written news text and on model-written news in the same language. How large is the difference, and what kinds of words account for it?
Judging a judge. Create pairs in which the second sentence contains one Turkic-specific error from Section 14.1. Ask an LLM judge which sentence is correct, with the order counterbalanced. Which error types does it miss, and does it prefer one position?

title: 15  Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Responsible Deployment
text:
15.1 Principles for Reading and Reporting Results
The preceding chapters report task scores and describe their limits. Chapter 14 also examines generation and dialogue, where a single score can hide different kinds of failure. This chapter brings the evaluation methods together: choosing metrics, checking benchmark exposure, estimating uncertainty and assessing errors in the intended use.
A score on exam questions, news text or translated sentences answers a specific question. Deployment may involve other domains, varieties and error costs. Human evaluation and task-specific checks connect those scores to the application; Chapter 17 develops the community and governance questions.
Start with the decision an experiment should support. A useful report makes five things clear:
These principles apply throughout the book. The following sections develop the task-specific metrics, contamination checks and human-evaluation choices. Community authority, consent and maintenance have their main treatment in Section 17.4.
crumbs: 15  Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Responsible Deployment

title: 15  Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Responsible Deployment
text:
Task and data. Name the language, variety, script, domain, release and split. Keep evaluation items and their source groups out of training and model selection.
Comparison. Include a simple baseline and use the same evaluation items. Record differences in training size, tuning budget, input length and inference settings.
Measurement. Define the unit, denominator, label mapping and exclusions. Coverage measures how often a system supplies an output; accuracy requires an appropriate reference. Human review supplies evidence about meaning and acceptability.
Uncertainty. Report sample size, variation across runs where measured, and paired uncertainty when comparing systems. A difference observed in one configuration motivates replication on other data.
Scope and provenance. Link the claim to its predictions, table or worked exercise. Identify model and dataset revisions, known training exposure and unresolved exposure. A diagnostic illustrates behaviour under its stated conditions; a deployment claim needs evidence from the intended use.
crumbs: 15  Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Responsible Deployment

title: 15  Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Responsible Deployment
text:
15.2 Evaluation Challenges for Agglutinative Languages

15.2.1 Features, Bundles and Sentences
Different metrics answer different questions. For gold Case=Acc|Number=Sing and predicted Case=Nom|Number=Sing, one of the two values is correct: feature accuracy is 50%, while exact-bundle accuracy is 0%. Predicting nominative plural instead gives 0/2, not 50%. Specify how absent and extra features count. Lemma accuracy and lemma-plus-bundle accuracy are separate measures.
If word analyses were independent and each had correctness probability 0.9, a ten-word sentence would be entirely correct with probability \(0.9^{10}\approx0.349\). Real errors need not be independent or equally likely. Measure sentence-exact accuracy directly.
Exercise 1 compares these measures using gold word boundaries, including punctuation. Stanza’s Turkish IMST predictions achieve 91.3% exact-bundle accuracy and 50.7% sentence-exact bundle accuracy. The sentence measure requires every feature bundle to match, leaving lemmas and syntax untested. Applying the same per-word probability to each sentence’s actual length gives a mean estimate of 50.3%. Its closeness to the observed rate cannot validate the independence assumption. The notebook’s length-bin estimates are rougher because they substitute one representative length per bin.
Kazakh’s observed and estimated rates are 89.0% and 84.0%. Treat both as replay diagnostics: checkpoint preparation creates a concrete test-exposure risk, and historical training membership has not been reconstructed (Chapter 8).


15.2.2 Surface and Lemma Novelty
Surface-form OOV includes unseen inflections of familiar lemmas. Lemma OOV tracks unfamiliar lemmas themselves. Define the training vocabulary and use gold lemmas consistent with the annotation scheme. Then separate four cases: seen surface/seen lemma, unseen surface/seen lemma, seen surface/unseen lemma (possible with ambiguity), and unseen surface/unseen lemma. Report counts and error rates for each; leave empty cells undefined. Subword unknown-token rates measure a different property.
On the Turkish IMST test set (Exercise 2), 33.2% of the non-punctuation words are surface-unseen in training but only 10.2% lemma-unseen; the feature-bundle error rate is 6.3% for seen forms with seen lemmas and 20.5% for unseen forms with seen lemmas. These cells show where errors occur; they do not isolate the cause of the difference.


15.2.3 Translation Metrics
BLEU compares token n-grams under a specified tokenisation; chrF compares character n-grams. A suffix error can break a word match while preserving some character overlap. Neither metric decides whether the changed suffix preserves meaning. Exercise 3 adds negation to one verb in each of 100 Turkish X-WMT references, for example söyledi ‘said’ → söylemedi ‘did not say’. Mean sentence chrF remains 97.7. Word deletion gives 92.3 on a separately selected set. Both edits can change meaning; these scores measure overlap, not the severity of the change. The generated edits still need contextual review.
Report the metric signatures and reference policy from Chapter 10, and validate learned metrics such as COMET against judgements in the target language/domain rather than assuming training-language coverage guarantees reliability.
Choose human-evaluation sample size for the desired interval width, error prevalence and subgroup analysis. A fixed sample of 100–200 outputs is not a universal adequacy threshold. Preserve paired outputs when comparing systems.


15.2.4 Benchmark Contamination
Native exam questions, translations and public games can appear in pretraining or adaptation data, including for languages with a small web presence. Save benchmark release and model cutoff information where available, search for overlap in accessible training sources, and distinguish known exposure from unknown exposure. A performance drop on rewritten questions can reflect changed difficulty as well as memorisation. Use independently authored held-out material as a complementary test (Isbarov et al. 2025).
crumbs: 15  Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Responsible Deployment

title: 15  Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Responsible Deployment
text:
15.3 Existing Benchmarks

15.3.1 TUMLU: Native Multiple-Choice Evaluation
TUMLU collects native middle- and high-school multiple-choice questions in 11 subjects (Isbarov et al. 2025). Its abstract and tables list nine languages: Azerbaijani, Crimean Tatar, Karakalpak, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Tatar, Turkish, Uyghur and Uzbek. Other passages describe eight languages and a total of 38,139 questions. Because these descriptions conflict, base experiments on audited counts from a pinned release. The Hands-On uses only Kazakh TUMLU-mini.
The TUMLU paper compares proprietary and open models by language and subject. Use the model-specific tables; differences in question content, subject coverage and training exposure prevent a language-level score from isolating a resource effect.


15.3.2 Kardeş-NLU: Cross-Lingual Transfer Evaluation
Kardeş-NLU (Senel et al. 2024) covers Azerbaijani, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Uyghur. Its tasks are natural language inference from XNLI, semantic textual similarity from STS-Benchmark and causal reasoning from XCOPA. English items were machine-translated and post-edited by one native speaker per target language. The Uyghur set uses Cyrillic, which matters when choosing a model or comparing it with Arabic-script data.
The paper tests Turkish as a source for intermediate training and downstream fine-tuning, reporting gains in its evaluated settings. These results motivate the source-language comparisons in Chapter 12 and Chapter 16.


15.3.3 Turkish Benchmark Suites
Mukayese (Safaya et al. 2022) groups Turkish datasets and baselines for language modelling, translation, named entity recognition, sentence segmentation, spell checking and correction, summarisation, and text classification. Each task has its own metric, and adding them up would not yield a measure of Turkish proficiency. Reading comprehension is also covered by Turkish XQuAD and Kazakh KazQAD, discussed in Chapter 13.


15.3.4 Kazakh and Multilingual Benchmarks
KAZ-LLM reports evaluation in Kazakh, Russian and English (Institute of Smart Systems and Artificial Intelligence (ISSAI) 2024). KazMMLU (Togmanov et al. 2025) provides 23,000 questions (10,969 in Kazakh and 12,031 in Russian) from authentic educational material, validated by native speakers and educators, on general and Kazakhstan-specific knowledge. These are not matched translations: KazMMLU’s university-level section is Russian-only. Language-level scores therefore also reflect differences in subject and education level.
Broader multilingual datasets include FLORES-200 for MT (11 Turkic varieties), SIB-200 for topic classification (11 Turkic varieties), and Belebele for reading comprehension (Bandarkar et al. 2024) (Turkish, North Azerbaijani, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, and Northern Uzbek).


15.3.5 X-WMT: Turkic Machine Translation Evaluation
X-WMT, produced as part of the Turkic Interlingua (TIL) project, provides machine translation test sets of at least 300 sentences for 88 translation directions involving eight Turkic languages (Azerbaijani, Bashkir, Karakalpak, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Sakha, Turkish and Uzbek) plus English and Russian (Mirzakhalov et al. 2021). The release covers intra-Turkic pairs (Kazakh–Uzbek, Turkish–Azerbaijani, and others) as well as Turkic-to-Russian and Turkic-to-English directions.
FLORES-200 complements X-WMT with aligned evaluation sentences for the eleven Turkic varieties in NLLB-200. Use the split and overlap checks in Chapter 10.


15.3.6 Beyond Multiple Choice: Generation and Interaction
Multiple-choice benchmarks measure answer selection under a specified protocol. Complement them with the methods in Chapter 14:

Human review of generation: assess meaning, fluency and use of the requested language on answers, summaries or rewrites.
Automatic language checks: use unrestricted language identification to select outputs for review. Keep predicted labels separate from confirmed language drift.
Interactive tests: use dialogue games with explicit rules, validated local word lists and recorded failures. Fresh instances help test beyond public examples, but do not by themselves rule out training exposure.

Exercise 5 illustrates the limits of automatic checks. It selects an abstention threshold from Kazakh-labelled news sentences, then applies it to whole model answers. The threshold is provisional, and it has not been validated as a multilingual detector: the sample lacks labelled non-Kazakh and mixed-language controls. One example per predicted category is a starting point for annotation, not enough to estimate error rates.


15.3.7 The Benchmark Gap
The catalogue verifies selected releases and leaves gaps in language coverage. For languages without a suitable public benchmark, work with the community on a domain-specific evaluation and document its sampling frame and limits. Check for overlooked or newer resources before concluding that a benchmark is unavailable.

title: 15  Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Responsible Deployment
text:
15.4 Human Evaluation for Turkic NLP

15.4.1 Evaluator Competence and Agreement
Recruit evaluators who know the target variety, register and domain. Native-speaker status alone may leave gaps in that expertise. Work with community partners, pay for expertise and annotation time, and pilot the guidelines before scaling. Seek representation beyond a single institution, and verify the competence of evaluators who speak a neighbouring language.
Report agreement before adjudication, along with category frequencies and a table of disagreements. State how the agreement statistic accounts for chance. There is no universal kappa cutoff or inherent agglutinative-language agreement ceiling. Feature-level agreement, exact bundles and span/attachment agreement expose different disagreements. Revise unclear guidelines on development material, keeping the final evaluation independent.


15.4.2 Scale and Uncertainty
Specify the population from which items and evaluators were sampled. Use paired uncertainty estimates for model differences and account for clustering by document, speaker or annotator. Small sets can support a pilot. They are too small to measure performance for every variety or rare error type. Plan sample size and annotation effort from a timed pilot rather than asserting a fixed limit on community capacity.
crumbs: 15  Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Responsible Deployment

title: 15  Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Responsible Deployment
text:
15.5 Responsible Deployment

15.5.1 Resource Imbalance and Model Quality
Training volume, sampling, tokenisation, domain and adaptation can all affect quality. Temperature sampling, for example, changes language exposure relative to raw corpus size (Section 16.4). Report results by task and subgroup. A single language comparison cannot separate these factors or justify predicting quality from speaker population or web volume.


15.5.2 Precision, Recall and Consequences
An entity F1 of 0.70 does not mean that 30% of entities were missed. For example, 7 true positives, 0 false positives and 6 false negatives give precision 1, recall 7/13 and F1 0.70: 6/13 of gold entities were missed. Swapping the false-positive and false-negative counts gives the same F1 with recall 1 and no missed entities. These arithmetic examples are checked by code/common/check.py.
Set acceptance criteria for the intended task: which false positives or omissions matter, when the system should abstain, and which outputs need review. Test those criteria on representative data, record who handles failures, and reassess after changes to the model or input domain. Aggregate F1 alone cannot make that decision.


15.5.3 Domain, Script and Variety
Good results on news say little about private messages, legal records, medical text or speech transcripts. Evaluate script variants and mixed-language inputs explicitly; a Cyrillic-trained model may degrade on informal Latin input, but failure is not guaranteed merely by the script difference. Preserve community names and variety distinctions instead of reducing language boundaries to a technical convenience.


15.5.4 Environmental and Community Costs
Record hardware, runtime and measured energy where available, stating the assumptions of any emissions estimate. Fewer trainable parameters do not automatically imply proportionally less compute. Discuss who sets the priorities, who bears annotation and maintenance work, and who can access the result; do not infer the geographic distribution of costs and benefits without project evidence.

section: 15.6 Hands-On: Evaluating a Multilingual Model on TUMLU
text:
15.6 Hands-On: Evaluating a Multilingual Model on TUMLU
Question. How does a small model compare with simple answer-choice baselines?
Inputs. The pinned Kazakh TUMLU-mini release and schema audit. The procedure uses mT5; the measured comparison below uses Qwen.
Compute. Model download and inference memory. The mT5 procedure is not run in full; the two Qwen probes use different precision/runtime settings.
Output. Per-item scores, exclusions, accuracy, uncertainty and answer-label distributions.
Interpretation. Compare the development-selected baseline and inspect option-order sensitivity.
Use the released TUMLU-mini, pinned at 3523de73e1d1d784118d328f40b49d53afd6f334. The verified Kazakh configuration contains 40 development and 799 test rows; the audit found two test rows with empty choices, leaving 797 schema-valid test questions under an explicit exclusion policy. Only one language subset of the mini release is used here; the full benchmark is larger.
python code/ch15-tumlu/tumlu.py --config kazakh --audit-only --output runs/tumlu-audit
python code/ch15-tumlu/tumlu.py --config kazakh --split dev --output runs/tumlu-dev
# Freeze the prompt and scoring rule before this final evaluation:
python code/ch15-tumlu/tumlu.py --config kazakh --split test --exclude-invalid --output runs/tumlu-test
The scorer reads question, choices, answer and subject. It checks the number of choices and the letter-to-choice mapping, creates stable hashes and rejects exact question-and-ordered-choice duplicates within or across development and test. Paraphrases and reordered duplicates require further checks. The prompt excludes the released CoT explanation.
audit.json identifies invalid rows by original index and content hash. Scoring stops when invalid rows are present unless --exclude-invalid is supplied. That option selects the audited 797-item subset and records its denominator; the score covers that subset of the 799-row release.
The prompt contains the question and all labelled options. For each possible answer letter, mT5 computes the sum of conditional token log probabilities, including EOS and excluding padded positions. This differs from the negative mean loss returned by the model. The predicted letter maximises that sum; exact score ties use the first option. Test robustness to option permutation on development data and freeze the policy. Inputs are not silently truncated.
Base mT5 was pretrained for span corruption, not instruction following. The result diagnoses one fixed conditional-likelihood protocol. It is not a validated measure of how instruction-tuned models reason. Report the exact checkpoint, prompt, length rule and scoring method when comparing it with another model.
The output includes every item’s scores and prediction, overall and per-subject support, accuracy, a Wilson interval and the analytical uniform-random expectation \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i1/K_i\). The interval is descriptive under an independent-item assumption; source-clustered uncertainty requires source metadata. Never substitute a random simulation for the analytical baseline or describe below-expectation accuracy as significant without uncertainty analysis.
The book reports no mT5 score: the release schema and all Kazakh rows were audited and tiny-model tests verify the scoring arithmetic, but the full mT5 run and an independently authored contamination check are left to the reader.

15.6.1 A measured pretrained TUMLU-mini baseline
A separate zero-shot run uses Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on the pinned Kazakh TUMLU-mini test split (Isbarov et al. 2025). Of 799 rows, two have empty choice lists (zero-based indices 362 and 390); the explicitly defined valid subset therefore contains 797 questions. The user message contains the native question and four choices, preceded by “Select the correct option. Reply with only its letter.” The model’s chat template is applied without a gold answer or explanation.
The score is the next-token log probability of each single-token answer label A–D, selecting the highest. This constrained-letter protocol differs from free generation, full-choice likelihood and the mT5 example above. Inputs are not truncated. The pinned weights, prompt, per-item label scores and exclusions are recorded with the run.



Table 15.2: Measured zero-shot constrained-letter Qwen score on 797 valid TUMLU-mini Kazakh test items; two malformed items of 799 are excluded and recorded. The letter-D baseline is selected from the 40 development items, not the test answers. Uniform accuracy is an expectation, not a model run. Source: run_tumlu.py; Isbarov et al. (2025).

Qwen answers 226/797 correctly: 28.36%, with a Wilson 95% interval of 25.34–31.58%. The most frequent answer in the 40 development items is D. Always choosing D scores 304/797 (38.14%) on test. That beats the model, even though the model itself clears the 25% uniform-choice expectation. Report this answer-label imbalance: uniform guessing is a weaker baseline than the simple strategy selected on development data.
The Wilson interval assumes independent items and excludes variation from prompts, option order and subjects. These results describe one small checkpoint on the valid Kazakh mini subset. They leave full TUMLU performance and independent contamination assessment open.
Exercise 4 uses an 8-bit version of the same model with a different inference implementation (230/797 correct, 28.9%) and measures option-order sensitivity on development data: under four cyclic rotations of the options, the model picks the same option content for only 4 of the 40 development questions, and it answers B in half of the 160 rotated prompts.
Status: completed for the Qwen probe; the mT5 scoring procedure is not run. The table above records the 226/797 main probe. Exercise 4 records a separate 8-bit probe (230/797) that also tests option order.

title: 15  Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Responsible Deployment
text:
What to Take Forward
An evaluation starts from the decision the score must support. The unit matters: all morphological feature bundles match in 50.7% of the Turkish sentences; this says nothing about whether their lemmas or syntax are correct. Across 100 automatically negated references, mean sentence chrF remains 97.7, illustrating why overlap alone cannot assess meaning. Define the task, denominator, baseline and held-out data before scoring, report uncertainty, and inspect consequential errors. Chapter 16 applies these principles to choosing source languages and transfer methods.

title: 15  Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Responsible Deployment
text:
Further Reading
Isbarov et al. (2025) describes TUMLU’s construction and evaluation; Senel et al. (2024) studies transfer through Turkish. Safaya et al. (2022) provides task-specific datasets and baselines for Turkish. For resource availability and limitations, see Çöltekin, Doğruöz, and Çetinoğlu (2023).
Marneffe et al. (2021) describes the Universal Dependencies annotation framework. Shared feature names support comparisons, but treebank conventions and reference quality still need checking (Chapter 8). For generation and dialogue evaluation, return to Chapter 14.

title: 15  Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Responsible Deployment
text:
Exercises

Compare feature, exact-bundle and observed sentence-exact accuracy on the same morphological predictions, for Kazakh and Turkish UD test sets. Explain the independence assumption behind a product estimate and where it fails.
Partition tagging errors by surface and gold-lemma novelty, reporting counts and undefined empty cells.
Measure how BLEU and chrF react to single-suffix changes that alter meaning (negation, case, person) in correct English→Turkish references, then compare two decoding settings of an MT model and prepare a blinded sheet for human judges. Document metric signatures.
Test TUMLU option-order sensitivity on development data, then freeze the scoring protocol before running the audited test subset.
Audit generated language with unrestricted LID, using human text to choose a provisional abstention threshold, and prepare a sample for fluent reviewers. Include Russian, other languages, code-switching and indeterminate short answers.

title: 16  Cross-Lingual Transfer within the Turkic Family
text:
16.1 Why Related Languages Can Help
Earlier chapters tested transfer in morphology, parsing, NER, translation and speech. Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 also compared native and converted text for classification and retrieval. This chapter brings those methods together: choosing source languages, controlling script conversion, pooling training data and evaluating target-language results.
crumbs: Cross-Lingual Methods and the Resource Frontier
16  Cross-Lingual Transfer within the Turkic Family

title: 16  Cross-Lingual Transfer within the Turkic Family
text:
16.1.1 Structural and Lexical Hypotheses
Transfer reuses a model trained on one language to make predictions in another. Shared suffix patterns can help a tagger recognise similar grammatical functions; shared words can give an encoder familiar inputs. Multilingual pretraining offers another route: it can place texts from different languages in a shared representation space. A source language is therefore a candidate to test, using the target task and data to judge its usefulness.
The morphology in Chapter 5 suggests which constructions to compare. Written overlap may come from inherited cognates or shared loans, such as kitap/kitab ‘book’. Script conversion changes that overlap. Compare sources on the same target sentences and record script, training size and domain alongside the score (Section 15.1).


16.1.2 Evidence from Tasks
Kardeş-NLU reports benefits from Turkish intermediate training in its evaluated settings (Senel et al. 2024). The parser comparison in Chapter 8 and TurkicASR in Chapter 11 provide further task-specific evidence. The parser table uses matched words and includes very small target samples, especially Sakha; interpret its scores under that evaluation convention.
“Zero-shot” here means applying a model without target task-labelled training. The model may have encountered the target language during multilingual pretraining. A proxy language is a chosen model input or routing configuration. Evaluate that choice on independent target annotations.

title: 16  Cross-Lingual Transfer within the Turkic Family
section: 16.2 Script Conversion as an Experimental Condition
text:
16.2 Script Conversion as an Experimental Condition
Script conversion supplies an alternative written input to the same task. The conversion conventions and their losses are explained in Section 3.4 and Section 3.6. Here the question is whether conversion helps transfer: compare it with native text under the model’s documented input conventions. Muller et al. (2021) motivates testing this for unseen scripts.

Identify the language and script on the original text.
Record the converter, version and supported direction. Native Latin is not automatically CTS.
Preserve original strings, whitespace, item IDs and an explicit character-boundary map.
Run the model, recording any additional automatic script bridging.
Map predictions back only where the alignment is unambiguous; report failures and coverage.

Digraphs, deletions and context-sensitive mappings can shift character offsets even when word counts stay the same. Rebuilding text with split()/join() can also change its spacing. Preserve a map to the original boundaries; a lossy conversion may have no exact inverse.

title: 16  Cross-Lingual Transfer within the Turkic Family
text:
16.3 Transfer Strategy by Available Evidence
Available annotation, domain match, model coverage and cost jointly determine which comparisons are feasible. No fixed sentence count marks the point at which a larger model or training from scratch becomes preferable.



Table 16.1: Candidate comparisons, not measured resource thresholds.










Available evidence
Initial comparisons
What to reserve




No target task labels
Native multilingual/proxy baseline; optional conversion; existing FST where relevant
Obtain independent target evaluation before claiming quality


Small labelled collection
Zero-shot, head/adapter tuning, pooled training
Source-disjoint development and test items


Labelled data plus unlabelled text
Continued pretraining vs. task tuning alone
Exclude all evaluation texts from adaptation


Larger task data and compute budget
Monolingual vs. multilingual; model-size and scratch-training controls
Same test set and comparable tuning budgets






Check existing resources before adapting a neighbouring language’s system. Nogai, for example, already has an Apertium module whose lexicon and rules can be extended. For translation, verify NLLB’s supported codes: adding a pivot cannot supply a missing language interface. Use development learning curves to estimate the value of further annotation or parallel data, and reserve separate gold sentences for final evaluation.

title: 16  Cross-Lingual Transfer within the Turkic Family
text:
16.4 Multilingual Turkic Training

16.4.1 Pooling Data Across Languages
Pool only after checking label conventions, tokenisation and split provenance. Language tags, language embeddings and separate adapters are alternative design choices; none is required by multilingual training. Compare a language-conditioned model with an otherwise matched shared model. A dominant corpus can influence training, but raw language percentages alone do not identify which linguistic mechanism produced a gain.


16.4.2 Evidence from Speech and Parsing
Speech and parsing provide two task-specific comparisons. In speech, the TurkicASR system (Mussakhojayeva et al. 2023) trains a single model jointly on transcribed speech in ten Turkic languages and reports improvements for languages with little data; these results do not isolate the contribution of shared phonetics. In parsing, TurkicNLP’s multilingual parser, trained on twenty UD-format treebanks of ten Turkic languages, is evaluated in the frozen matched-word comparison in Chapter 8. Its gold/silver reference mixture and small samples limit interpretation (Hakimov 2026).
Transfer failures should be analysed by language, domain and task. Report branch and script alongside the results, without treating them as explanations by themselves.


16.4.3 Language-Specific Adapters
State each training stage. One recipe begins with a shared pretrained encoder, optionally updates it on pooled text, then freezes it while training a target adapter and task head. Another trains shared weights and adapters jointly. Compare these as separate experiments. Distinguish bottleneck adapters from LoRA and report the modules trained, parameter counts and measured inference overhead.
Freezing shared weights prevents those weights from being overwritten during that stage, but does not guarantee preservation of end-to-end predictions: adapters and heads change outputs. Save all trained components and check reload equivalence.


16.4.4 Addressing Data Imbalance
Temperature sampling chooses language \(i\) with probability
\[p_i=\frac{n_i^{1/T}}{\sum_j n_j^{1/T}}.\]
With a synthetic 9:1 corpus-size ratio, \(T=1\) samples 90%/10% and \(T=2\) samples 75%/25%. The figures are illustrative arithmetic. In an actual run, track examples and updates per language. Choosing one language per batch controls exposure across steps; mixing all languages into every batch needs a compatible batch design. Select temperature on development data and check both smaller and larger languages.

title: 16  Cross-Lingual Transfer within the Turkic Family
text:
16.5 Pivot Translation as Data Augmentation
A pivot translates source→pivot→target when both component directions are supported. Verify the actual released pair/model and script for each leg; a development repository is evidence neither of released coverage nor of translation quality. Compare direct translation, pivoting and any synthetic-data adaptation on the same independent target test set (Chapter 10).
Evaluate the complete source→pivot→target output. Scores for the two legs cannot simply be combined: the second model may preserve, introduce or repair errors.
Back-translation uses a target→source system to pair real target sentences with synthetic source text. Document filtering and keep source-document groups intact across splits. Check the real text too. Round-trip consistency can reward copying or repeatable mistakes, so combine it with language checks, alignment diagnostics and independent human review.
Compare filtered data with random subsets of equal size. Exercise 4 measures reference overlap on such subsets without training on them. To test their value for adaptation, generate separate training data and reserve the benchmark test set for final evaluation.






Figure 16.1: An evaluation workflow for choosing a cross-lingual transfer strategy. Target task labels determine the initial comparison. Script conversion and an available finite-state transducer are options to test; final selection depends on held-out target performance, coverage, cost and error analysis.

title: 16  Cross-Lingual Transfer within the Turkic Family
text:
16.6 Code-Switched and Mixed Text
Distinguish an established borrowing from an active switch between languages, and state the annotation convention for ambiguous cases. A shared script cannot identify language boundaries. Preserve mixed-language segments and evaluate token-level language labels, task labels and segment boundaries separately. Turkish–German SAGT and Turkish–English BUTR resources must be named according to the exact released treebank; consult the official inventory in Chapter 8 rather than treating every Turkish treebank as monolingual.
Inserting words synthetically perturbs the input. Natural code-switching may look quite different. Have proficient speakers check naturalness and preservation of the task label, and report real mixed-language evaluation separately.
